verses.1:
Al-Mizan treats the opening praise as an introduction that contains the chapter’s central teaching of monotheism, from which its subsequent arguments arise. It expresses astonishment and blame at the polytheists’ assignment of equals to God, and introduces the admonition and threat that follow. The first three verses set out the knowledge on which the religious call, the substance of the sharīʾah, rests: the universal order of existence, human existence, and human conduct. Together they praise God for creating the macrocosm, creating man from clay to his decreed term, and knowing man’s inward thoughts, utterances, and deeds. The third verse further develops the first two and prepares for the account of God’s knowledge of secret, open, and acquired acts.

The creation of the heavens and earth and the making of darkness and light indicate the universal created order. Within the world’s ordered system, light and darkness underlie continual generation, transformation, appearance and disappearance, renewal and decay; their combined movements form the great universal movement that carries things toward their end. Al-jaʾl, “to make,” here means al-khalq, “to create,” but al-khalq originally suggests composition from components, whereas al-jaʾl does not. Perhaps this explains why “create” is used for the composite heavens and earth, and “make” for darkness and light. And God knows better.

Al-Mizan explains the Qur’an’s plural al-ẓulumāt and singular al-nūr by holding that darkness is only the absence of light in what ought to be illuminated. It therefore has varying degrees according to distance from light, whereas light is an existential reality and does not truly multiply in relation to non-existence.

“Yet those who disbelieve set up equals with their Lord” conveys astonishment together with blame. Since God alone created the heavens and earth and made darkness and light, He alone possesses divinity and godship, without likeness or partner. Yet the disbelievers, despite acknowledging that creation and management truly belong to God rather than to their idols, make idols and images into His equals. The delaying thumma (“then, yet”) portrays the shock of juxtaposing God’s exclusive creative sovereignty with the claim that carved wood and stone can equal the Lord of the universe: astonishment momentarily interrupts the speech before the rebuke resumes.
verses.2:
Al-Mizan explains that, after describing the macrocosm, the verse turns to the human microcosm: God created man from clay and governs his worldly bodily abode by decreeing a term, so human existence extends from clay to the terms associated with death. Human progeny continued through marriage and sexual intercourse. Possibly, “the term” includes return to God through resurrection, since the Qur’an apparently counts the life of barzakh as part of worldly life. Its indefinite expression makes this term unknown to man by ordinary means.

A named term is a specified, settled end-point, as with a fixed period in agreements or loans. In the Divine Speech, both “the term” and “the named term” apparently mean the end of the life-span rather than its entire duration. There are thus two terms: a vague or unnamed term and the named term that is with God. Because it is “with Him,” the named term is enduring, determined, and incapable of change. The unnamed term is conditional and undetermined: it may fail to occur if its conditions are not fulfilled. The named term, being unconditional and determined, necessarily occurs.

In light of …for every term there is a book; Allah erases and establishes what He pleases, and with Him is the basis of the Book (13:38–39), Al-Mizan identifies the named term with the basis of the Book and the unnamed term with the “tablet of erasure and affirmation.” The former concerns events dependent on perfect causes that do not fail in their effects; the latter concerns events dependent on incomplete causes, or requirements, which obstacles may prevent from producing their effects. The distinction resembles the sun: its illumination may be obscured by cloud, eclipse, or another impediment, but if it rises with no barrier between it and the earth, illumination must result. Thus the illuminating effect resembles the tablet of erasure and affirmation, while the sun’s timely rising without hindrance resembles the basis of the Book, the Preserved Tablet.

A human body’s constitution normally requires a lifespan that may be around a hundred or a hundred and twenty years; this is an example of what is written in the tablet of erasure and affirmation. But uncomputable interactions among the causes and impediments affecting human existence may bring death before that natural span, which is called sudden death. The two terms are therefore both required by the divine order: the ambiguous term does not conflict with the fixed named term; they may coincide or differ, but what actually occurs is the named term.

Al-Mizan records several other explanations as strange without undertaking to assess them: that the first term runs from creation to death and the second from death to resurrection, reportedly from Ibn ʿAbbās; that the first is the worldly term until death and the second the endless next-worldly term, ascribed to Mujāhid, Jubbāʾī, and others; that they refer respectively to those already dead and those remaining or yet to come, attributed to Abū Muslim; that they mean sleep and death; or that both designate one and the same named term.

The shift from third person in the preceding verse to second person here is deliberate. The former concerns universal creation and management, about which people might be oblivious; this verse confronts human beings directly because it concerns their own creation and appointed term. Its rebuke is therefore: even if they were excused for overlooking the implications of the heavens, earth, darkness, and light, what excuse have they for doubting the One who created them, decreed their term, and holds the named term with Himself?
verses.3:
Al-Mizan explains that, since the preceding verses establish God’s sole creation and management of the universe and man, “He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth” rejects the idolaters’ multiplication of gods and intercessors for particular functions, places, species, nations, and groups. His divinity encompasses the heavens and earth without difference or limitation, elaborating the preceding argument and preparing what follows.

God’s knowledge of “your secret and your open” concerns acts performed privately and acts performed openly. What people “earn” is the inward, psychological condition acquired by the soul through those acts, whether good or evil. The repetition of “knows” likely reflects the difference between external actions, characterized as secret or open, and their inward effects upon the soul.

Because God knows every hidden and open deed and its inward consequence, and manages human affairs, it belongs to Him to send a messenger with a divinely legislated religion for human guidance, contrary to the idolaters’ denial of any need for prophethood. And because He knows deeds and their consequences for the soul, He must call people to account on a day that excludes none, rather than treating believers and the righteous as He treats mischief-makers and the wicked.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains that their turning from every divine sign springs from arrogance deeply rooted in their souls. This arrogance makes them averse to all signs leading to the truth and heedless of them indiscriminately, because they have rejected the ultimate end: the truth itself when it came to them.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan reads the verse as a warning and threat: what the rejecters mock is the truth, and truth must eventually emerge from mere report into realized fact. Falsehood is blotted out, while truth is confirmed, perfected, and made to prevail despite the unbelievers’ and polytheists’ aversion; like scum, falsehood passes away, whereas what benefits people remains.

When that truth appears, believers and unbelievers, and those humble before it and those who mocked it, will not be treated alike. God’s promise of aid and victory for His messengers and host entails that the chastisement mocked by the rejecters will finally descend upon them.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan explains al-qarn as a people living in one era, with qurūn as its plural. Midrāra, “abundance of rain,” is figuratively derived from words literally connected with copious milk.

The shift from the third person to “you” in “as We have not established you” apparently prevents the pronoun from being mistaken as referring back to the earlier generations; otherwise, the chapter’s context is in the third person. Their destruction “on account of their faults” shows that sins and evil deeds bear upon afflictions and general calamities, just as obedience and good deeds affect the bestowal of bliss and blessings.
verses.7:
Al-Mizan holds that the polytheists’ arrogance had become so extreme that no sensory proof would guide them. Even if a written message on a sheet of paper were sent down and directly touched, seen, and heard, they would still call it clear enchantment; their senseless demand for a book they could read therefore need not be heeded.

“Writing” is an indefinite common noun because the revealed book came gradually and in portions. Its qualification as being “on a paper” brings it nearer to what they demanded and further removes the notion that the Qur’anic verses were the Prophet’s own written composition rather than revelation brought to his heart by the Faithful Spirit.
verses.8:
Al-Mizan takes the demand, “Why has not an angel been sent down to him?”, as an attempt to expose the Prophet’s supposed inability, although he had already said that the verses he recited were brought by a noble angel from God. The demand may have had two meanings.

First, they may have demanded the threatened punishment. If an angel descended in a manner that brought the unseen into the visible realm, their persistent arrogance and unbelief would require a just decision against them, namely death, without further respite. Human beings bound to the material realm cannot enter the angels’ realm and mingle with them except by passing from the physical to the metaphysical level, which means death. Thus the verses about guilty people seeing angels refer to the day of death or to later stages, apparently including the Last Day.

On this reading, the verse answers their demand for punishment: God will not send the angel because its descent would decide their case and end their respite. Yet this community has been granted a respite until an appointed time; punishment is deferred while the Prophet is among them and while they seek forgiveness. They will continue in their course until their day comes, when God will give them what they demanded and judge between them. Possibly, however, they asked for an angel merely as a sign; then the reply means that, because their arrogance and hatred of truth are entrenched, they still would not believe, and judgment without respite would follow.

Second, they may have wanted an angel to assume the mission of calling them to God, or to accompany the Prophet as a confirming co-warner. They considered it unfitting for a divine messenger to share ordinary human conditions such as eating and earning a livelihood in markets, and expected instead a heavenly life or an unmistakable visible confirmation. The following verse answers this expectation: even if the messenger were made an angel, he would be made a man.
verses.9:
Al-Mizan explains al-labs as hiding or covering, and al-lubs as covering the truth; hence the phrase means making truth and falsehood confused. Its omitted object apparently gives it a general scope: it includes the disbelievers’ confusion of themselves and their confusion of others.

They confuse others when corrupt scholars or leaders mingle truth with falsehood, exploiting their followers’ ignorance or weakness. They confuse themselves when, despite the human nature that distinguishes truth from falsehood and recognizes right and wrong, they follow base desire and anger. Arrogance toward truth then makes wrongdoing attractive; they knowingly embellish it and treat truth as falsehood and falsehood as truth. A person may therefore go astray while knowing the matter, as is evident in deeply rooted bad habits that one knows to be evil but does not abandon. This is straying with knowledge and an inward confusion of truth with falsehood, produced by delight in imagined pleasures rather than steadfast practice of truth.

The commentary understands “And if We had made him an angel, We would certainly have made him a man” as answering the request for an angelic warner. This world is the abode of choice: people attain happiness or harm by what they freely choose and earn, and divine guidance shows the way without compelling either gratitude or disbelief. The divine call would be meaningless if a heavenly manifestation forced acceptance. Therefore its messenger must be one of the people, speaking their language, so that obedience and disobedience remain their own choices.

If God sent an angelic messenger, He would necessarily make him a man like them. The righteous could then benefit by their deeds and the evildoers would lose through the confusion they choose for themselves and their followers. God’s making them confused is consequently like His making hearts turn aside after people themselves have turned aside: it is not an initial misguidance attributable to God, but follows their preferred misguidance. An angel thus would bring no added effect beyond a human messenger; they would again doubt and confuse the matter, so their demand is futile.

The verse does not specify whether making the angel a man means changing his angelic essence into humanity or merely giving him a human form. Most verses about angels support the latter, as when the Spirit appeared before Maryam and angels came to Abraham and Lot as human guests, though “And if We please, We could make among you angels to be successors in the land(43:60)” somewhat points to the former. It is also said that the wording “a man,” rather than “a human,” indicates both that a messenger can only be a man and that the angel would assume human form rather than have his essence changed.

Most exegetes argue that ordinary humans cannot see angels in their true form, so an angel sent to them would appear as a human and provoke the same doubt. Al-Mizan judges this insufficient. Sunnī and Shīʿī traditions report that the Holy Prophet saw Gabriel twice in his original form, and God could enable all people to see angels and believe; the real difficulty is the compulsion such a sign would create. Nor does seeing angels in human form necessarily entail doubt, since Abraham, Lot, and Maryam recognized them without confusion. But giving everyone a soul like those purified friends of God, so that all would recognize the angels with certainty, would alter their natural dispositions and again create compulsion, nullifying test and trial.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains al-ḥayq as staying or descending. The earlier communities’ mockery of their messengers was in fact mockery of the divine punishment with which the messengers warned them; consequently, the very punishment they mocked descended upon and encompassed them. The first verse consoles the Prophet while warning the polytheists, and the command to travel through the land is admonition and advice to observe the end of the rejecters.
verses.11: Al-Mizan explains al-ḥayq as staying or descending. The earlier communities’ mockery of their messengers was in fact mockery of the divine punishment with which the messengers warned them; consequently, the very punishment they mocked descended upon and encompassed them. The first verse consoles the Prophet while warning the polytheists, and the command to travel through the land is admonition and advice to observe the end of the rejecters.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan begins the proof of resurrection from God’s absolute ownership of all that is in the heavens and the earth. Since every creature—including idols and the beings invoked by polytheists—ultimately derives its existence and affairs from God, He alone owns and may administer them as He wills. Nothing, whether death, absence, disorder, or the complexity of an act, can prevent Him from giving life, providing sustenance, causing death, or resurrecting.

The question is posed and immediately answered because both the Prophet and his opponents already acknowledge this ownership. This argumentative form resembles a benefactor who asks an ungrateful recipient who fed, clothed, and provided for him, then answers the question himself. Divine ownership is thus the first premise; the second is that God has ordained mercy on Himself, while His ownership of whatever dwells in night and day supplies a further premise.

Al-Kitābah, “writing,” here means firm affirmation and decree. Mercy is an attribute of action: bestowing blessings upon those entitled to them and bringing things to their due happiness. It may therefore be said that God has affirmed mercy for Himself. By contrast, life, knowledge, and power are attributes inseparable from the Divine Person and are not described as having been affirmed for Him.

Because many servants, including human beings, are fit for enduring life and its happiness, God’s affirmed mercy entails completing His blessings by gathering them on the Day of Resurrection and recompensing their words and deeds. Believers will gain and the others will lose. The verse therefore emphatically concludes that He will gather them, without doubt; those who have lost their souls will not believe.

This proof reaches resurrection through mercy. It differs from proofs based on the fact that God does not create in vain, or that it would be unjust to treat believers and the pious as equal to mischief-makers and the wicked when they are not distinguished in this world; those arguments require another life in which blessing and unhappiness distinguish them.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan explains that dwelling in night and day means existing within this natural world, whose order is governed by the changing conditions of light and by a system through which every element and being is brought toward its appointed completion. Night and day are the comprehensive environment affecting the formation and life of their inhabitants, just as a person’s land, food, water, air, and surroundings affect his life and bodily growth.

God alone created night, day, and all that dwells in them. He consequently owns not only their inhabitants but also the events, actions, words, and universal order consequent upon their existence. Human life, cognition, will, emotional powers, society, languages, customs, laws, and judgments concerning good and evil, justice and injustice, obedience and disobedience all arise within this divine ownership. God therefore hears every word, voice, and sign, and knows every deed and what each soul gains of happiness or misery.

Such knowledge follows from ownership and creative governance. Good and evil, obedience and disobedience, and meaningful speech are themselves intelligible only through knowledge: an act is not called good, bad, obedient, or disobedient unless its meaning is known, nor is a sound called speech apart from its understood meaning. It is inconceivable that a created human being should know himself while his ultimate Owner remains unaware of him.

The commentary illustrates this practical knowledge through the innumerable stages by which God creates and governs the universe, human society, language, speech, understanding, assent or refusal, human generation, and a person’s passage through the chain of causes into the world of free choice. God remains present with every cause and every stage; hence He cannot be oblivious to human acts or conditions. “And to Him belongs whatever dwells in the night and the day” thus yields the conclusion, “and He is the Hearing, the Knowing.”

Hearing and knowing are, in one respect, attributes of the Divine Person and inseparable from it. Yet hearing, seeing, and knowing may also be attributes of action when related to created things: sounds are heard and made to be heard by Him, lights and colors are seen and made to be seen by Him, and all things are known and made known by Him. Such attributes arise with the relevant divine action, not before it; this introduces no change into the Divine Person because it remains at the level of action.

The verse therefore establishes practical knowledge from divine ownership. By repeating the ownership expressed in the preceding verse and linking it to hearing and knowledge, it supplies a premise that completes the proof of resurrection: God’s ownership of creatures necessarily includes His awareness of them and of what they say.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan begins the argument for God’s Unity by explaining that idolatry arose from two motives. People either sought the causes they imagined could secure their needs—especially food and the other means of preserving life—or feared supposed powers behind calamities and worshipped them to avert their harm. The verses answer polytheism by accepting the underlying reasoning from need and fear, but showing that it can establish worship only of God and excludes every alleged partner.

The present verse addresses the first path, the path of hope for benefits. God alone is the walīy, the guardian and source of the blessings enjoyed by human beings and others: He feeds but is not fed. He originated the heavens and earth from non-existence, gave them existence, and then bestowed the countless bounties that preserve them. Food, the most obvious need of living beings, and every cause by which provisions reach their recipients ultimately return to His origination and making. Therefore, sustenance belongs to Him, and He alone deserves worship.

The term walīy is used because the proof concerns God’s beneficence in providing food. “The Originator of the heavens and the earth” explains why provision is confined to Him, while “He is not fed” alludes to the dependence of beings taken as gods, such as Jesus. The phrase may also indicate a higher proof of Unity: since God originates the universe and everything returns to His creation, one must surrender to Him. The proofs from hoped-for bounty and feared punishment make worship incumbent for the sake of gaining benefit or escaping wrath; this higher path makes worship incumbent because He is God Himself.

After the rational proof, revelation confirms it: the Prophet is commanded to follow the conclusion to which reason leads, namely monotheism, and forbidden to join the polytheists. “The first who submits himself” may mean the first among his community to submit; if it is unrestricted, the priority is one of rank rather than time. Islam is used rather than īmān because the conclusion is servitude, submission, and humility—the purpose of worship.

A translator’s note adds that, if the Prophet’s spiritual creation is considered, he was first in time as well as rank, and reports his saying: “The first thing that God created was my light,” citing ʿAbdu al-Ḥaqq Dehlawi’s Madārij al-nubuwwah and al-Sīrah al-Ḥalabiyyah.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan identifies this as the second path by which polytheists adopted gods: they worshipped them to guard against their wrath and chastisement. The verse takes the greatest object of fear, the punishment of the Hour of Resurrection, just as the preceding argument took food as the most evident human need.

“If I disobey my Lord” stands in place of saying, “if I ascribed anyone with my Lord,” and thus refers back to the prohibition of polytheism. The meaning is that worshipping God alone is rationally incumbent in order to escape the punishment of the grievous Day. This conclusion is not based only on revealed guidance; reason itself reaches it. Like the preceding verse, the verse first establishes a rational proof and then supports it by revelation, compressing this comprehensive meaning into the word “disobey.”

A translator’s note, concerning the preceding expression “the first who submits himself,” reports that if the Prophet’s spiritual creation is considered, he was first in time as well as rank. It attributes to him the saying, “The first thing that God created was my light,” and cites ʿAbdu al-Ḥaqq Dehlawi, Madārij al-nubuwwah, and al-Sīrah al-Ḥalabiyyah.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse completes the preceding proof. The Prophet’s statement that he fears punishment if he disobeys God might seem to establish monotheism only for himself, since the prohibition of polytheism was addressed to him. An inattentive opponent could therefore claim that the fear of punishment and obligation to affirm God’s Unity apply only to the Prophet.

The verse answers that divine chastisement encompasses everyone, and none escapes it except through God’s mercy. Every person must consequently fear the chastisement of that Day as the Prophet fears it for himself. The proof for monotheism and rejection of partners is thus universal, not confined to him.
verses.17:
Al-Mizan says that the preceding arguments used food as an example of what people hope for and the punishment of Resurrection as an example of what they fear. This verse extends the point to every other harm and benefit: if God afflicts a person with harm, only He can remove it; if He grants good, none can prevent His grace, for He has power over all things. Fear of harm and hope for good therefore require taking Him as the God worthy of worship.

One might concede that God deserves worship because He brings harm and good, yet still claim that intermediary causes or powerful intercessors deserve worship as well, since idolaters regard them as effective in benefit and injury. The verse refutes this by God’s omnipotence. No being is above or equal to Him; alleged partners, their acts, and their effects are under His domination. They act only through His creative permission and will, are independent in no affair, and possess no harm, benefit, or other power for themselves. Every good or evil effect attributable to them terminates in His command, will, and permission.

Thus whatever good or bad reaches a person is from God in the manner appropriate to His divine station. He alone possesses divinity and alone deserves worship. The use of “touching” for harm and good indicates their insignificance before His unlimited power: no limited creature can resist or master what He touches it with. “He has power over all things” means both that no one can repel the harm He inflicts and that no one can avert the good He bestows.

Although harm and good are here addressed specifically to the Prophet, the following statement concerning God’s supremacy over His servants is general, as is the preceding declaration that mercy is shown to whomever is spared punishment. An author’s note adds that some leading idolaters allowed God’s worship but deemed devotional worship irrelevant to His unlimited existence, whereas ordinary people often worshipped Him alongside other gods, as reflected in the pre-Islamic Meccan talbiyah.
verses.18:
Al-Mizan explains al-qahr as domination by which one thing overcomes another and compels an effect contrary to the latter’s own tendency, as water extinguishes fire or fire turns water to steam. Created causes serve as intermediaries in the appearance of events and produce their effects, yet all are compelled to obey what God wills in and through them. They are therefore dominated by Him.

Although al-Qāhir may be applied to God and to creatures, divine domination differs completely from creaturely domination. Fire overcomes wood while both exist on the same level of being, with fire merely stronger in imposing its effect. God’s domination is wholly comprehensive: He dominates a thing through the limited existence, properties, conditions, powers, and causes He has bestowed upon it. In burning firewood, for example, He owns the fire, its essence and effect, the conditions of the wood, and the removal of resistance from it. There can consequently be no resistance, defiance, or rebellion against His will.

God is thus omnipotent over His servants while exalted above them, not a being that overpowers equals. The Qur’an qualifies al-Qāhir in this chapter with “above His servants” in this verse and verse 61. Al-qahr is especially used of domination over rational beings, and al-Rāghib explains it as degradation or abasement, though it may also apply to non-rational beings.

God, who touches His servants with harm and good and compels them to obey Him, remains supreme over their actions and effects because He owns what He has placed in their ownership and controls whatever power He has granted them over others. Since harm and good are sometimes ascribed to other than God, the verse distinguishes His action by calling Him “the Wise, the Aware”: He never acts haphazardly or ignorantly, and neither errs nor makes mistakes like others.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that testimony is to apprehend news with clarity, akin to eyewitnessing, and to convey it. Its force differs with the witness’s perception, the clarity of what is witnessed, and the witness’s capacity to report it: one impaired by heedlessness or forgetfulness is not like one who accurately retains what he sees and hears, nor is a specialist like an uninformed person. God is therefore greatest in testimony, for He creates all things, to Him return amr and khalq, and His knowledge encompasses everything without error, forgetfulness, or omission.

Because this is self-evident, the verse need not explicitly answer that God is greatest in testimony; “Allah is witness between me and you” itself supplies the answer. It is also possible that “witness” is predicated of an omitted “He,” so that the statement both answers the question and begins a new assertion. God’s command to the Prophet to announce this testimony is itself God’s testimony to his prophethood; there is consequently no need to seek other forms of Qur’anic testimony for his messengership or for the Qur’an’s divine origin. The qualification “between me and you” places God between the Prophet and his people, who differed from him only over his claim to prophethood, messengership, and revelation. Thus, God’s testimony is specifically testimony for his prophethood.

The revelation of the Qur’an is joined to this testimony. Its stated purpose, warning, follows the more effective path for the general public: hope creates desire, whereas fear of a possible harm rationally impels one to avert it. Since Islam summons people to the religion implanted in their nature, while polytheism and sins have concealed it and brought misfortune and divine wrath upon them, it is more reasonable to begin with warning. This apparently explains why the Prophet is described here only as a warner. The particular servants of God, however, worship out of love rather than fear of Fire or desire for a garden; they fear Fire as distance from God and His wrath, and desire the garden as proximity to Him and His pleasure.

Although “you” apparently addresses the Meccan polytheists, Quraysh, or Arabs generally, its contrast with “whomsoever it reaches” shows that the call includes everyone reached by it, whether during the Prophet’s lifetime or afterward. The Prophet was thus sent with the Qur’an to all who hear it from him or through another until the Day of Resurrection; the Qur’an remains God’s truthful proof for the people of the world throughout that time. “With it I may warn you,” rather than merely with its recitation, means that its proof reaches anyone who hears its words, understands its meaning and purposes, or has its contents interpreted for him. A divine written message need not be in a community’s own language if its purpose is made comprehensible to them.

Having mentioned God’s supreme testimony for the Prophet, whose mission is to summon to monotheism, the verse treats testimony to other gods as astonishing and unacceptable: once God has testified that He has no partner in divinity, none may testify to other gods beside Him. The Prophet is commanded to reject their testimony and instead testify that God is one and disavow the partners they associate with Him.
verses.20: Al-Mizan explains that the verse reports God’s testimony in the scriptures given to the People of the Book: their prophets’ books repeatedly gave glad tidings of the Prophet of Islam and described his attributes without ambiguity. When these attributes were brought before their scholars, they recognized him as unmistakably as they recognized their own sons. Yet some scholars concealed the tidings and descriptions found in their books and disdainfully refused belief; by doing so, they lost their souls and would not believe.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains injustice as deviation from the middle course of justice. All sins are blameworthy in proportion to the injustice they contain, and injustice increases both with the character of its doer and, especially, with the rank of the one against whom it is directed. Since none is more honourable than God or His guiding signs, no injustice is greater than forging lies against Him or rejecting His communications; in reality, however, the wrongdoer harms only his own soul.

To forge a lie against God is to assign Him a partner, falsely claim prophethood, or falsely attribute a command to Him. To deny His communications is to reject a true prophet and his divinely supported call, the true religion, or the Creator Himself. The verse particularly concerns idolaters, who posited independent partners managing worldly affairs and serving as intercessors, while denying the signs of prophethood and resurrection.

The commentary rejects the claim that seeking the intercession of the Prophet, the Purified Ones of his progeny, or spiritual masters is polytheism. God confirms intercession when it is by His permission, without restricting it to this world or the next: Who is he that can intercede with Him but by His permission? (2:255). He also confirms it for those who bear witness to the truth and know it (43:86). Prophets, including Muḥammad, are among such truthful and knowledgeable witnesses; the Qur’an further establishes knowledgeable witnesses in this ummah. The Prophet’s Household are divinely purified, and, as the purified ones who touch the protected Book, are identified as scholars of the Qur’an and certified witnesses to the truth, untouched by falsehood.

Al-falāḥ, like al-fawz, al-najāḥ, al-ẓafar, and al-saʾādah, denotes success, victory, and the attainment of one’s desired felicity. It includes worldly well-being and the hereafter’s enduring life, freedom from need and humiliation, and knowledge without ignorance. It is so called because it means overcoming the obstructions to one’s goal.

Thus, “surely the unjust will not be successful” means that wrongdoers cannot attain through injustice the victory and happiness they seek. Every real end has a path suited to it within the ordered causal system of the universe; pursuing it by a contrary path suspends and corrupts the causes needed to reach it. Creatures that act through perception and will must conform their actions to the reality they know, or their actions are negated and, if the deviation persists, they perish.

Human beliefs concerning creation and resurrection, and practical norms governing worship and transactions, arise from this universal order and constitute the natural paths to human felicity. To follow them is to attain one’s true end; to abandon them is injustice. Even if injustice seems temporarily to secure an aim, it cannot endure, because the interconnected order of things resists it until its supposed felicity is ruined.

A wrongdoer may violate monotheism, others’ rights, property, honour, lives, or the sanctities of worship through such acts as falsehood, slander, and cheating, and may sometimes obtain what he wants. Yet he incurs loss in both worlds. In this world, his course is one of disorder: if it became general practice, social life would be destroyed, while every system preserving human continuity necessarily contests and eventually nullifies its unlawful gains. In the next world, his injustice is recorded in his book of deeds and impressed upon his soul, and he is requited according to it. The verse therefore comprehensively establishes that injustice, whether against society or the individual, never yields true success.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan takes “the day” as elliptical for “remember the day,” and “all together” as affirming that God’s knowledge and power encompass every one of them: none will escape His enumeration or gathering.

The verse explains why wrongdoers do not prosper. God will gather the idolaters and ask for the partners they had asserted; these associates will be lost to them, and they will deny their own polytheism by falsely swearing, “By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists.” Had their attribution of partners been successful, they would have found those partners with the alleged power and intercession and benefited from them.

Al-fitnah, rendered “excuse,” may mean their reply—namely, their false oath; the final outcome of their involvement with idols; or their excuse. Each interpretation is linguistically justifiable.

verses.24:
Al-Mizan explains that on the Day of Resurrection the polytheists will lie against themselves by swearing that they were not polytheists, thereby denying the very partnership they had obstinately asserted in the world despite clear proofs. Their end proves that their injustice has not brought them success.

“What they forged has passed away from them” means that God’s sole rule, kingdom, and power will become manifest. Their idols and alleged associates will be exposed as possessing neither harm nor benefit for themselves or anyone else. The divinity and intercession they ascribed to them belong to God alone; what they took for such powers was an illusion, like a mirage. If they appeal to their associates, every hope will be cut off, as those associates disown their worshippers.

The fact that they lie and swear falsely although the realities of the next world are unveiled does not mean that they seek some worldly advantage or concealment there, for the next world is a place of recompense, not action and acquisition. Rather, having made false oaths and forged claims a habitual means of escaping danger and gaining benefits in the world, they have rooted lying in their souls. A deeply fixed disposition compels the soul to display itself; hence, on the day hidden things become manifest, the heart bound to lying manifests only lying. Likewise, the disputes of the people of the world will appear among the people of the Fire, whereas the purity and safety of the people of Paradise will appear in their speech of peace.
verses.25: Al-Mizan explains al-akinnah as covers that conceal a thing, al-waqr as heaviness in the ear, and al-asāṭīr as fabricated false stories, usually arranged and collected in written form. The verse’s wording, “those who disbelieve say,” rather than simply “they say,” apparently indicates that their disbelief is the cause of their dismissing the Qur’an as “the stories of the ancients.”
verses.26: Al-Mizan explains that they prohibit others from following it and themselves go far from it; al-naʾy means being far away. The restriction that they destroy only their own souls reverses their intention: they imagine that opposing the message will destroy the Prophet and frustrate his mission, but God wills to complete His light, so their effort brings about their own unnoticed destruction.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan describes these verses as the outcome of the deniers’ persistence in disbelief and rejection of the divine communications. When they stand before the Fire, they will wish to return to the world, not reject their Lord’s communications, and become believers in order to escape punishment. This wish, like their future denial of polytheism and false oath, manifests a trait ingrained in them: they habitually long for benefits they have forfeited through their own evil choices and defective actions.

“What they concealed before shall become manifest to them” refers to the same polytheists and to their worldly life. What becomes newly manifest is the Fire before which they stand—a reality they had concealed by disbelief, by hiding the truth, and by concealing it after it had become evident. The truth that they had rejected had already been made manifest to them in the world; the context does not support the view that the mere disclosure of that truth, apart from the Fire and the terror of Resurrection, causes their wish to return.

The commentary reports that al-Manār lists several other explanations: that what appears is their evil deeds recorded and testified to; their futile supposed means of felicity; disbelief concealed after their false denial of polytheism; truth concealed by arrogant enemies, leaders from followers, or hypocrites beneath an outward Islam; resurrection and requital, whose denial is called concealment; or the evil consequences and punishment of concealed disbelief and sins. Al-Manār finally prefers a broad reading that all disbelievers find exposed whatever they had hidden in the world from themselves or others. Al-Mizan holds that the principles already given reveal the defects of these interpretations and does not discuss them further.

If they were returned to the world, they would return to what they had been forbidden. Their wish is prompted by the next world’s unveiled reality and punishment; but a return would restore the conditions of worldly life, including free choice, the desires of the soul, Satanic whispering, human natural disposition, arrogance, and oppression. The same causes that made them oppose the truth and deny the communications would remain, so they would revert to their original polytheism and enmity toward truth.

They are called liars regarding their wish because it implicitly contains both a request and a promise: that God return them and that, if returned, they will believe and do good. In that sense it is open to truth or falsehood, and it is false. It is also possible that they are called liars because their hope itself proves false by never being realized. The suggestion that the phrase instead condemns every statement they make about recognizing and believing the truth is not worthy of consideration.

verses.29:
Al-Mizan explains that the idolaters openly deny any life beyond this worldly one and deny that they will be raised after death. Their belief in the intercession of alleged partners concerns only worldly benefit and protection from harm.

The image of their being made to stand before their Lord answers this denial in the form of “And could you see”: they will certainly verify and acknowledge what they denied when they see the meeting of God after death. Thus, the “raising up” they rejected is explained as meeting God, as the following reference to “the meeting of Allah” and the Hour—the Hour of meeting—also indicates. When asked, “Is not this the truth?” they will confess, “Yea, by our Lord!” and then be commanded to taste the chastisement for their disbelief and concealment.

verses.31:
Al-Mizan explains baghtah as something that comes suddenly, al-ḥasrah as grief and remorse over what has been lost, and al-wizr as a heavy burden, hence also a sin or its consequences.

The verse gives another consequence of denying resurrection: the Hour will overtake them suddenly. They will lament their neglect of it, while their sins, burdens, or the consequences of their sins appear for them to carry upon their backs. This is a most grievous and perilous human condition.

Those who reject the meeting of God are losers because they exchange the comfort of the next world and the felicity of meeting God for denial of resurrection and its resulting painful chastisement.
verses.32: Al-Mizan presents this verse as the conclusion of the discussion and a comparison of worldly and otherworldly life. Worldly life is play because it revolves around reflective beliefs and imagined aims, and idle sport because it diverts people from the important life of the next world. The Hereafter is the real and enduring life; therefore it is better, and only the pious attain it.
verses.33:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse consoles the Prophet: the deniers’ speech should not grieve him, because he only conveys God’s message and their rejection is directed against God’s communications, not against him personally. This is according to the reading lā yukadhdhibūnaka with the doubling sign. According to the reading lā yukdhibūnaka without it, they have neither established that he lies in his call nor refuted his proof with a counter-proof; rather, they wrong the divine communications by rejecting them.

The expression “the unjust” rather than “they” shows that their denial arises not from ignorance or deficiency, but from transgression, rebellion, and haughtiness. Likewise, the shift from “Our communications” to “the communications of God” emphasizes that their conduct opposes the station of divinity, which nothing can withstand.

Other explanations say either that they do not inwardly believe him to be a liar but deny him outwardly from obstinacy, or that their denial of him is really denial of God; a third says that they did not find him to be a liar. Al-Mizan judges its initial explanation to be correct.
verses.34:
Al-Mizan says that the verse directs the Prophet to follow the way of earlier messengers: to endure rejection and persecution patiently in God’s cause until divine help comes. Their eventual help demonstrates and confirms God’s promise to grant victory to His messengers.

“No one can change the words of Allah” excludes change from either side: God does not reverse, erase, or cancel what He has decisively willed, nor can another overpower Him and make Him alter it. Thus, God’s “word,” “speech,” and “promise” in this Qur’anic usage denote a definite, unchangeable conclusion, beyond the tablet of eraser and affirmation.

The statement that information about the messengers has already reached the Prophet confirms that previous messengers were rejected. Al-Mizan adds that this may indicate that Sūrah al-Anʿām was revealed after Meccan chapters recounting prophetic stories, such as al-Shuʿarāʾ and Maryam, and therefore belonged to a third stage of Meccan revelation before the hijrah. God knows best.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains al-nafaq as a penetrating path or tunnel in the earth, and al-sullam as a ladder or means of ascent. The response to the conditional is omitted but understood: if the Prophet can obtain such a passage or ladder, then let him do so.

The “sign” sought is a sign that would compel people to believe. The verse consoles the Prophet through the Qur’an, the divine sign proving his mission and one especially accessible to eloquent and intelligent Arabs. Their refusal should not distress him, for the call to truth and its acceptance rest on free choice. God has not created a sign that compels belief, because He does not will faith from them except through their free choice. Had He willed to compel them, all would have been gathered upon guidance. The suggestion that the verse asks for a sign superior to the Qur’an conflicts with the context, especially the statement that God could have gathered them all on guidance, which points to compulsion.

The apparent meaning is that, had God willed, He would have made them accept faith forcibly, thereby negating free will. Yet related verses explain that His not guiding every soul also rests on His decreed word concerning Hell, following Satan’s undertaking to mislead mankind except God’s purified or devoted servants. Satan himself will acknowledge on the Day of Resurrection that he had no authority over people except to call them, and that they obeyed him. Thus sins, including polytheism, bring about a person’s deviation, and that deviation ultimately belongs to the person himself.

Human willing depends, in its realization, on God’s will; nevertheless, God affirms a person’s will when that person is prepared by the goodness of his inner self and is exposed to divine mercy. He guides those who turn to Him, but does not will guidance or encompass with mercy the transgressor whose heart has deviated, who clings to the earth, and who inclines to error. Religious invitation and divine signs therefore proceed with regard to free choice, and God guides to Himself only one who becomes ready for guidance through free choice and exposure to mercy.

Although God could, considered in itself, make every person freely choose faith as He makes believers do so, this would contradict the universal order of cause and effect and of divine ability and munificence. Guidance is granted to one who fears God and purifies the soul, while misguidance—meaning being withheld from guidance—befalls one who turns from remembrance and corrupts the soul. God aids every soul from His bounty according to what it seeks: one who seeks good receives it, while one who seeks evil is withheld from good. Were God to make every person, good or evil, freely desire goodness, faith, and piety, this general order would be negated. The following verse, “Only those accept who listen,” supports this explanation.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan says that the verse explains why the Prophet cannot turn the rejecters away from their refusal or produce for them a sign leading them to faith: they are like the dead, without perception or hearing, and therefore cannot grasp the religious call or hear its caller.

People are of two kinds. Those spiritually alive and hearing respond positively; those who turn away are dead, though outwardly living, and do not hear. They will hear only when God raises them in the Hereafter, when they will understand what they failed to hear in this world. Thus “those who listen” alludes to believers, while “the dead” denotes all who refuse the call, whether polytheists or others. Divine speech commonly portrays believers through life and hearing, and disbelievers through death and deafness.

Although most exegetes take these descriptions as allusion and simile, Al-Mizan notes that another real meaning for them has been discussed elsewhere. The verse proves that God will certainly make unbelievers and polytheists understand the truth and hear His call in the Hereafter, just as believers understand and hear it in this world. No person, believer or unbeliever, can ultimately escape understanding the truth.
verses.37:
Al-Mizan explains that the idolaters’ demand for a sign was meant to expose the Holy Prophet’s supposed inability. The Qur’an itself, descending chapter by chapter and verse by verse and recited to them, was already the greatest sign; thus they were seeking some other sign because, in their folly and frenzy, they would not accept it as sufficient.

Their attachment to their deities made them speak of a sign from “his Lord,” not from “our Lord” or from God. By this wording they dissociated themselves from God and belittled the Prophet’s cause: if his call were true, then let the Lord to whom he called aid him by producing a sign that established his truthfulness.

This request arose from ignorance in two respects. First, the idolaters regarded their gods as independently controlling the affairs assigned to them—war, peace, land, sea, love, hate, and the like—despite calling them intercessors. They therefore imagined that God, having distributed affairs among these helpers, could not overturn their gods’ authority by a sign disproving their divinity. This belief was reinforced by what they had heard from the Jews of Ḥijāz: that God’s hand was fettered and that He could not alter the established causal order.

Second, they did not distinguish between signs God grants a messenger without a people’s request and signs sent in answer to a people’s demand. The former prove the messenger’s truthfulness without bringing immediate peril upon those invited; examples include Moses’ staff and bright hand, Jesus’ raising of the dead, healing of the blind and leper, and creation of the bird, and the Noble Qur’an for Muḥammad. But when a demanded sign descends, God’s established way is to judge the people: if they believe, it is well; if they persist in rejection, chastisement comes and they are not respited, as with Noah, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, and others. Thus the verse indicates both God’s power to send any sign and the peril inherent in their demand.

The reply changes their word “Rabb = Lord” to “Allah.” This establishes the judgment: unrestricted divinity comprises every perfection and is subject to no condition or limit, and therefore possesses unrestricted power. Their demand was prompted by ignorance of the divine station and by a wish to show the Prophet incapable. They also did not know that the requested sign would not serve their welfare, but could expose the entire group to destruction and uprooting. This sense is supported by: Say: “If that which you desire to hasten were with me, the matter would have certainly been decided between you and me; and Allah best knows the unjust”(6:58).

The intensified forms nazzala and yunazzilu indicate that they demanded a gradual sign, or several signs descending one after another, as their other reported demands likewise show. Ibn Kathīr is reported to have recited these two verbs without intensified pronunciation.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains that al-dābbah includes every animal that moves upon the earth, though the word is mostly used for the horse; al-dabb and al-dabīb denote soft crawling. Al-Ṭāʾir is what glides through the air with its two wings, and its plural is al-Ṭayr. An ummah is not merely a numerous group, but a body united by one comprehensive purpose, whether a religion, culture, time, place, or another aim; its root conveys intending. Al-ḥashr means gathering people by force, as for battle or evacuation.

The phrase “that flies with its two wings” corresponds to “that walks upon the earth”: the verse thus encompasses every terrestrial and aerial animal. It also prevents “flying” from being understood figuratively as swift motion, just as crawling can denote light movement. The animals are said to be ummahs like human beings, not simply because each species contains many individuals, nor merely because animals share forms of food, reproduction, shelter, and cohabitation. The closing words, “then to their Lord shall they be gathered,” show that the likeness includes a further and more fundamental matter: their gathering to God.

Gathering to God presupposes a kind of conscious life connected with felicity and wretchedness. Human happiness does not consist simply in pleasant food, marriage, and dwelling, nor is it destroyed merely by hardship: a person may enjoy worldly ease yet be wretched through injustice and iniquity, or endure distress while rejoicing in human perfection and the light of servitude. Human nature, supported and detailed by the prophetic call, establishes a way of belief and action. Whoever takes it up, together with society or alone, attains felicity in the Hereafter, and perhaps in both worlds; whoever wholly or partly abandons it incurs wretchedness. Its summary is commanding goodness, obedience, justice, and steadfastness, while restraining evil, disobedience, injustice, and deviation from truth. Sound human nature itself loves justice and dislikes injustice, and divine religion confirms this disposition and explains its particulars.

The commentary holds that attentive consideration of animals that live alongside human beings shows that they too have individual and collective beliefs and opinions underlying their movements and stillness. A human being perceives needs such as food, marriage, offspring, and freedom from injustice or poverty, and acts according to judgments about what should be pursued or avoided. Likewise, an animal systematically seeks food, cohabitation, and shelter in ways that show perception of its needs and of the means of satisfying them. It pursues benefit, repels harm, and often employs individual or collective devices for obtaining prey or escaping enemies that human beings understood only after long observation. Research into ants, bees, and termites has found traces of civilization, social organization, manufacture, norms, and policy usually associated with developed human societies.

The Qur’an urges reflection on animal creation and action: “And in your creation and in what He spreads abroad of animals there are signs for a people that are sure(45:4).” It also directs attention to cattle, birds, bees, and ants. Animal opinions and beliefs entail motives of attraction and repulsion, approval and disapproval, and some sense of justice and injustice. Differences of temperament within a species—such as one horse, ram, or cock being fierce and another tame—together with love, hate, generosity, mercy, hardness, and transgression, support this conclusion. In human beings, corresponding traits affect judgments of good and evil, justice and injustice, and underlie gathering, reckoning, reward, and punishment in the next life. Thus it may appear that animals too are subject to al-ḥashr.

The verse itself sufficiently answers whether animals other than human beings will be gathered: “then to their Lord shall they be gathered.” The same is indicated by “And when the wild animals are gathered (81:5).” Numerous verses also speak of the return or presentation of the heavens, earth, sun, moon, stars, jinn, idols, stones, and other things; but the term al-ḥashr is not used in the same way for such things as it is for beings gathered and driven together. Reckoning and judgment are concomitants of this gathering. Scripture gives final judgment over disputed truth, reward for the good-doer, and retribution against the unjust as the purpose of human gathering; and good-doing and injustice are present in animal activities to some degree. The apparent sense of “And were Allah to punish men for what they earn, He would not leave on the back of it any creature, but He respites them till an appointed term… (35:45)” also supports this, if “creature” is taken in its general sense rather than as restricted to human beings: injustice is injustice, and it occurs among human beings and animals.

That animals may undergo censure, requital, reckoning, and recompense does not make them equal to human beings in perception, will, psychology, or spirituality. Even among human beings, equal subjection to reckoning does not require that a wise person and an idiot, or one sound in mind and one weakened, be questioned with equal strictness. Yet the Qur’an attributes to certain animals an understanding and intelligence not far from that of an ordinarily informed human being, as in the ant of Sulaymān and the hoopoe that reported on Sheba and its people’s worship of the sun. Such reports indicate that their awareness rests on numerous simple and complex cognitions. Zoological observation likewise discloses animal conduct that ordinarily could arise only from substantial will, understanding, and perception.

Whether animals receive duties through a messenger and revelation, and whether such a messenger belongs to their own species or comes from humankind, cannot usefully be determined. The animal world remains veiled from human knowledge; the Divine Speech does not apparently explain this matter, and nothing reliable on it is found in traditions from the Holy Prophet and the Imāms of Ahl al-Bayt. The conclusion is therefore that animal societies, like human society, contain an element of divine religion nourished by their nature and preparing them for gathering to God and recompense. Nevertheless, the observable difference between animals and human beings, together with Qur’anic indications of humanity’s general superiority and of other things’ subjection to it, shows that animals have not received the detailed human cognitions or the intricate burdens imposed on human beings.

Accordingly, the verse establishes that every animal species forms a society directed to perceptible common ends, despite differences in its perception and will. These ends are not confined to bodily nutrition, growth, and procreation in this world; they extend to affairs after death and to another life of felicity or wretchedness rooted in perception and will.

The objection that animals lack free choice, and that their acts are therefore natural and involuntary like those of plants, rests on a mistaken account of choice. Human perception and will enable a conscious being to distinguish harm from benefit and to manage external things for the continuation of its existence. Where a benefit is clear, awareness of it immediately gives rise to willing and acting, as with many innate capacities; deliberation is unnecessary. Where benefit is uncertain because of defects, obstacles, or other considerations, a person considers the alternatives until determining whether the act is beneficial or harmful. Thus a hungry person who finds food may hesitate over its soundness, whether it is poisonous, whether it belongs to him, or whether some circumstance prevents its use. Once its permissibility and benefit are known, he acts; had these been clear from the outset, he would have acted without deliberation.

Free choice, then, consists in choosing what one judges beneficial, whether that judgment follows deliberation or is immediate; deliberation is needed only to remove impediments to decision. Even among human beings its degree varies greatly according to courage and cowardice, continence and greed, energy and laziness, dignity and brazenness, strength or weakness of discernment, and soundness or unsoundness of thought. The greedy person may feel compelled where the virtuous person feels no attraction; a coward may count a slight harm an excuse for inaction where a brave person disregards grave danger; an idiot may choose on a baseless fancy; and children may choose after a measure of reflection that a mature person would not need. People also falsely call certain acts compelled by appealing to addiction, laziness, or poverty.

Religion and social custom consequently treat as voluntary what is voluntary for average members of society, and on this basis apply commands, prohibitions, punishments, rewards, and rights, while excusing those lacking ordinary capacity and understanding. This boundary is a religious or social determination intended to preserve welfare; from the standpoint of nature, the range of voluntary action is broader. On this basis, animals are not wholly deprived of choice, though their choice is weaker than that of average human beings. Their hesitation amid obstacles, especially among domesticated animals, and their refraining under rebuke, threat, or training, show that their nafs can decide to act or not to act. Their deliberation is very weak, but the root of free choice is present. It is therefore possible that God makes the level of choice appropriate to them the basis of duties that human beings do not comprehend, or deals with them in another manner proportionate to that gift, so that obedience may be rewarded and disobedience censured and punished; God knows this better.

“We have not neglected anything in the Book” is a parenthetical clause. It declares the Book perfect and complete: nothing whose consideration, due fulfillment, or necessary description was required has been omitted. If “the Book” means the Preserved Tablet, which contains past, present, and future, the verse means that the generic systems of animal species fall under divine grace. Their creation is not vain or aimless, and they are not deprived of the perfection their capacity can receive. This accords with “...and the bounty of your Lord is not confined (17:20)” and “...there is no living creature but He holds it by its forelock… (11:56).”

If “the Book” means the Noble Qur’an, it means that, as a book of guidance, it neglects none of the matters whose knowledge is necessary for human success and happiness in this world and the next: “...and We have revealed the Book to you explaining clearly everything…(16:89).” Knowledge of the connection between the formation of nations in this world—including animal species—and their gathering in the Hereafter is needed for understanding the Hereafter. It also discloses God’s oneness, subtle power, care for creatures, and the general order of the universe, especially the chain by which existents advance from deficiency toward perfection through graduated ranks, including plants, animals, and humankind. Reflection on animals is a means to certainty of God.

Possibly, the verse includes both meanings of “the Book.” God neglects nothing in the book of creation, decreeing for each species the existential perfection it deserves and preparing it for social organization where it has the capacity for it; nor does He neglect anything in His revealed speech that concerns human welfare in both abodes. The verse thereby describes animals as conscious genera granted an existential happiness and moving toward God, to Whom they will be gathered like human beings. The use of pronouns for beings possessing perception and intelligence in “then to their Lord shall they be gathered” indicates that they possess the basis upon which pleasure and displeasure, reward and punishment, revolve. The shift from the third person to “We have not neglected anything in the Book,” and then back to the third person, occurs because the first-person plural clause is parenthetical and particularly addressed to the Holy Prophet.

Al-Mizan rejects as evidently invalid an attempted proof of transmigration of souls from the verse. That view claims that after death a human soul enters an animal body corresponding to its entrenched vile trait—such as a crafty person becoming a fox, a spiteful mischief-maker a wolf, a seeker of people’s shameful secrets a swine, or a greedy glutton a cow—while blessed souls enter better human bodies. It consequently reads the animal genera as human nations changed into animal forms. The verse’s explanation and, especially, “then to their Lord shall they be gathered,” are incompatible with this interpretation, so there is no benefit in examining it further. The commentary likewise rejects the claim that the animals’ gathering means only their death, or death together with resurrection. Death cannot be described as going “to their Lord”; and adding death to resurrection is unwarranted, since neither the wording nor the meaning of the verse requires it.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan explains that those who reject God’s communications are spiritually deprived of hearing, speech, and sight: deafness prevents them from hearing and answering the true word; dumbness prevents them from speaking truth or testifying to monotheism and prophethood; and utter darkness prevents them from seeing and following the way of truth.

God’s causing them to err by making them deaf, dumb, and enveloped in darkness is not the cause of their rejection, but its recompense. He does not will error for anyone except one who deserves it through rejecting His communications. Conversely, guidance is God’s gift of hearing, responsive speech to the Caller to God, and sight of the truth; He grants it to one who does not reject the communications and exposes himself to divine mercy.

The commentary further notes the wording, “deaf and dumb, in utter darkness”: deafness and dumbness are conjoined, while darkness is stated separately. Probably this distinguishes two groups. The deaf are ignorant followers who follow their leaders and therefore do not hear the call of truth. The dumb are leaders who know the truth of monotheism and the falsity of polytheism, but whose enmity and transgression prevent them from acknowledging or testifying to it. Both groups share utter darkness, in which they cannot see the truth and no one can effectively point it out to them.

This differs from the description of hypocrites as “Deaf, dumb, blind,” where all these defects are combined because they are cut off from God’s mercy on every side. It also differs from the description of disbelievers whose hearts and hearing are sealed and whose eyes are covered, which distinguishes the sealing of hearing from the sealing of hearts.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains araʾaytakum as meaning “Tell me.” The verse renews the argument against polytheism by asking what the polytheists would do if Allah’s chastisement overtook them or the Hour arrived. In the face of a calamity, human nature seeks help from one able to remove it. They would not call their idols and images, which are themselves subject to the creative order and can bring no benefit; they would call Allah. When hardship overwhelms a person, he forgets all but himself and the Lord in whom he hopes for deliverance. Thus, their calling upon God and forgetting their alleged partners proves that God alone is their Lord and the only one worthy of worship.

The removal of the affliction is qualified by “if He pleases”: God is not compelled to answer a prayer, but has power over everything in every circumstance. The verse includes both worldly punishment and the Hour; denial of the Hour does not affect its coming. Its point is that, in the supposed situation, the one called upon would be God alone. This is a proof of monotheism. The natural turning to God when all other hopes are cut off is a distinct proof that there is a Maker, although the two proofs accompany one another.

Al-Mizan holds that “if He pleases” establishes God’s absolute power even in relation to matters definitively decreed, such as the Hour or a final punishment. His decision that something will occur does not remove His power to do otherwise; yet He always fulfills what He has decisively willed and promised, and does not break His promise. Similarly, His promises to answer prayer—“And when My servants ask you concerning Me, then verily I am near, I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he calls on Me, (2:186)” and “Call upon Me, I will answer you…(40:60)”—do not deprive Him of the power not to answer. Nevertheless, He always answers the real prayer of one who truly prays to Him; this is His unchanging custom.

On this basis, the commentary rejects the objection that the verse conflicts with the certainty of the Hour, the irreversibility of an exterminating punishment, or the statement that “…and the call of the unbelievers is only in error, (40:50).” The verse establishes only that God does whatever He wills and has power over all things; it does not say that He wills or does every possible thing. His final decree to bring the Hour or punish a people does not cancel His power to do the opposite, though He does not act contrary to His promise or settled will.

The phrase “…and the call of the unbelievers is only in error, (40:50)” concerns the unbelievers’ plea in Hell for its punishment to be removed or lightened. Since resurrection and requital according to deeds belong to divine lordship, a request that God not resurrect people or not punish the people of Hell has only the appearance of prayer and lacks its reality. A real prayer is a sincere address to God and is not rejected; moreover, one who sincerely prays in that way does not remain an unbeliever, at least at the time of praying. This is illustrated by: “So when they ride in the ships, they call upon Allah, being sincerely obedient to Him, but when He brings them safe to the land, lo! They associate others (with Him), (29:65).” Thus the erroneous call is their call while they remain unbelievers. Disbelief cannot leave them in the abode of recompense, though in the abode of action it may leave through repentance and faith.

Their request in the Hereafter resembles their lie, “By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists, (6:23).” Neither benefits them, but both manifest there because the habits rooted in their souls in this world disclose themselves when hidden things are exposed. Their food, drink, and disputes in Hell likewise manifest their inner character. Their asking the keepers of Hell to call on their Lord to lighten the punishment, rather than calling directly with hope themselves, shows that they have no hope of their own prayer being accepted; a prayer lacking hope of acceptance is not a true invocation.

Finally, Al-Mizan takes “and you forget what you set up (with Him)” in its real sense: when engulfed by calamities, a person concentrates on himself and forgets everything except God. It therefore finds no need for the interpretation that they merely turn away from idols as though forgetting them, even though such a figurative use of “forgetfulness” is plausible and occurs in the Qur’an.
