verses.42:
Al-Mizan explains al-baʾsāʾ as distress such as poverty, drought, and famine, while al-ḍarrāʾ includes adverse psychological, bodily, or social conditions. Their combination indicates outward calamities and their human consequences. Al-taḍarruʾ is self-abasing humility before God in the hope that He will remove affliction.

The verse begins a description of God’s established way with earlier nations. He sent messengers calling them to divine unity, sincere return, and humility, then afflicted them with hardships that did not compel them to implore Him. The purpose was that they might freely turn to God, their hearts soften, and they abandon satanic temptation and dependence on material causes. Instead, worldly absorption hardened their hearts; Satan beautified their evil deeds and caused them to forget God.

After they forgot God, He opened to them the doors of every blessing. Delighted by these gifts, they became proud and regarded themselves as self-sufficient; then He seized them suddenly and unawares, when they had lost hope of escape and saw their means declining. The cutting off of the unjust is therefore God’s al-istidrāj: granting respite and blessings that make evildoers secure while gradually drawing them toward a severe punishment.

The commentary holds that this does not conflict with the natural human disposition toward monotheism, which becomes manifest when hope in material causes is wholly lost. The distress in this verse had not reached the coercive point at which all ordinary causes are forgotten; “that they might humble themselves” expresses hope, which would have no place under compulsion. Their reliance on the means and actions available to them, made fair-seeming by Satan, kept them from humble dependence on God.

Al-Mizan consequently rejects the view that earlier nations remained averse to monotheism even under hardships that necessarily force a person to turn to God. That view would deny, or undermine, the natural basis of monotheism. The religion of divine unity is grounded in an unchanging human nature: whenever people are disillusioned with material causes, they sincerely turn to their Lord. This instinctive acknowledgment of the One God is the same in past and present humanity.
verses.43: Al-Mizan explains that “Yet why did they not” conveys a negative meaning in its context. Their hearts had hardened—that is, they were no longer affected by sights or words that normally move a person—so, when punishment came, they neither humbled themselves nor turned to their Lord. Instead, satanic deeds kept them from remembering God, and they relied on natural causes as sufficient to improve their condition.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains that opening for them “the doors of all things” means granting, without measure or restriction, every kind of worldly blessing people seek—wealth, children, health, comfort, abundance, security, prestige, and power. Unlike a measured bestowal, whose door is opened only to a fixed extent, this is unrestricted provision; the expression is therefore used despite “opening” being more naturally associated with blessings than with misfortunes, which imply deprivation and closing.

When they had turned away from the admonition, God gave them these varied blessings to allure them, until their enjoyment was complete and they rejoiced in what they had received. He then seized and destroyed them suddenly, because they deserved it. “They were in utter despair” (mublisūn), derived from ablasa and iblāsan, denotes the extreme hopelessness that leaves one silent and unable to produce an argument: they were silenced, with no argument in their support.
verses.45: Al-Mizan derives dābir, “the end” or “root,” from dubr, the rear of a thing, and explains “their roots were cut off” as total destruction: either no trace remained or none was spared. Repeating “the people who were unjust” instead of a pronoun identifies injustice as the basis of judgment and prepares the praise of God’s Lordship. Their calamity and disgrace came from their own injustice and wrongful choice; God handled their affair only according to profound wisdom, so nothing is attributable to Him except good praise.
verses.46:
Al-Mizan explains that taking away hearing and sight means depriving a person of their powers and making him deaf and blind. Sealing the heart means shutting its door so that nothing external enters it for reflection or for distinguishing obligatory from non-obligatory deeds, and beneficial good from harmful evil, while the heart still retains the basic faculty of understanding; otherwise, the person would be insane. Because the polytheists would neither heed the true words concerning God nor see the signs of His oneness, what came through their ears and eyes could no longer enter their hearts to distinguish truth from falsehood. The verse therefore argues against their belief in partners of God.

That belief is self-refuting, for the alleged partners are supposed to be intercessors and intermediaries who procure benefit and avert harm. As mere intermediaries, they cannot oppose God, who may act freely in His kingdom. If He removes hearing and sight and seals hearts, they cannot restore what He has taken, since they are not sources of creation and invention. What neither benefits nor harms cannot meaningfully be called a god. Human nature seeks the origin of the good and evil occurrences it witnesses in the world and is thereby compelled to acknowledge a God; God is the One who creates, destroys, and does what He wills in the universe.

A sound and discerning person cannot regard a humanly carved image of stone, wood, or metal as the creator or as possessing power to create and destroy. Nor can an idol, itself a servant of God nurtured by Him, be the God worthy of worship who originated the world without a prior model.

The commentary gives the argument another form: divinity requires originality in creation and invention, freedom to do what one wills, and the humility of created and sustained beings before it. If the supposed intermediary is free in what it does, it is an originating principle rather than an intermediary; if it lacks such freedom, it is only an instrument, not a god. Material causes likewise are instruments: eating satisfies appetite, drinking quenches thirst, parents bring forth a child, a pen produces writing, and walking covers distance.

Al-Taṣrīf means presenting the communications in different forms to make them clearer, while al-Ṣudūf means ignoring or discarding them; ṣadafa, yaṣdafu, ṣadufan are used of turning away from something.
verses.47: Al-Mizan explains that al-Jahrah, “openly,” denotes a fully manifest chastisement leaving no doubt, whereas al-baghtah, “suddenly,” overtakes its victim unexpectedly, after it has engulfed him and left no escape. The verse generally argues that divine chastisement is directed only at the unjust: chastisement is the recompense by which the guilty are brought to what harms and destroys them, and guilt entails injustice. Their injustice consists in turning from the Islamic call and rejecting God’s communications; the following two verses specify that the unbelievers are the unjust.
verses.48:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses identify the unbelievers as the unjust: when God’s chastisement comes, it harms only them, and only because of their injustice. The address is turned directly to the Prophet so that his warning more decisively removes their excuse; the divine first-person wording emphasizes that the statement issues from the arena of divine glory and greatness.

God has sent messengers solely as bearers of good news and warning. Whoever believes and acts aright will face neither chastisement, fear, nor grief; whoever rejects God’s communications will be afflicted because of fisq—deviation and straying from submission. The unbelievers are therefore called to consider which of these two groups they belong to.

verses.50:
Al-Mizan explains that “the treasures of God” perhaps means the treasures of His mercy. Divine mercy emanates upon things, giving them existence and its effects; its source is the divine command “Be.” As indicated by “And there is not a thing but with Us are the treasures of it, and We do not send it down but in a known measure,(15:21),” these treasures are the station from which God bestows whatever He wills without depletion or incapacity. This belongs to God alone. Every other possessor is limited, and what he gives diminishes from what he has; hence he cannot independently remove poverty, fulfil every request, or answer every supplication.

The Prophet’s denial that he knows the unseen denies independent knowledge naturally possessed without divine revelation, not knowledge of the unseen conveyed through revelation. Revelation to messengers can include such knowledge, as shown by the revealed accounts of Joseph, Mary, and Noah and by: “The Knower of the unseen! So He does not reveal His secrets to any, except to him whom He chooses of an apostle…(72:26–27).” Likewise, his denial of being an angel denies angelic nature: angels are free of bodily needs such as food, drink, marriage, and its attachments. It answers the unbelievers’ objection that a messenger who eats and goes about in the markets cannot be genuine.

The commentary holds that the repeated denials apparently answer the unbelievers’ demands for miraculous displays, wealth, gardens, an angelic companion, access to hidden matters such as the Hour, and other signs. The Prophet did not claim divine treasures, independent knowledge of the unseen, or angelhood; they therefore have no basis for imposing such demands on him or discrediting him for ordinary human needs. His claim is only that God reveals to him whatever He wills.

“I do not follow aught save that which is revealed to me” does not merely state a claim but shows that he is commanded to convey revelation, for conveying it is itself following it. Thus, although he shares their humanity and dependence, he follows revelation in giving glad tidings to those who obey, warning those who disobey, and calling to monotheism. The comparison of the blind and the seeing means that revelation has granted him insight not granted to them. Reflection therefore shows that the blind should follow the seeing, just as the ignorant should follow the learned.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan explains that “with it” means with the Qur’an, the revelation which the Prophet follows. The description of those who fear being gathered to their Lord, when they will have no guardian or intercessor besides Him, portrays the condition underlying their fear of the Resurrection. Here fear has its ordinary meaning, not knowledge or realization, since the context provides no indication for that wider sense.

The verse singles out such people for warning without restricting the Prophet’s warning to them; the Qur’an elsewhere declares its warning to all whom it reaches: “… and this Qur’an has been revealed to me that I may warn you and whomsoever it reaches…”(6:19). Fear of the gathering makes a soul more receptive and a mind nearer to the call, so the Prophet is directed to give these people particular attention rather than treat them like others. Thus he must warn people generally, and especially those in whom fear of returning to their Lord gives hope of faith.

“There is no guardian for them, nor any intercessor besides Him” absolutely negates the independent power and intercession claimed for beings other than God. Other verses qualify intercession by God’s permission or approval, such as: …who is he that can intercede with Him but by His Permission? (2:255); …and they do not intercede except for him whom He approves… (21:28); And those whom they call upon besides Him have no authority for intercession but he who bears witness of the truth and they know, (43:86). But the qualification is deliberately absent here because the idolaters held their idols to be absolute guardians and intercessors by their own essential power, not by divine permission. Such a belief does not rest on knowledge derived from revelation and prophethood, which they denied. Although an exception for divinely permitted intercession is true in itself, it would not answer their particular claim; the unqualified denial directly corresponds to their unqualified affirmation.

Accordingly, the command concerns anyone in whom signs of fear of the gathering appear when God’s verses are recalled: those who believe in it, such as believers among the People of the Book, and those who doubt it, such as idolaters and others. Fear can arise from the possibility of an event even without certainty that it will occur. Al-Mizan therefore rejects views limiting the verse to believers in the gathering, including the view that it addresses only those mentioned in the following verse, and the view that its special warning concerns believers because the proof is stronger against those who confess the Resurrection. It also reports the claim that it concerns idolaters who believed in resurrection after death, but notes that there is no evidence that the Meccan or Arab polytheists addressed in this sūrah held that belief.

The verse itself makes fear, rather than certain belief, the criterion. The religious call is founded on gathering before the Lord, accounting for good and evil deeds, and requital. Its least effect appears in one who regards the gathering as possible and therefore fears it; as the probability of it becomes stronger, fear and receptiveness increase, until conviction eliminates its opposite and produces complete acceptance.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan explains that the polytheists of the Prophet’s tribe asked him to dismiss the socially weak believers, and God forbade this. Their demand resembles the arrogant chiefs of earlier communities who asked their prophets to expel poor believers. Those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, whether by prescribed prayer or general supplication, are believers whose worship shows their pure attachment to Him; this also prepares for the following statement that God knows the grateful best.

The believers “desire only His wajh,” rendered here as His favour. Wajh literally means face, and by extension what faces another thing: its outward, foremost, or noble aspect. Al-Rāghib records views that in such verses it means God’s Person, or turning to Him through good deeds. He also reports that when this interpretation was put to Abū ʿAbdillāh b. al-Riḍā, he rejected it, explaining that wajh is that toward which one turns: deeds perish except those done for God’s sake. Thus, “they desire only His wajh” means that they seek only God’s pleasure or favour.

The commentary maintains that wajh cannot properly mean the person or essence itself. Things are encountered through their manifest names, qualities, and effects, not through their inner reality; even knowledge of a created person proceeds from perceived attributes to the person by intellectual inference. God’s essence, being unlimited and infinite, is still more beyond comprehensive knowledge, for perception requires limitation. A thing’s wajh is therefore what others face of it, or its direction and point of reference.

Accordingly, good deeds may be called God’s wajh, just as evil deeds are Satan’s wajh. God’s wajh also includes the attributes by which He faces creatures—such as mercy, creation, sustenance, and guidance—and such attributes of His Person as life, knowledge, and power, through which He is known to the extent possible. In “But the face of your Lord (the master of glory and honour) will endure forever, (55:27),” it appears that “the master of glory and honour” qualifies “face,” not “your Lord.”

Whatever is connected with God through nearness—His names, attributes, religion, and good deeds—and those established in His proximity—prophets, angels, martyrs, and forgiven believers—are likewise His wajh. The verses concerning what is with God, those who are with Him, the slain in God’s way, and His treasures show that such realities endure through His everlastingness and are untouched by destruction. Thus “everything is perishable but His wajh” means that these things are in God’s direction and with Him. Likewise, what a person seeks from his Lord—His grace, pleasure, mercy, nearness, and His way—belongs to His wajh, because these are attributes of His action. The believers’ desire for His wajh is therefore their exclusive orientation to God’s pleasure and nearness.

Regarding “neither are you answerable for any reckoning of theirs, nor are they answerable for any reckoning of yours,” Al-Mizan prefers to take reckoning as the accounting of deeds for recompense. Since recompense belongs to God, reckoning belongs to His jurisdiction. The Prophet is not charged with accounting for their deeds and rewarding or punishing them, and so cannot expel them because he dislikes their conduct or company. Nor are they charged with his reckoning, so that he would expel them through fear of their scrutiny, punishment, or arrogant dislike. The two clauses are independent.

Other possible readings are that he bears none of the burden of their deeds, with the second clause added merely for balance; that the two clauses simply deny a connection between him and them in reckoning; or that reckoning concerns provision, which God alone apportions. These readings are possible, but the first is preferred.

To drive away those who call upon God would make the Prophet one of the unjust. Although this consequence normally would follow immediately after the prohibition, the intervening clarification about reckoning lengthens the statement. The phrase “drive them away” is therefore repeated to reconnect the consequence to the initial command, not as a defective self-predication.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan explains that Fatannā means testing and trial. The disparity between people is a divine test that distinguishes the ungrateful from the grateful. The polytheists’ question, “Are these they upon whom God has conferred benefit from among us?”, was mockery of poor, humble believers whom Meccan aristocrats considered socially contemptible.

Human social norms judge nobility, baseness, and even deeds by the standing of those who perform them. Thus the wealthy and powerful discounted the faith embraced by the poor, labourers, and slaves; the Prophet’s regard and association with them became, in the eyes of the arrogant, evidence that the faith itself was insignificant and unworthy of the notable class.

“Does not God best know the grateful?” answers this ridicule: the believers, not the polytheists, were grateful, so God preferred them with the favour of Islam. God knows who is thankful for His blessing, and the Benefactor favours the thankful. Gratefulness includes affirming God’s Unity and denying any partner to Him. The verse therefore exposes the polytheists’ ignorant measure of honour through worldly vanities—wealth, children, and status—which have no value or honour before God. Real honour rests on gratefulness and true benefit, namely the Divine Authority.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan explains that God commands the Prophet to welcome believers with peace and to gladden them with the promise of forgiveness and mercy when they sincerely repent of sin. God’s having “ordained mercy on Himself” means that mercy cannot be separated from His actions. Aṣlaḥa, “acts aright,” means reforming oneself or amending one’s deed.

This is a verse about repentance from sins committed by believers, not repentance from unbelief or polytheism. The “ignorance” in which they do evil is opposed to deliberate disbelief and obstinacy: one who believes and seeks God’s favour does not disobey out of arrogance, but may be overcome by desire or anger.

Repentance is inseparable from acting aright. True return to God and refuge in His nearness cannot coexist with the impurity of sins; it is not merely a verbal declaration that fails to reach the heart. Although mercy is ordained upon God, His action-attributes of being Forgiving and Merciful are manifested when His servant commits a sin in ignorance, then repents and reforms.
verses.55:
Al-Mizan explains “We make distinct the communications” as the clarification of Divine Knowledge and the removal of ambiguity from it. The la in “so that the way of the guilty may become clear” expresses a purpose, connected with an unspoken statement whose omission magnifies its significance, as in: …and We bring these days to men by turns, and that Allah may know those who believe…(3:140), and: And thus did We show Abraham the Kingdom of the heavens and the earth and so that he might be of those who are sure (6:76).

Thus God clarifies the divisions of Divine Knowledge and dispels their ambiguities for important ends, one of which is to make known the path followed by the guilty so that believers in His verses may avoid it. This path opposes the verses concerning God’s Unity and the true knowledge related to it; it is disbelief, obstinacy, turning away from the divine verses, and ungratefulness. Although it has been said that “the way of the guilty” means God’s way of dealing with them—cursing in this world and an evil reckoning and painful chastisement in the hereafter—the first interpretation is preferable in the context of these verses.
verses.56: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is commanded to tell the polytheists that he is forbidden to worship the beings they invoke besides Allah, thereby also conveying the prohibition of their worship. Idol-worship is the following of low desires; its rejection rests on the fact that such following is misguidance and removes one from those distinguished by accepting divine guidance. It disrupts the continuity of guidance in the soul and prevents the constant, beneficial illumination of the heart by monotheism. Thus the verse gives a complete rationale: worshipping their idols follows low desires, and following those desires entails misguidance and separation from the rightly guided.
verses.57:
Al-Mizan explains that al-Bayyinah, “the manifest proof,” derives from al-bayān, clarity through separation: it distinguishes truth from falsehood so plainly that the truth can be recognized without difficulty. The pronoun in “you call it a lie” refers to the Qur’an, which is among the proofs supporting the Prophet’s messengership. The polytheists reject this proof while demanding a different sign, namely the punishment they seek to hasten. That punishment is neither in the Prophet’s possession nor delegated to him; thus they reject what he has been given and demand what he has not been given.

“I have not with me that which you would hasten” indirectly denies the Prophet’s power over it. Things ordinarily given or bestowed are under a person’s possession and control; denying possession here therefore denies control. “The judgment is only Allah’s” gives the reason: judgment belongs exclusively to God, with no share for anyone else.

Al-Ḥukm originally signifies joining and strengthening parts so that they do not break apart. In human conventions, a ruler’s command imposes a binding duty, and a judge’s ruling restores and confirms the connection between an owner and his property or a right-holder and his right, ending a dispute and excluding interference. The term is then applied to creation: a seed’s development into a plant and a sperm-drop’s development into a living, sentient body occur through God’s ḥukm and decree. In both spheres, ḥukm establishes a firm relation or correlation.

Tawḥīd establishes that every real effect in the universe proceeds from God alone, who has no partner. Although the Qur’an sometimes attributes creation and such qualities as knowledge, power, life, will, sustenance, and beauty exclusively to God and sometimes attributes them to others, the creative decree, al-ḥukm al-takwīnī, belongs exclusively to Him. If another possessed an independent ḥukm, that person could oppose the Divine will. Legislative judgment, al-ḥukm al-tashrīʾī, likewise belongs to God in origin and independently. When judgment is attributed to just witnesses, David, the Prophet, or other prophets, it is a secondary judgment exercised by God’s permission and according to what He revealed. God is therefore the best of judges, because judgment belongs to Him primarily and independently.

Attribution of ḥukm to others is confined to conventional matters; as far as the commentary recalls, creative command is never attributed to anyone besides God. Other Divine qualities and actions may be attributed to creatures by His will and permission. This distinction perhaps preserves the sanctity of Divine independence: terms such as al-Badīʾ and al-Fāṭir, which convey a special exclusivity in creation, are not attributed to others.

In this verse, ḥukm means God’s creative decree. It explains why the Prophet cannot bring the punishment: the final decision between him and his opponents belongs to God alone. Their demand for a sign other than the Qur’an is, indirectly, a demand that he bring about the judgment between them. This also explains the repeated wording “that which you desire to hasten” in the following verse: what they seek entails the final judgment, according to the Divine practice. It is also possible that the indirect and direct senses of the expression are reversed between the two verses.

The reading yaquṣṣu means cutting off and separating, while another reading derived from qaḍāʾ conveys judgment or decision. Both yield the same sense: God declares the truth and separates it from falsehood through a judgment founded on truth. Yet “He is the best of separators” particularly suits yaquṣṣu in its sense of separating. Al-Mizan rejects interpretations of yaquṣṣu as merely narrating stories, since the context contains no such narration, and as following the truth, since—even though God judges only by truth—the Qur’anic decorum does not describe God as following something on which He depends. The truth is from God, not something with Him; He is not characterized by weakness or dependence.

The commentary consequently maintains that God’s action and judgment are actual truth, not actions merely conforming to a truth external to Him. A thing is true when it has real existence rather than being imagined; a report is true when it accords with independent reality; and a command or judgment is true when it accords with the governing order and the relevant general or particular good. Thus commands to establish justice and avoid injustice are true because social harmony and welfare are required for human success, whereas commands to commit injustice or withhold justice are false. al-Tawḥīd is true because it leads a human being to success in his real life, while al-shirk is false because it leads to ruinous suffering and perpetual chastisement. A legal judgment is true when it accords with the welfare properly relevant to all people, a group, or a community.

Yet the world, its order, and its norms are all God’s act: they begin from Him, are sustained by Him, and return to Him. Truth and good therefore follow His action and exist through attribution to Him; God does not follow truth. He is the True in Himself, while all else is true through Him.

Human beings, by contrast, are needy and imperfect, and seek to complete themselves and attain success through voluntary, social action. They therefore consider general welfare, follow laws and norms, and characterize actions with such notions as good, evil, obligation, prohibition, permission, ownership, and right. These laws and evaluations are conventional and relative rather than independently existing realities: they arise from human needs and social life and are used to distinguish beneficial from harmful action. Hence communities differ in what they approve, forbid, retain, or abandon as their purposes change. Such evaluations nonetheless have a real basis in the actual order of creation and in the human being’s natural need for social life and success. Where general aims are universally acknowledged—such as the need for society, justice’s positive value, and injustice’s negative value—there is no practical disagreement requiring such evaluative classifications.

Al-Mizan rejects two opposing theological extremes. The mufawwiḍah make benefit, harm, goodness, and evil eternal, unchanging realities that govern God’s creation and legislation; by doing so, they remove God from His authority and deny His absolute power. The mujabbirah deny purposes and reasons in creation and legislation, holding that goodness results only from God’s command and evil only from His prohibition, and that human beings have neither responsibility nor power over their acts. The former make acts purely human creations beyond God’s power, while the latter deny human responsibility; neither position is correct.

God has presented religion through the pattern of social norms so that people can understand it. He presents Himself as the worshiped Lord and people as nurtured servants; He sets out fundamental beliefs and practical laws, with reward and punishment, and explains obedience as their benefit, good end, and success. This allows people to seek religious knowledge as they seek social knowledge and to understand that Divine commands contain goodness and that prohibitions concern what corrupts religion or worldly life. Divine action is not purposeless or evil, and reason approves what God commands and avoids what He forbids.

Nevertheless, two qualifications are essential. First, the reality itself is far greater than the social concepts through which people understand it; such concepts do not ascend to the level of the elevated, wise original of the Book. Al-Mizan cites the Prophet’s reported saying: “Verily, we the assembly of the prophets, have been commanded to speak with the people according to the level of their intelligence.” This transcendence does not entail denying goodness or benefit in God’s acts, nor treating them as childish or purposeless; it only removes deficiency from Him.

Second, goodness and benefit relate differently to human and Divine action. Human beings derive these meanings from the created order and are guided and compelled by them: they act and legislate to gain a good they lack and to secure their success. God’s action, however, is the real world from which such meanings are derived, and His legislation generates reality rather than following it. Goodness and benefit are thus inseparable from His actions and commands as their beneficial consequences, not external compelling causes or purposes through which He acquires something absent from Himself. People are accountable because their acts depend on such aims; God is not accountable to anyone, nor can His judgment be repelled. If His action were like human rational action, some benefit would compel Him and limit His ability to do whatever He pleases. The Qur’an’s linking of His commands with life, goodness, and the rejection of indecency shows that benefits belong to Divine commands without compelling God.
verses.58: Al-Mizan explains that, if the Prophet possessed the punishment the disbelievers demanded be hastened, its descent upon a messenger would conclusively judge between him and his people: one party would be saved and the other destroyed. The punishment would seize only them, because they are the unjust; God cannot confuse the unjust with the innocent and punish the Prophet instead. “Allah best knows the unjust” therefore both indicates and justifies this outcome: His chastisement does not pass from the unjust to others, reaffirming (6:47).
verses.59:
Al-Mizan relates this verse not merely to the preceding words, “and Allah best knows the unjust,” but to the two preceding verses together. The demanded decisive sign and the judgment it entails are wholly in God’s power and knowledge, not the Prophet’s. God neither overlooks anything nor confuses the unjust with the innocent when judging them. Thus, the verse establishes both His exclusive knowledge of the unseen and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, completing the point that the decision sought by the polytheists cannot be known or controlled by anyone else.

Mafātīḥ may be the plural of maftaḥ, meaning treasures, or of miftaḥ, meaning keys; a non-canonical recitation supports the latter. Either meaning implies knowledge of, and power over, what is contained in the treasures. Nevertheless, Al-Mizan judges “treasures of the unseen” the more appropriate meaning, because the Qur’an repeatedly speaks of God’s treasures and treasures of mercy without speaking of their keys. In either case, no one besides God has access to the unseen treasures, since none besides Him knows them or their keys.

The first part of the verse concerns the exclusive knowledge of the unseen, whereas its latter part includes all things, whether unseen or seen. The treasures of the unseen contain things before they descend into a state of limitation, measure, time, and visible existence. Such things have with God a kind of abstract, unmeasured existence which human beings cannot comprehend; the temporal things of this world existed in that manner before their material existence. Perhaps those treasures also contain things incomparable to the time-bound things familiar to us. This is al-ghayb al-muṭlaq, the absolute unseen: what has not emerged into visibility and is inaccessible to all but God.

Al-Mizan distinguishes this from al-ghayb al-nisbi, the relative unseen. Once things have descended into limits and measures, they may be known or unknown according to the knower. What is inside a house is seen by those within and unseen by those outside; lights and colours are seen by the eyes but not the ears, while sounds are apprehended by the ears but not the eyes. Thus, the land, sea, falling leaves, grains in the earth’s darkness, and all that is green or dry belong to the relative unseen: they are limited and measurable things that may be perceived by some and hidden from others.

The “clear book” does not mean that these external things themselves exist in it as letters exist in an ordinary book. Rather, its relation to events is like that of a written programme to the event it specifies. It is an entity distinct from the things recorded: it precedes them, remains after they perish, and records them without error or omission. Although worldly events and persons change, the verses describing the Book as guarded and preserving show that change, variation, and error do not reach it. The Book is therefore distinct from the treasures of the unseen. The treasures are beyond limit and measure, while the Book contains the detailed limits and measures of things after their descent from the treasures, before their material realization, during their existence, and after their demise.

The Book is mentioned to display God’s all-encompassing knowledge of all events and things, visible or hidden from people. Everything created has its origin and sustenance in the treasures of the unseen, while everything created is contained in the clear book before, during, and after its physical existence. The clear book is lower in rank than the treasures and cannot be compared to material parchments or papers, which cannot even record their own history, much less the perpetual history of all things. While no one can know what is in the divine treasures, some verses indicate that others may know what is in the Book: “In a book that is hidden; none do touch it save the purified ones,(56:78–79).”

Thus, “the keys of the unseen” are the divine treasures containing things before they assume the mould of measure, as indicated by: And there is not a thing but with Us are the treasures of it, and We do not send it down but in a known measure, (15:21). The clear book, by contrast, is like a programme containing the measured determination of things, existing before them, with them, and after them, and embodying God’s knowledge without error or forgetfulness. It is sometimes surmised that the clear book means the real status and material realization of things, on the ground that an existent does not change after it has come to be. Yet the Book contains all past, present, and future occurrences, including records subject to erasure and reaffirmation: “Allah erases what He pleases and establishes (likewise), and with Him is the basis of the Book; (13:39).” The erasing and establishing, especially when contrasted with the basis of the Book, occur in the Book. A translator’s note summarizes this by identifying within al-Kitābu al-Mubīn the unchangeable Ummu al-Kitāb or Lawḥ Maḥfūz and the changeable Lawḥ Maḥw wa Ithbāt, which concerns partial knowledge given to some angels and prophets; it also states that the Book may be accessible to chosen humans by God’s permission, unlike the treasures.

The verse consequently confirms that the decisive punishment requested from the Prophet lies in God’s knowledge and power alone. God knows that the opponents are unjust and so does not mistake them for others; none can know or control His ultimate decision, because the keys of the unseen belong to Him alone. The phrase “none knows them but He” shows that the keys belong to the category of knowledge, but not knowledge as people ordinarily conceive it—images derived from things after they have materialized and acquired measurable boundaries. They are God’s unlimited knowledge of things in their abstract state before materialization and measurement.

God’s knowledge of what is in land and sea includes things that may be visible to some and hidden from others; land is mentioned first because it is more familiar to the audience. The falling leaf is specified because the immense number of leaves, their distinctions, and their changing states make it impossible for human beings to monitor them. The darkness of the earth denotes its dark depths, containing grains that may grow or perish. Thus no grain, green thing, or dry thing falls there without God’s knowledge, and “but (it is all) in a clear book” takes the place of “but that He knows it”: all is written in that Book. Al-mubīn may mean a book that clarifies every thing in its true form without change, alteration, or concealment, or a book that is itself clear, free of ambiguity and concealment.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains al-tawaffā as taking something in full. God uses it both for death and for sleep: each suspends the soul’s function in the body, but sleep does so partially and death completely. Likewise, al-baʾth denotes both awakening from sleep and resurrection after death, because in each case the soul’s function is restored, partially in awakening and completely in resurrection. Nightly taking and daytime raising describe the usual human pattern of sleeping by night and waking by day.

The expression “He takes your souls in full” shows that the soul is the human being’s complete essence—the referent of “I”—not merely one component, an accidental quality, or a form attached to the body. The objection that a person is lost when the body disintegrates in the earth rests on identifying the person with the body. The answer is that the angel of death takes the soul completely; therefore nothing of the human essence is lost.

“Jaraḥtum—you acquire” derives from al-jarḥ, an act performed by a limb, and here means what people acquire through their deeds during the day. Al-Mizan prefers to read “and He knows what you acquire in the day” as a circumstantial phrase—“while He knows”—rather than as a separate conjunction. Thus, “then He raises you up therein,” meaning during the day, follows directly from His taking souls at night. The verse thereby sets out the divine ordering of human life, death, and the return to God: He takes people in sleep while knowing their deeds, then restores them to wakefulness.

Awakening is called baʾth in deliberate contrast with the tawaffā of sleep. God raises people each day so that their appointed term of death, known to Him and neither advanced nor delayed, may be completed. Although He knows the evil deeds they acquire, He does not retain their souls to finalize their death before that fixed term. Were it not for the prior determination of the term, He would seize them swiftly for their deeds and their evil consequences. After death and resurrection, all return to Him, and He informs them of what they were doing.
verses.61:
Al-Mizan takes the unqualified sending of “keepers,” joined to the arrival of death, as indicating angels who guard human beings against calamities, misfortunes, and tribulations until their appointed death. Worldly life is marked by rivalry and mutual domination: each thing seeks a fuller share of existence, often at another’s expense. The human bodily constitution is especially delicate and surrounded by many natural rivals and dangers; therefore God assigns angels to preserve people from destructive events. When the fixed term arrives, however, they leave a person to the tribulations that bring death, as mentioned in the aḥādīth.

The “keepers” in And most surely there are keepers over you, honourable recorders, they know what you do, (82:10–12) are angels who record deeds. Although some exegetes interpret the keepers in this verse likewise, the wording “until when death comes to one of you” favors the interpretation that they are protectors.

“Our Messengers take him completely, and they are not remiss” apparently means that the angels charged with taking the soul are never negligent or careless in carrying out God’s command. Since every nation has a determined term which neither precedes nor lags, they take each person’s soul precisely at the assigned time and under the assigned conditions, without even momentary neglect.

The verse does not decide whether the angels who take souls are the same keepers, though it remotely suggests this. In any case, the angels of death are helpers of the Angel of Death: Say: “The angel of death who is given charge of you shall take you completely, then to your Lord you shall be brought back.”(32:11). The attribution of taking souls to these angels, to the Angel of Death, and to God—Allah takes completely the souls at the time of death…(39:42)—marks levels of agency. All things end with God, the absolute Master; the Angel of Death acts through his helpers, who are his instruments, like a pen moved by a hand and, behind both, the writer.
verses.62:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse concerns humanity’s return to God in resurrection after death. Calling Him “their Master, the True One” shows that He alone is responsible for their sleep, awakening, preservation, death, and resurrection. A master owns the slave and may dispose of him as he wills; because God possesses real ownership and brings about creation, governance, and resurrection, He is the True Master whose mastership cannot be diminished.

Since God alone possesses the treasures of the unseen, knows the clear book containing everything, and governs creatures from their origin until their return to Him, judgment belongs exclusively to Him. “He is swiftest in taking account” means that He does not postpone reckoning beyond its proper time; any delay serves only to complete its determined term.
verses.63:
Al-Mizan explains that deliverance from “darkness of the land and the sea” means rescue from the hardships of travel—cold, rain, snow, storms, robbers, and the like—which darkness of night, clouds, or dust-bearing winds intensifies by increasing anxiety, hopelessness, and confusion. The verse therefore links deliverance to darkness because it is especially associated in people’s minds with the calamities of land and sea journeys, although God delivers from every distress.

Citing al-Rāghib, the commentary explains that al-Taḍarruʾ is the open display of humiliation, humbleness, and submission, contrasted with al-khufyah, private and concealed prayer. One afflicted by a calamity may first pray secretly and in whispers; when the danger becomes severe and hope of safety is cut off, he openly implores as well. The two expressions indicate that God delivers from both severe and lighter calamities.

The promise, “If He delivers us from this, certainly we shall be of the grateful ones,” is a pledge to become grateful and abandon prior ingratitude. Such promises resemble ordinary human dealings, in which the helpless seek aid from one able to remove their hardship and offer praise, wealth, service, or loyalty in return, since people act for hoped-for benefit. But God is exalted above need or loss, and whatever He does benefits His creatures.

Thus, when disaster removes all apparent means of safety and rescue, a person realizes that God alone can remove his grief and that He has governed him and all means from his creation onward. Seeing himself as unjust and sinful, and therefore undeserving of relief, he promises gratitude and obedience in hope that his prayer will be accepted. Yet once delivered, he forgets this pledge and promise of gratitude: “yet again you associate (others) with Him.”
verses.64:
Al-Mizan explains, citing al-Rāghib, that al-karb means severe distress, akin to al-kurbah; its proposed derivations evoke inner agitation and constriction. By adding “every distress” to the darknesses of land and sea, the verse encompasses all people, for everyone encounters distress and anxiety and therefore pleads for relief, openly or secretly.

When people are cut off from ordinary means of rescue, their human nature makes them recognize Allah as their only Lord and become certain that worshipping another is unjust and sinful. Their humiliated open and secret prayer, together with their promise to be grateful and not disbelieve if delivered, proves this recognition. Yet once Allah delivers them, they break their pledge and return to disbelief. Thus the two verses argue against the polytheists and rebuke their breach of oath and pledge.
verses.65:
Al-Mizan explains, citing al-Rāghib, that al-baʾth fundamentally denotes raising something and directing it onward. Its meaning varies with its object: it may be a human act, such as setting a camel moving or dispatching a person, or a divine act, including creation and raising the dead. Thus, the “sending” of chastisement suggests that chastisement is directed towards and comes upon its people; what prevents this necessary consequence is a barrier such as faith and obedience to God.

Citing al-Ṭabrisī, the commentary explains yalbisakum as mixing and confusing matters, while al-Shiyaʾ denotes sects, each group being a separate faction. The verse therefore threatens that God may confuse people by mixing them together as divided groups and sects.

Although the opening words apparently establish only God’s power to send a chastisement from above or beneath, and ability does not itself entail action, the context shows more than a bare assertion of power. The people deserve chastisement, and it will be directed upon them if they do not agree upon faith in God and His revelation. The later statement, “For every prophecy is a term and you will come to know (it),” confirms that this is a clear threat. Similar Qur’anic warnings concern communities that reject their messengers and divide their religion into sects.

It has been said that chastisement from above includes such afflictions as the cry, stones, flood, and wind, while that from beneath includes being swallowed by the earth. It has also been interpreted as oppression from elders and tyrannical rulers above, and harm from lowly people and evil slaves below; another view applies it to destructive weapons, including aircraft, tanks, bombs, and submarines. Al-Mizan holds that the wording can apply to all of these explanations, as well as to similar chastisements occurring after the verse’s revelation. Their common opening is the disagreement and division that arose in the ummah against the Prophet’s summons to unity upon the truth: This indeed is my straight path, so follow it, and do not follow (other) ways, for they will separate you from His way… (6:154).

Apparently, the confusion into parties and the making of some taste the fighting of others refer to the factions that emerged after the Prophet, whose schools acquired partisan and jāhiliyyah zeal. This led to wars in which each group treated the other’s sacred things as violable and denied the other the sanctity of faith and the territory of Islam. These words describe one chastisement, not two: division itself culminates in mutual fighting. Though they may in one respect be viewed as separate chastisements, taking the fighting as a separate qualification of the general confusion would require an added emphasis absent from the wording; the conjunction supports their unity. Division also brings gradual weakness, depleted power, and fragmented resources.

The verse consequently instructs the Messenger to warn those who refuse to unite under Islam and heed the true call: God can seize them with an inescapable chastisement from above or below, or make them form hostile factions that dispute, fight, and taste one another’s fighting. The repeated display of signs is meant to bring them to understanding.
verses.66:
Al-Mizan takes the Prophet’s “people” to mean the Quraysh, Muḍar, or Arabs generally; other verses indicate that a messenger’s people are those whose language he speaks. Their calling “it” a lie justifies the realization of the preceding warning: they were required to unite upon their Lord’s monotheism and the true word, lest an inescapable punishment come from above or below, or division lead to armed conflict. Their rejection therefore makes them deserving of the threatened punishment.

The pronoun in “call it a lie” most clearly refers to the chastisement, as al-Ālūsī attributes to the majority of commentators, or at least to the news of chastisement in the preceding verse. Referring it to the repeated display of signs or to the Qur’an is far-fetched. The statement is the first report preparing the threat: the Prophet’s people, including those of his time and later members of his ummah, hastened to violate what they were bound to affirm by denying the warning. Although Jews, other contemporary communities, and later peoples also rejected the Prophet, the Qur’an’s particular attribution of rejection to his people supports the connection between their rejection, their divisions, and the warning of punishment.

The commentary holds that the later weakness, disintegration, and loss of unity of the Muslim ummah can be traced to disputes after the Prophet’s death, and further back to the early hijrah and to his own tribe’s bold rejection and ridicule of him. Though they later assembled under Islam after it prevailed, the religious society retained a substantial element of hypocrisy, whose harmful influence it could not fully eliminate during the Prophet’s life and whose embers were soon rekindled.

“Say: ‘I am not placed in charge of you’” indirectly instructs the Prophet to leave them: he is neither responsible nor liable for their deeds, nor required to prevent their rejection; his duty as Messenger is only to warn them of a severe, hidden punishment. This also shows that “For every prophecy is a term, and you will come to know (it)” belongs to the Prophet’s speech addressed to his people, rather than directly to God’s speech.
verses.67:
Al-Mizan reads “For every prophecy is a term and you will come to know (it)” as an explicit threat of an imminent event. The warning properly concerns the Meccan polytheists, because the divisions and troubles later faced by the Muslim ummah have their roots in them. Humanity is one community: later generations are affected by what earlier ones do, and defects appearing later may be traced to the first generation whether people recognize this connection or not.

The commentary cites (44:9–15) as an instance of God’s punishment reaching later communities for their predecessors’ crimes, and relates this pattern to Yūnus (10:47–56), al-Anbiyā (21:92–97), and al-Rūm (30:30–45). Many Qur’anic verses, it holds, warn of the evil consequences and misfortunes that will overtake the ummah after Divine favor, forgiveness, and blessings. It reproaches Qur’anic commentators for gravely neglecting reflection on these numerous and important verses, despite their bearing on the ummah’s condition and good fortune in this world and the hereafter.
verses.68:
Al-Mizan explains, citing al-Rāghib’s al-Mufradāt, that al-Khawḍ originally means entering and passing through water, then came to denote entering into other matters, chiefly blameworthy ones in the Qur’an. Here it means becoming deeply involved in vain talk about God’s signs—for example, citing true Qur’anic verses only to ridicule and insult them.

To “withdraw from them” is to demonstrate non-participation, by leaving their gathering or the like. The restriction, “until they enter into some other discourse,” shows that withdrawal is not an absolute prohibition on associating with such people, even for a rightful purpose; it applies while they persist in mockingly engaging with the Divine verses. The verse thus contains an understood qualification: when they turn to another subject, there is no impediment to sitting with them. Though revealed amid the argument against the polytheists, its criterion is general. The pronoun in ghayruhu refers to the discourse in which they had been negatively engaging with the verses.

Such engagement is injustice, and the command forbids participating with unjust people in that injustice; as the similar verse says, “…surely then you would be like them… (4:140)”. Thus the required withdrawal is from their conduct for as long as it continues, not a permanent withdrawal from the people themselves.

The commentary holds that the clause concerning Satan-caused forgetfulness strongly emphasizes that, once the prohibition is remembered, one must not delay leaving. Those who fear God must not participate in gatherings where His verses are ridiculed. Although the wording addresses the Holy Prophet, its real addressees are the ummah: prophets do not forget the Divine Law in this sense, since such neglect would furnish opponents with an argument against them. This is supported by the following address to the pious and, more decisively, by the Medinan verse: And indeed He has revealed to you in the Book that when you hear Allah’s communications disbelieved in and mocked at, do not sit with them until they enter into some other discourse; surely then you would be like them; surely Allah will gather together the hypocrites and the unbelievers all in Hell; (4:140). Its reference to what had already been revealed in the Book is this verse of Sūrah al-Anʾām, showing that the earlier command was addressed to the believers, though phrased to the Prophet.
verses.69:
Al-Mizan explains that those who mock or engage negatively with God’s verses bear their own sin; another person bears none of its reckoning unless he joins in it or approves of it. Yet those who guard against evil must be reminded, because even attendance at such a gathering without participation, inward approval, or intent to support it can dull one’s sensitivity to the transgression. Once a sin seems less serious, a heart inclined to sins may fall into it. Thus the pious, as well as those already sitting with such people, must avoid their company lest they become accustomed to insolence toward God and His verses and so approach perdition: whoever hovers around fire is likely to fall into it.

The verse singles out the pious as free of the mockers’ reckoning, although in principle no one bears another sinner’s punishment, in order to stress that one who sits in such gatherings is not secure from sharing their punishment. Its implied sense is that those who do not engage in this conduct incur no responsibility so long as they protect themselves from it; nevertheless, they are forbidden to sit with the offenders so that they preserve, or increase, their piety and sensitivity to God’s prohibitions.

Al-Mizan takes taqwā in “those who guard (against evil)” as general avoidance of everything displeasing to God, while in “haply they may guard” it concerns the particular sin of negatively engaging with God’s verses. Alternatively, the first may denote the initial degree of taqwā and the second its perfection, or the first its general meaning and the second its application in this particular case. Another possible reading makes the first address believers and the second the offenders themselves: they are to be advised so that they desist.

Grammatically, dhikrā may be the unrestricted object of an implied verb—God counsels them by it—or may be construed through an omitted subject or predicate, yielding either “this command is a reminder” or “it is your duty to counsel them.” Al-Mizan considers the interpretation that the command itself is a reminder closer to the mind.
verses.70:
Al-Mizan explains al-Baṣl, following al-Rāghib, as separation or constraint; in this verse it means being deprived of reward. Unlike al-ḥarām, which may be a prohibition by law or force, al-baṣl denotes constraint by force. Ṭabarsī reports that it may mean surrendering someone because he cannot escape; al-Akhfash glosses tublaṣa as being punished or mortgaged, meanings that are close.

Taking religion as play and idle sport means following evil desires in relation to the true faith to which pure nature calls them. They should have adhered to and safeguarded that faith, but instead altered it according to desire. Their deception by worldly life is closely connected: becoming absorbed in acquiring and enjoying material life compels abandonment of true faith and its treatment as amusement.

The command to remind them thereby means to counsel them by the Qur’an, lest a soul be fettered by its sins—that is, deprived of God’s reward or surrendered for reckoning and punishment. Such a soul will have no guardian or intercessor besides Allah, and no gold-weight or other ransom will be accepted, for that Day is for recompense of deeds, not buying and selling. Those fettered by what they earned will receive boiling water and painful punishment because of their disbelief.
verses.71:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as a rhetorical argument against polytheism. People worship or seek nearness to a god through hope for benefit or fear of harm; therefore, beings that can neither benefit nor harm provide no reason to be invoked or worshipped.

To be “returned back on our heels” after Allah’s guidance is to abandon the straight path after finding and walking it, and is thus misguidance. The image is of one cast down and bewildered by the Shayāṭīn: lacking insight and firm resolve to attain felicity, he leaves the sound path already traversed by his rightly guided companions. He is torn between Satan and his agents, who draw him toward ruin, and companions who have reached the goal and call him, “Come to us.”

The commentary rejects the inference drawn from this expression, and from Shuʾayb’s words in (7:88–89), that prophets were unbelievers before their missions. The prophets speak in the language of a religious society whose members had been idolaters until Allah guided them; this does not mean that disbelief can literally be ascribed to every individual in that society, including its prophet. The community was polytheistic before receiving true faith through the prophets, whereas the prophets were always guided by Allah. Yet, without His constant guidance, nothing would remain for them but misguidance, since supposed gods possess neither benefit nor harm. In this sense it is proper to deny returning to polytheism after Allah’s deliverance. The Qur’an, moreover, affirms the prophets’ purity even from the smallest minor sins, let alone shirk, the gravest major sin.

Allah’s guidance is the only true guidance because it accords with human fiṭrah, whereas Satan’s call rests on evil desires and treating faith as play and sport. Guidance is inseparable from the truth manifested in creation and invention, both of which belong to Allah alone. Since people seek truth in religion and belief, and all their origin, final destination, and worldly and otherworldly needs lie with Allah, His guidance must be followed rather than the satanic call.

The commentary takes “we are commanded that we should submit” as an explicative appositive to “Surely the Guidance of Allah, which is the (true) guidance”: Allah’s guidance is applied in the command to submit to Him. The subject, Allah, is left unexpressed so that “to the Lord of the worlds” may state the reason for submission: He alone is Lord of all worlds, leaving no god for all or any part of them, contrary to dualism. Submission apparently means entrusting all affairs to Allah, not merely pronouncing the two testimonies of faith; this is also the apparent sense of Surely the religion with Allah is Islam (3:19).
verses.72: Al-Mizan reads the verse as continuing the preceding command: believers are commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds, maintain prayer, and be mindful of their duty to Him. Mindfulness of God summarizes the detailed religious obligations, while the daily prayer is singled out to emphasize its special importance and rank in the Qur’an. Submission and God-consciousness are obligatory because all human beings return to Him, and reckoning and recompense are in His hands.
verses.73:
Al-Mizan explains that the divine names and attributes in this verse complete the justification for the preceding assertions: God alone possesses true guidance; submission, prayer, and fear of Him comprise faith; and all people must be gathered to Him. The attributes named here establish why this guidance cannot be disregarded and why return, reckoning, and compensation are necessary.

“He has created the heavens and the earth with truth” means that all creation is His act and is founded on truth rather than falsehood. Since an act not founded on falsehood has a purpose, creation has the purpose of returning to God for reckoning and compensation. This is the import of: And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in vain; that is the opinion of those who disbelieve… (38:27). Thus, creation with truth entails the gathering of creatures to Him at resurrection. “With truth” qualifies the act of creating, not a supposed “true word” by which He created the heavens and earth; that latter interpretation is far-fetched.

In “and on the day He says: ‘Be’, it is,” the context most apparently makes the Day of Resurrection the object of “Be”: on the day He commands the Resurrection, it will come to be. Although “Be” can apply to every created thing, as in His command, when He intends anything, is only that He says to it, “Be,” and it is,(36:82), the alternative interpretation—that the command addresses a thing which then exists—is less fitting here. The first occurrence of “day” is consequently an adverb denoting the time at which the command is issued, not the Resurrection Day itself.

“His word is the truth” justifies the preceding statement and is therefore an independent sentence. al-Ḥaqq, “the truth,” is that which possesses real, external existence rather than merely mental existence. Since God’s word is His act and creation, as the command “Be” shows, His word is truth itself; no one can oppose or alter it: He said: The truth then (it) is and the truth do I speak,(38:84).

“His is the Kingdom on the day when the trumpet shall be blown” concerns the Day of Resurrection. The kingdom belongs to Him always, but on that day its exclusive reality will become manifest: all supports will disappear and every relationship and family tie will be severed. The specific mention of the trumpet emphasizes the universal character of the gathering stated in the preceding verse. al-Ḥashr, “the gathering,” is the resurrection and marshalling of all people together in confusion. As a trumpet gathers soldiers for an important matter, the second trumpet will gather people at the place of assembly for judgment; no soul will then be wronged, and each will be recompensed only for what it did: So this day no soul shall be dealt with unjustly in the least; and you shall not be rewarded aught but which you did, (36:54). The second occurrence of “day” means the Day of Resurrection itself.

“The Knower of the unseen and the seen; and He is the Wise, the Aware” includes the basis of reckoning and compensation. Nothing outward is concealed from Him by its visibility, and nothing inward is concealed by its inwardness. By wisdom He perfectly administers creation and assigns the required compensation without injustice or blindness; by awareness, neither the smallest thing because of its minuteness nor the greatest because of its greatness escapes Him.

The commentary concludes that these attributes establish the gathering of all people, the truth of God’s guidance, and the truth of the religion of fiṭrah that He commands. He created the universe for its return to Him; when He wills that return, His irresistible true word will bring it about. On that day His kingdom alone will be evident, no creature will have power over another, and, through His knowledge, wisdom, and awareness, He will distinguish those who obeyed Him from those who disobeyed.
verses.74:
Al-Mizan notes that, in the seven canonical recitations, Azara bears faṭḥa and is an apposition to abīhi, “his sire.” A non-canonical reading gives Azaru with ḍumma, making it a vocative: “O Azar, do you take idols for gods?” Another reading begins with interrogative ḥamza, a azraʾa, followed by azraʾa, a verbal noun of azara, yaʾziru, “to support,” and thus asks whether Abraham took idols as a means of strength and support.

Commentators dispute whether Azar is Abraham’s father’s proper name, a laudatory or derogatory nickname, or otherwise; this is connected with reports naming Abraham’s father Tāriḥ or Tārikh, a name also found in historical sources and the present Old Testament. They also dispute whether ab means a biological father, uncle, maternal grandfather, or an authoritative elder. Some reports make Azar Abraham’s actual father, for whom Abraham will unsuccessfully intercede on the Day of Judgement before God transforms him into a foul-smelling hyena; other reports deny that he was Abraham’s father, maintaining that Abraham’s real father, like the Prophet Muḥammad’s ancestors, was a monotheist. Such tradition-based and historical elaborations have generated remote conclusions, sometimes even diminishing Abraham’s prophetic rank, and lie outside sound Qur’anic exegesis.

The commentary holds that the Qur’anic account itself shows that Abraham first encountered the man called his father, Azar, called him away from idols to monotheism, and sought to guide him. When Azar rejected him and ordered him away, Abraham peacefully promised to ask forgiveness for him, hoping to draw him to faith and guidance. His words that he would withdraw from Azar and what he invoked besides Allah show that this was a promise of prayer in this world, not a promise of intercession for a disbeliever on the Day of Judgement.

Abraham subsequently fulfilled that promise in his prayer for his father, describing him as one of the misguided. This was either after Azar’s death or after Abraham’s separation from and abandonment of him; in either case, the prayer was made to fulfil the earlier promise. The Qur’an then explains that Abraham’s asking forgiveness for his sire was only because of that promise, and that, once Azar’s enmity to Allah became clear, Abraham disassociated himself from him (9:114). The context makes both the prayer and the disassociation acts of this worldly life: a present legislative prohibition cannot meaningfully exempt a future act to occur at the Resurrection.

This sequence belongs to the earlier period of Abraham’s migration, his prayer for wisdom and righteous offspring, and his separation from his father and people. God then relates his migration, the granting of Isaac and Jacob, and the withdrawal from those who worshipped other than Allah. By contrast, Abraham’s final Qur’anic prayer was made in Mecca toward the end of his life, after migration to the blessed land, the birth of his children, Ishmael’s settlement in Mecca, the establishment of the town, and the building of the Kaʿbah. In that prayer he asks forgiveness for his parents. It cannot refer again to Azar, from whom he had already disassociated himself after learning that he was Allah’s enemy.

Al-Mizan further argues from Abraham’s use of wālidayya, “my parents,” in that final prayer. Wālid denotes the true father from whom one is born, whereas ab can designate a grandfather, uncle, stepfather, guardian, or another elder vested with authority. The Qur’an itself calls Abraham and Ishmael the ābāʾ of Jacob, though Abraham was his grandfather and Ishmael his uncle; it likewise calls Abraham and Isaac Joseph’s ābāʾ although they were his great-grandfather and grandfather. Thus Azar was not Abraham’s biological father, but someone to whom ab and the address “O my father” properly applied. The Qur’an does not name Abraham’s real father; traditions and the Old Testament support the name Tārikh.

The commentary therefore finds no exegetical need to resolve speculative linguistic, traditional, or historical disputes over whether Azar was a proper name, a nickname, or an idol’s name. Most of the proposed constructions—relocating words, deleting them, or supplying unstated phrases—lack proof and disturb the verse’s apparent meaning and context.

It rejects the claim that the Qur’an, because it pursues guidance through storytelling, may employ popular but unverified, incomplete, imaginary, or false narratives. Although storytelling may use such devices, the Qur’an is neither a history book nor a collection of fictional tales. It is Divine Speech, protected from falsehood, which guides by truth to truth; God does not advance truth through falsehood or guidance through misguidance. An interpreter seeking the Qur’an’s purpose must consequently treat its speech, reports, and explanations as true and factual, in accordance with its own claim to guide people to their real success. This is not merely an appeal to inherited belief or an instruction to deny every perceived difficulty without inquiry; it is the necessary methodological consequence of interpreting a book that presents itself as God’s truthful guidance.

Accordingly, apparent discrepancy or conflict must be addressed through the Qur’an itself. The verse, “Do they not then mediate on the Qur’an? And if it were from any other than Allah, they would have found in it many a discrepancy;”(4:82), indicates that some verses remove the ambiguity of others: the interpreter must make verses explain, support, and speak for one another. The Qur’an’s aim is guidance, not the provision of genealogies, dates, locations, political and social circumstances, or the other details required by historical research or fiction. Questions of establishing its divine origin, comparing it with the Bible or Avesta, or measuring it against historical, natural, mathematical, philosophical, or social disciplines are separate from Qur’anic exegesis and must not be merged into it. This does not mean that the Qur’an neglects useful knowledge or forbids inquiry into the universe, past peoples, and social conditions; rather, it repeatedly praises knowledge, reflection, deliberation, and meditation.

On the phrase, “Do you take idols for gods? Surely I see you and your people in manifest error,” al-Rāghib, as cited by the commentary, defines ṣanam as a body of silver, copper, or wood worshipped to gain nearness to God, with aṣnām as its plural. These materials are illustrative rather than exhaustive: idols may be fashioned from any suitable material, including stone and clay, or may be pictures. They may represent intangible objects of belief, such as a god of heaven, earth, or justice, or visible things such as the sun and moon. The people of Abraham had both kinds and worshipped them to approach their gods and, through them, Almighty God.

For Al-Mizan, this exposes the manifest irrationality of idolatry: a human being gives the utmost humility due from a creature to its Creator to an image that the human being has made. The worshipper, possessing knowledge and power, bows before a product that lacks knowledge, hearing, sight, power, benefit, and harm. Abraham’s bare use of aṣnām signals their insignificance and abasement: they are things made by their worshippers’ own hands and devoid of the most evident attributes of divinity. His question therefore means that taking such insignificant, powerless products as gods is manifest error in contrast to the greatness proper to God.

This statement is a concise form of Abraham’s arguments and his first argument for monotheism: he first challenged his father and those associated with him over idol worship. His argument against worshipping the star, moon, and sun came afterward. His argument with the king occurred later still, after his mission and opposition to paganism and Sabianism had become known and after the breaking of the idols.
verses.75:
Al-Mizan holds that “thus” refers back to Abraham’s declaration that his sire and people were in manifest error: God had already shown him the Kingdom of the heavens and earth, by which he argued against their idols. The following account of the night and the star continues this state of divine support. Thus, “We show,” though expressed in the present/future form, concerns a past event, as in And W e desired to bestow a favour upon those who were deemed weak in the land…(28:5). The commentary therefore rejects the view that the clause is parenthetical or that Abraham was first shown the Kingdom only when he saw the star.

Al-malakūt, derived from al-mulk, denotes intensified authority or dominion. Human social dominion is conventional, relative, and transferable: it may be granted, seized, or lost. But the deeper and real sense of mulk is inseparable, non-transferable mastery, like a person’s command over his own hearing, sight, and actions. The limbs and their acts subsist through the person; without him, neither they nor their acts would exist. Incomparably, every creature depends upon God in its being, powers, actions, and place within the whole order of the universe. God’s dominion rests on His creation and continued existence of all things; it has no partner, cannot cease, and cannot be delegated so that He becomes unnecessary. This is the sense indicated by Say: “O Allah, M aster of the Kingdom!”(3:26), Allah’s is the Kingdom of the heavens and the earth…(5:120), and Blessed is He in whose hand is the Kingdom, and He has power over all things; who created death and life…W ho created the seven heavens one above another… (67:1–3).

The commentary explains God’s Kingdom of every thing through His command, “Be,” by which things exist: malakūt is God’s exclusive relation to their existence and survival. Since this creative and sustaining relation admits no partner, neither lordship nor the management of affairs can belong independently to another. Reflection on this Kingdom therefore leads to tawḥīd, as in Do they not consider the Kingdom of the heavens and the earth and whatever things Allah has created, and that may be their doom shall have drawn nigh; what announcement would they then believe in after this?(7:185).

To show Abraham the Kingdom was to guide him to see every thing’s dependence on God. He consequently recognized that hand-made, falsely named idols could neither own nor nourish their makers, and that changing celestial bodies which appear and disappear could not govern the universe. The lām in li-yakūna is explanatory and is joined to an implied purpose: God showed him this and other matters so that he might be among those who are sure.

Al-yaqīn is knowledge wholly free of doubt. The verse probably refers to certainty concerning God’s signs, like that of those described in And We made of them Imāms to guide by Our command as they were patient, and they were certain of Our signs(32:24); such certainty brings conviction in God’s Beautiful Names and great attributes. The Prophet is likewise described as being shown divine signs in Glory be to Him Who made His servant to go on a night from the Sacred Mosque to the remote mosque of which We have blessed the precincts, so that We may show to him some of Our signs…(17:1) and The eye did not dazzle, nor did it exceed the limit. Certainly he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord,(53:17–18). But God’s Exalted Essence lies beyond the reach of doubt and even knowledge, and can only be acknowledged with submission. One effect of certain knowledge of the signs is that, to the extent God wills, the material veil is lifted from created realities, as indicated by Nay! If you had known with knowledge of certainty, you should most certainly have seen the hell (102:5–6) and the witnessing of the record in ‘Illiyīn by those brought near to God (83:18–21).
verses.76:
Al-Mizan explains that the night’s “over-shadowing” means that darkness covered Abraham, not merely that the sun had set. The episode continues the preceding account of God’s showing Abraham the Kingdom of the heavens and the earth: through that showing he had refuted idol-worship, and it continued when, in the darkness, he saw the star.

The indefiniteness of kawkab does not identify the particular star because the argument applies to every rising and setting star; yet Abraham was not pointing to an arbitrary star among countless stars. The context indicates that it was a particular object of his people’s worship. The commentary considers it most likely to have been Venus. The Sabaeans, unlike peoples who revered fixed stars, sanctified the planets and assigned worldly affairs to them. Since the moon and sun are separately mentioned, and Mercury is seldom visible, the star would be one of Venus, Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn. Venus especially fits the sequence: it can appear shortly after sunset in the west, set after a short time, and be followed by the moon’s rising. Some narrations from the Imāms of Ahl al-Bayt likewise identify the star as Venus. On this account, Abraham saw Venus in the latter half of the lunar month, while people worshipped it through devotion, prayer, and sacrifice.

By saying, “This is my Lord,” Abraham did not mean that the planet was the Creator and Originator of the heavens and earth. Rabb means the owner and manager of what belongs to him. God is not a body, does not occupy space, and cannot be pointed out as an object; Abraham’s prior knowledge of God and His signs had already shown him that God transcends bodily form, image, and limitation. Idolaters and Sabaeans did not necessarily posit equals to God in creation. Rather, they attributed the management of particular affairs or creatures to beings that were themselves created by, or dependent on, God: gods of beauty, justice, fertility, particular peoples, tribes, rulers, or other domains.

Thus Abraham’s inquiry concerned whether the Lord who manages affairs was God Himself, the sole Originator, or a created being to whom management had been delegated. His eventual declaration of freedom from the partners associated with God and of turning wholly to the Originator concerns the rejection of polytheism, not the proof of God’s existence. He tests the star, then the moon and sun, as possible managers of the universe and of human affairs.

The commentary first presents Abraham’s words as a genuine hypothesis entertained before decisive proof.
