A person passing from ignorance to religious discernment must seek the truth, examine whether there is a Creator and whether He is one or has partners, and test such propositions against the signs in the universe. Until proof is complete, he remains in a state of consideration rather than settled belief. Abraham’s statements concerning the star, moon, and sun would therefore not be firm polytheism but propositions considered in the course of seeking sound faith; there is no blame in this movement from lack of distinction toward full knowledge. Human beings generally acquire the capacity and obligation for true belief and good action gradually, after reaching discernment and maturity, though exceptional individuals such as Jesus and John (Yaḥyā) displayed knowledge before the normal age.

However, Al-Mizan then argues from Abraham’s speech to his father—where he says that knowledge has come to him and calls his Lord affectionate—that Abraham already knew that God alone managed his affairs. On this reading, “This is my Lord” is an argumentative procedure: he temporarily speaks as though he shares his opponents’ premise, then demonstrates its weakness. Such a method is more likely to restrain their prejudice and bring them to hear the proof.

His rejection of the setting star refutes its lordship because a body that sets is cut off from those over whom it supposedly exercises management. Lordship creates a real relation between Lord and servant, and this relation entails love: the dependent is naturally drawn to the one on whom he depends. But what perishes, changes, disappears, and loses the beauty for which it is loved cannot be a true object of love or a lord. The Lord must be ever-living and beyond such alteration. The argument may mean either that Abraham does not love the star because it sets, and therefore cannot worship it, or that its setting explains why it lacks the love inseparable from lordship. The context apparently rests on the latter point. A narration from Imām al-Ṣādiq says, “Is religion anything but love?”

The same quality of rising and setting can invalidate the moon’s and sun’s lordship. Abraham’s repetition may reflect either his earlier lack of knowledge that they also set, or the presence of distinct groups devoted to each celestial body. Finally, his use of al-āfilīyn, a form used for intelligent beings, subtly indicates that what lacks perception and reason cannot deserve lordship. This accords with his challenges to worshipping what neither hears, sees, benefits, nor harms: God must possess intelligence, knowledge, and power.
verses.77:
Al-Mizan explains al-Buzūgh as rising. Abraham’s words, “This is my Lord,” concerning the moon are spoken in the manner of temporarily going along with the belief of others. When the moon sets, the same proof that refuted the star’s lordship applies: what sets is unfit for lordship, for Abraham has said, “I do not love the setting ones.” Thus, had he persisted in affirming the moon as lord, he would have joined those in error who believed in its lordship.

The commentary infers that, just as some people held the star to be lord, others held the moon to be lord; the following declaration, “O my people! Surely I am clear of what you set up (with Allah),”(6:78), also indicates this. Abraham was seeking divine guidance and awaiting his Lord’s grace in the form of sound belief and an indisputable view, whether the account is taken literally as a genuine search or rhetorically as an initial acceptance of a hypothesis in order to expose its flaw.

He was nevertheless certain that he had a Lord who managed his guidance and all his affairs. His inquiry, whether real or enacted for argument, was to identify whether this Lord was Himself the Creator of the heavens and earth or one of His creatures. Once the setting of the star and moon showed their incapacity for such lordship, he looked to his Lord to guide him to Himself and deliver him from the error of the misguided.
verses.78:
Al-Mizan explains that “Then when” joins Abraham’s statement about the sun to the preceding argument concerning the star and moon. His words, “This is my Lord,” are not an actual confession of the sun’s lordship, but either a hypothesis or a provisional assent intended to disprove the view. Since the star and moon had already failed as possible lords, he calls the sun “the greatest” as the final and strongest hypothesis; when it sets, he declares, “O my people! Surely I am clear of what you set up (with Allah).”

The commentary holds that Abraham’s use of the masculine demonstrative hādhā for the grammatically feminine sun indicates that he did not yet clearly distinguish the thing to which he pointed. A person who sees a distant or indistinct form and cannot tell whether it is male or female, living or inanimate, may use hādhā. Probably Abraham had only then emerged from isolation among his uncle and people and, seeing the star, moon, and sun as shining lamps without complete knowledge of them, said of each: “This is my Lord.” His delaying the repudiation of the star until it set may indicate that he initially supposed it to be lord, for otherwise he would have rejected it at once, as he rejected idols. It is also possible that he waited until its setting to establish a fact perceptible to his people, just as he broke the idols except their greatest one so that their incapacity would be evident.

Al-Mizan rejects several grammatical explanations of the masculine hādhā. Some exegetes say it refers not to the sun but to an understood masculine expression such as “this celestial bright body.” Although such usage is possible, it needs a reason; otherwise feminine terms could arbitrarily be made masculine. Others maintain that the demonstrative follows the masculine predicate, “my Lord” or “the greatest.” The commentary replies that those who recognized feminine gods could have said rabbah or Ālihatī, so the same alleged rule could equally require the feminine. Moreover, the elative form in “greater” is gender-neutral when predicative and cannot explain a masculine demonstrative.

The explanation that the masculine protects the divine from femininity is also rejected, because the relevant polytheists did not regard femininity as beneath divinity: Babylonian religion included female deities, and some Arab polytheists called angels God’s daughters and gave their gods female names, as reflected in: They did not call besides Him on any thing but females;(4:117). Nor does the report that Abraham’s people considered the sun a male god with a wife named Anuunit justify changing the feminine grammatical form of “sun.” Abraham himself uses a feminine pronoun for the sun in his challenge to Nimrod: So surely Allah brings the sun from the east, then bring it (you) from the west; (2:258).

Likewise, Al-Mizan finds unpersuasive the claim that Abraham spoke Syriac, whose speakers allegedly used masculine demonstratives without gender distinction, and that the Qur’an preserved this wording. Qur’anic quotations of speech normally follow the grammar appropriate to their meanings despite differences of language, and Abraham’s other Qur’anic arguments and prayers observe feminine forms where required; his feminine reference to the sun in (2:258) confirms this. The commentary considers still more surprising the claim that Abraham, Ishmael, and Hājar spoke ancient Arabic. Its proponents appeal to alleged early Arab domination of Chaldea and Egypt, an alleged Arab identity and contemporaneity of Hammurabi, and reports of Abraham’s settlement of Ishmael and Hājar in Mecca, his visits to them, his building of the Kaʿbah with Ishmael, and his dealings with Jurham. Al-Mizan answers that proximity, migration, or political dominance does not prove a change of language; Egypt and the Chaldean-Assyrian lands had their own languages, though contact may exchange individual words. The available historical evidence, Babylonian remains, and the Code of Hammurabi do not corroborate Hammurabi’s alleged contemporaneity with Abraham; proposed dates for Hammurabi differ from Abraham’s approximate date, and Hammurabi was an idolater who invoked gods to preserve his laws. Nor do Abraham’s settlement of his family in Arabia, the Kaʿbah, propagation of God’s religion, or communication with Arabs prove that he spoke Arabic.

The wording “then when” also indicates that the moon had set before Abraham saw the rising sun. The commentary says this could occur in autumn or winter at northern latitudes, during long nights in the latter half of a lunar month, especially if the moon was in a southern constellation such as the Archer or Capricorn. It further infers that the earlier star was Venus, first seen descending in the west, then setting before the moon rose in the east.

On this reconstruction, Abraham disputed with his people about idols in the daytime until night overtook him. Seeing Venus and those who worshiped it, he provisionally joined their claim of its lordship and watched until it set. During that long night the moon rose; after it set, he rejected its lordship, continued seeking his Lord, and sought refuge from error until sunrise. The sun appeared larger than the star and moon, so he again provisionally accepted its lordship on the ground of its greater size, even though the falsity of the other two claims was already apparent and they too were luminous heavenly bodies. When the sun set, he renounced its lordship and his people’s polytheism, then affirmed the lordship and divinity of God as the Originator of the heavens and earth: “Surely I have turned my face, being upright, wholly to Him—that is, being submissive to the Divinity—W ho originated the heavens and the earth,—without any deviation to the right or the left—and I am not of the polytheists,”—by associating anything from His creation and invention to Him in worship and submission, (6:79).

Al-Mizan argues that the intervening statement, And thus did We show Abraham the Kingdom of the heavens and the earth and so that he might be of those who are sure, establishes that Abraham derived his arguments from what God showed him of that Kingdom and received sure conviction in his heart. His argument, including “I do not love the setting ones,” is therefore demonstrative proof arising from certainty.

In response to Rāshīd Riḍā’s apparent view that Abraham merely made a popular allusion—namely, that star-worshipers worship something hidden from and unaware of them—Al-Mizan maintains that the argument is demonstrative, not merely rhetorical. The wording about the Kingdom shows that it rests on Abraham’s certain vision of God’s signs. More importantly, the argument rests on love and the lack of it, not simply on setting. Human beings worship their lord because he manages their affairs and supplies life, sustenance, health, wealth, safety, power, knowledge, and every need; by nature they love what they need and the one who provides it, seeking benefit, protection from harm, or both. Human nature does not attach itself to what has no permanence, unless greed or desire distracts it with passing pleasure. Thus something that disappears and has neither stability nor permanence does not merit love or attachment. The God whom one worships must be one whom one can love and not lose; consequently, the setting celestial bodies do not deserve divinity. This proof is accessible both to ordinary people and scholars.

The commentary further says that this view confuses rising (al-buzūgh) with appearance (al-ẓuhūr). Rising, which means appearing after concealment, is itself incompatible with divinity and is not the basis of the argument; asserting that rising is suitable to lordship because the Lord must be manifest does not explain why Abraham reasoned from setting (al-ufūl) rather than rising. Al-Zamakhsharī’s answer in al-Kashshāf—that setting provides a clearer argument because it involves disappearance and concealment, whereas both rising and setting are changes—is consequently redundant: the point is not change as such but the absence of love for that which sets and disappears.

Abraham’s proof, moreover, negates the lordship of the three bodies in the sense of managing the world and human life, not lordship in the absolute sense of creating and sustaining all things. Star-worshipers and idolaters did not deny the one Creator, God, who has no partner. The theological explanations that make setting prove contingency and dependence on the Necessary Being, or movement and dependence on the unmoved First Mover, are demonstrative in themselves but address atheists who deny the Creator. They do not answer the Sabaeans and other star-worshipers whom Abraham addressed, since such people could regard heavenly bodies as dependent, created, perpetual, and in continual motion, while still assigning them worldly governance. In addition, ‘setting’ does not linguistically mean contingency, createdness, change, or motion; it may be used to infer those things, but its own meaning is disappearance after visibility and concealment after appearance. This is incompatible with divinity, though compatible with lesser lordship in the sense admitted by those worshipers.

Al-Mizan also notes a difficulty in explaining the argument through physical disappearance alone. God is absent from human perception without change in Him or a real disappearance after appearance; one may say that this is due to human distraction, not a limitation in God. But this does not distinguish the heavenly bodies, since their apparent daily disappearance—especially that of the sun—is likewise from human perspective: the earth’s rotation turns people away from their direction, so it is in reality people who pass away from them. Hence treating the observed setting itself as a proof based on contingency or motion does not establish the intended point.

The commentary cites al-Rāzī’s attempt to combine these interpretations. Al-Rāzī says that rising and setting alike demonstrate createdness through motion, but prophetic proof must be clear to every level of understanding. The learned connect ufūl with contingency and dependence upon the Omnipotent Being; average people connect it with movement and the need of every moving, created being for the Eternal and Omnipotent; ordinary people see a setting star’s fading radiance and declining power, like an abdicated ruler, and deny it divinity. He further says Abraham argued against astrologers, who regarded a star as powerful when rising toward the zenith and weak near the western horizon; Abraham therefore used their own belief in its declining effectiveness to expose the defect in its lordship.

Al-Mizan finds no support for al-Rāzī’s elaborate classifications or explanations in the verse itself. They do not refute the belief of Sabaeans and star-worshipers, who did not make celestial bodies the supreme, unlimited God, but considered them dependent beings whose motion governs the earth. Al-Rāzī apparently recognized this objection and tried unsuccessfully to escape it by further elaboration. His argument from movement is also incomplete, for movement proves the createdness of a moving entity only with respect to its quality of movement, not in itself.

Abraham arranged his reasoning according to the signs of the Kingdom of the heavens and earth which God showed him and according to occasions for speaking with his father and people. He used perceptible objects either because he had not previously observed the celestial bodies’ daily changes or because he wished to argue from what his audience could observe. Thus he called each bright rising body “my Lord” and repudiated it when it set. The fact that he began with a star rather than the sun, although he had been with his people during the preceding day, may be because the daytime allowed only his argument about idols and discussion continued until night; other possibilities are clouded skies, gatherings for worship and sacrifice only at sunrise, or his desire to establish the proof through direct observation.

The preceding statement, “If my Lord had not guided me, I should certainly be of the erring people;” shows that guidance comes from God and that, if left merely to himself, a human being would fall into error without his Lord’s guidance. This accords with: …and were it not for Allah’s grace upon you and His mercy, not one of you would have ever been pure… (24:21), and Surely you cannot guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He pleases… (28:56). When misguidance is attributed to God, however, it means punitive misguidance for disregarding divine guidance, not an initial misguidance imposed by Him.

Finally, Al-Mizan defines ufūl as losing something after having found it. It is incompatible with the love that warrants worship of the beloved. If setting is repellent in material things because it implies cessation, death, destruction, and passing away, it decisively refutes polytheism and idol worship. The argument also reaches those idolaters who posit lofty, immaterial, luminous gods beyond body and movement: they still acknowledge that such beings perish before the Eternal Light and are humble under Divine Power. Their love, therefore, should attach only to the One who manages them, not to the various gods.
verses.79:
Al-Mizan explains that, after Abraham progressively rejected association with God—first by declaring that he did not love the setting ones, then by acknowledging that without his Lord’s guidance he would have been among the erring, and finally by disavowing what his people associated with God—he affirms the absolute oneness of lordship and worship: “Surely I have turned my face, being upright, wholly to Him Who originated the heavens and the earth, and I am not of the polytheists.”

According to al-Rāghib’s lexical account, al-faṭr originally denotes a splitting or rending; faṭara, when attributed to God’s creation, means that He creates a thing in its particular form. From it comes al-fiṭrah, nature: the innate disposition through which human beings know the Supreme and are able to recognize the true religion. Al-Ḥanf means turning away from error to rightfulness, whereas al-janf is turning from rightfulness toward error. Thus ḥanīfan means that Abraham turns exclusively to God while departing from every alleged partner.

“Turning my face” signifies exclusive worshipful attention to God. The dependent servant must attach himself wholly to his Lord, pray to Him, and refer all his affairs to Him; turning the face therefore indicates worship, prayer, and concentration upon God. Abraham identifies the One worshipped by the unique and undeniable attribute that He originated the heavens and the earth: everything is connected to Him in its origination and creation. His statement accordingly establishes servitude to God and rejects every partner, closely corresponding to lā ilāha illa ‘llāh—there is no god but God.

The choice of al-Fāṭir, rather than other terms for Creator, points to the religion of fiṭrah. The Qur’an describes the true faith as Abraham’s pure religion and as the religion rooted in the unchanging nature and creation of the human being. Religion is the path to real success, and real success is the end for which a being has been created and furnished with means of perfection. No creature can attain that end by a way contrary to its created constitution and equipment. True religion must therefore accord with fiṭrah; God does not guide a person, or any creature charged with religion, to a blessed end without creating and equipping it for that end. In God’s sight, religion is Islam: submission to God according to the guidance grounded in His creation.
verses.80:
Al-Mizan explains that this verse is the second part of Abraham’s argument: after he had initiated the discussion, his people disputed with him when he renounced their gods. Though their precise objection is not stated, Abraham’s declaration, “I do not fear in any way those that you set up with Him,” shows that they urged worship of the idols through fear of their displeasure and power. Idol worship arises from fear or hope, but fear is the stronger motive: people generally regard the material advantages they possess as their own acquisition or inheritance, so promises affect them less than threats. The Qur’an likewise mentions the prophets’ warnings more often than their good tidings, although both belong to their mission.

The people’s appeal had two connected claims: it denied the exclusive lordship of God and affirmed the lordship of their gods. Abraham answers both. “Do you dispute with me respecting Allah? And He has guided me indeed” does not merely mean that, having found God, he no longer needs to investigate. On deeper reflection, it is itself an argument: God guided Abraham by teaching him the proof that other alleged lords are false and that God alone is Lord. Guidance to the Lord is an act proper to lordship; had God not been Abraham’s Lord, the true lord would have guided him instead. Nor can this guidance to reject the idols be ascribed to one of the idols, because nothing guides someone to what destroys its own claim and existence.

The idolaters might nevertheless have alleged, as the people of ‘Ād alleged of Hūd, that one of their gods had maliciously misled Abraham through anger at him. Abraham’s reply, “and I do not fear in any way those that you set up with Him, unless my Lord pleases,” refutes this doubt and independently disproves their gods’ lordship. They threaten him with harm from associate-gods, but he does not fear them because they are creatures under God’s management and possess no benefit or harm for him. Thus their appeal to fear collapses.

“Unless my Lord pleases” is a hypothetical argument. If Abraham were to fear those gods, the fear would not proceed from them, for they have no power; it would be from his Lord’s will. That fear would therefore prove God’s lordship and unity, requiring exclusive worship of Him, rather than prove the lordship of the associate-gods. “My Lord comprehends all things in His knowledge” supplies the ground: God knows every good and evil occurring in His Kingdom, which He created for sound purposes. He cannot know of something beneficial or harmful and be silent about it, neither preventing it nor permitting it. Any fear arising in Abraham would thus arise by God’s will and permission and would still testify against the lordship of others. “Will you not then mind?” rebukes them to reflect upon what intelligence and pure nature show.

Accordingly, “I do not fear” both follows from “And He has guided me indeed” and forms a complete proof in its own right. The exception, “unless my Lord pleases,” does not concede that the idols could cause fear: even a supposed fear would be from God’s will. The comprehensiveness of His knowledge shows that nothing occurs in His Kingdom apart from His will, management, and sustaining. The verse’s final question indicates that this argument rests on pure nature.

Al-Mizan rejects several alternative explanations. Most exegetes take “And He has guided me indeed” to mean simply that Abraham needs no further argument after guidance. The context does not support this, because Abraham is actively arguing; the clause must itself be an argument for monotheism.

Some explain “unless my Lord pleases” to mean that Abraham would fear the idols if God gave them life and power to harm or benefit. Although this is near the intended meaning, it wrongly attributes benefit and harm to associate-gods, whereas ultimately these come only from God. Further, proving that such gods were created would not move idolaters, who do not deny that their gods are God’s creatures; even their belief in the eternity of some gods does not, in their view, make those gods independent of the truly Eternal God. Another interpretation makes the exception a general fear that God might create as initial harm or punishment for Abraham’s sins. Al-Mizan calls this arbitrary.

Explanations of “My Lord comprehends all things in His knowledge” as mere praise after the argument, or as an implicit criticism that the idols lack knowledge, are also inadequate: if the point were praise or contrast with the idols, God’s power would be more relevant than knowledge. Likewise, to say that Abraham praises God’s knowledge because He spared him distress, and therefore acts only beneficially, calls rather for mention of wisdom; and to say that God knew beforehand that the idols might harm him calls for power and wisdom as well as knowledge.

One commentator makes the clause a denial of all influence, including intercession: because God knows everything, no intercessor can inform Him of something unknown and thereby affect His acts. He appeals to …who is he that can intercede with Him but by His Permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they cannot comprehend anything out of His Knowledge except what He pleases… (2:255). Al-Mizan answers that denying such influence requires not comprehensive knowledge alone but absolute power and will; will is an attribute of action, not of person as that interpreter assumes. Since this verse mentions only the breadth of knowledge, that interpretation is not established. Nor do the verses on intercession negate intercession: they affirm intervention in causes by God’s permission. The Qur’an throughout confirms the general principle of causality, so causes in the visible world cannot be denied.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan explains that Abraham exposes a contradiction in the idolaters’ position: they demand that he fear idols, although there is no proof that these lesser or greater idols independently harm or benefit, while they themselves do not fear God by associating partners with Him. Since creation, the Kingdom, and command belong to God, any partner whose worship were obligatory would have to be made known by God Himself, through revelation or tangible proof. No such proof exists. Thus Abraham’s question, “which then of the two parties is surer of security, if you know?” concludes that he, rather than they, has grounds for security.

The clause, “…for which He has not sent down to you any authority,” is not meant to allow that God might actually authorize partners for Himself. It is a hypothetical form of argument, like telling one who threatens another with a superstition that he has no evidence for his claim. Its logical form is: if God had sent down proof that idols could harm, fear of them would be valid; but He has sent down no proof; therefore such fear is invalid. The first premise has no reality, so the clause need not be taken as sarcasm or as suggesting that divine authorization could be a condition for valid idol worship.

The commentary notes that the bā in lam yunazzil bihi means “with” or “for.” Abraham calls himself and the idolaters “the two parties,” rather than saying “you and me,” to avoid stirring prejudice or egoism and to make clear that their division concerns a fundamental, irreconcilable tenet of faith.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan holds that this verse is Abraham’s own answer to his preceding question about which of the two parties is more secure. Because the answer is evident and undisputed, he need not wait for his opponents to reply. Their admission in the account of the broken idols confirms the point: when challenged to ask the idols if they could speak, they said, “Surely you yourselves are the unjust,” before admitting, “Certainly you know that they do not speak.”(21:63–65) The context does not support taking the verse as the people’s statement or as God’s independent judgement between the parties.

Its repeated nominal constructions emphatically establish that believers who do not mix faith with injustice certainly possess security and guidance. Security and right guidance are fruits of faith, on the condition that it is not so mixed. al-Labs means covering or concealing; thus the mixing of injustice with faith does not eradicate faith’s root, but covers it, nullifies its effect, and prevents its proper result from appearing.

Al-Mizan explains al-ẓulm as departure from the equilibrium of justice. Though the word is indefinite in a negative construction and therefore general, the verse concerns only that injustice which damages faith and prevents its beneficial effects, not every thing that may broadly be called injustice. The term originally denotes violation of another’s social rights—life, honour, or property—but was extended to violations of law and custom, sins, disobedience, and even acts done through mistake, forgetfulness, or ignorance, as well as neglect of advice or health-preserving means. Yet acts that are not sins or disobedience, including mistaken, forgotten, or ignorant acts, do not impair faith’s function of bringing one near to blessedness and success through God’s pleasure. The verse therefore makes the security bestowed by faith conditional on freedom from sins and disobedience that obstruct its effect.

Intentional sin, however, has degrees according to the believer’s standpoint. For one standing between monotheism and polytheism, who recognizes the Creator, Sustainer, and the One to whom human life requires submission, the decisive injustice is shirk: ascribing partners such as idols, stars, or other gods to God. For one who has attained belief in God’s oneness, the relevant injustice includes major sins—such as distressing parents, consuming an orphan’s property, killing an innocent person, adultery, and intoxicants. The manifestation of such a person’s faith depends on avoiding them; if major sins are avoided, God promises forgiveness of minor sins: If you avoid the great sins which you are forbidden, W e will expiate from you your (small) sins and cause you to enter an honourable place of entering; (4:31). Punishment for major sins deprives one of faith’s result, but, unlike the punishment for shirk, is not everlasting and may end when its term ends or through intercession.

At a higher degree of righteousness and awareness of the Lord, injustice includes doing disliked acts (makrūh), omitting recommended acts (mustaḥab), and indulging in permissible acts (mubāh). At further degrees, it includes neglecting one’s noble traits and spiritual capacities, and then whatever obstructs love of God and seeking nearness to Him. At every level, faith grants security and repels misfortune only when the believer avoids the injustice corresponding to that level.

Thus ẓulm is general, while its application differs with the level of īmān. In Abraham’s immediate debate with idolaters, it means polytheism, and the resulting security is from perpetual misery and everlasting chastisement. Independently of that immediate context, however, the verse teaches generally that security and guidance arise from faith unclouded by every injustice that neutralizes its effect. The īmān in the verse is general belief in divinity, capable of being preserved or destroyed by what accompanies it; qualified by the absence of injustice, it becomes belief in God’s divinity and rejection of associate-gods. The dispute is not with atheists: both parties acknowledge a lord, but Abraham’s belief in the Creator and Governor rests on proof, while the idolaters’ belief in created associate-gods, from whom they seek protection from evil despite their inability to harm or benefit, has neither proof nor divine authorization. Accordingly, faith here concerns divinity rather than mere belief in a Creator; security is generally security from the misery of sins and disobedience, and guidance is freedom from misguidance, although both are contextually applied to shirk. The scope of ẓulm likewise varies with faith’s levels.

Al-Mizan then rejects a commentator’s broader construction. That commentator maintained that complete freedom from every injustice toward oneself, one’s faith, worldly and religious actions, or other beings brings security from both religious punishment and worldly consequences such as poverty and illness; he also said that no accountable person can be wholly safe from all fears, except those of the highest perfection. Alternatively, he restricted the verse to freedom from shirk and hence security from eternal punishment, while believers remain between fear and hope in this world. He appealed to a report that the Companions were distressed by the verse and asked the Prophet who had not wronged himself, whereupon the Prophet said that the injustice meant shirk.

The commentary raises four objections. First, the Companions understood injustice as sins and disobedience, whereas the commentator’s proposed general injustice is wider. Second, the verse is not about every consequence of injustice, especially things that are not sins, such as inadvertently eating harmful food. It makes faith its subject, conditions it by absence of injustice, and identifies security and guidance as its effects; it does not make injustice the subject. Therefore, the claim that this broad interpretation is correct in itself is invalid. Third, admitting that no accountable person enjoys comprehensive security from every fear shows that the alleged general security has no actual application. Fourth, restricting the general wording of ẓulm to shirk is also unwarranted without an indication. Shirk is indeed one application that blocks faith’s effect, but a general expression cannot simply be reduced to that particular case. Nor does the reported Prophetic statement clearly establish that shirk is the verse’s literal and exclusive meaning; this is to be examined further in the Traditions section.
verses.83:
Al-Mizan explains that the distant demonstrative tilka, “that,” magnifies Abraham’s argument: it is a conclusive argument grounded in nature and drawn from its premises.

“We exalt in ranks whom We please” means that God grants ranks of moral perfection and true virtue. These include attainable qualities such as knowledge and piety, and divinely bestowed gifts such as prophethood, messengership, and sustenance. Although darajāt is indefinite and general, the context specifies ranks of knowledge and guidance: God exalted Abraham through guidance, showing him the Kingdom of the heavens and the earth, and granting him certainty, decisive proof, and knowledge. “Allah will exalt those of you who believe, and those who are given knowledge, in high rank… (58:11).”

The closing words, “surely your Lord is Wise, Knowing,” stress that granting Abraham these arguments, like the arguments earlier given to the Messenger of God, proceeded from God’s wisdom and knowledge. The shift from the first person to the third person concerning Abraham consoles the Prophet and confirms the preceding discussion.
verses.84: Al-Mizan says that Isaac and Jacob were given and each guided; Noah was guided before, as were David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron among his descendants. Thus are good-doers rewarded.
verses.85: Zachariah, John, Jesus, and Elias were all among the righteous.
verses.86: Al-Mizan says that Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot were each preferred above the nations.
verses.87: Al-Mizan says that God chose some of their fathers, descendants, and brethren, and guided them to a straight path.
verses.88: Al-Mizan says that this is God’s guidance, by which He guides whom He wills among His servants; had they associated others with Him, their deeds would have become ineffectual.
verses.89: Al-Mizan says that they received the book, judgment, and prophethood; if these disbelieve in it, God has entrusted it to a people who do not disbelieve in it.
verses.90:
Al-Mizan explains these verses as a continuation of Abraham’s account, but not merely as a catalogue of favors bestowed on him and other prophets. They show the blessings that follow acceptance of divine guidance and the innate monotheism embedded in human fiṭrah. They also show that God has continuously preserved monotheism through a connected chain of guided persons; otherwise satanic desire could wholly prevent human nature from realizing its purpose, rendering creation purposeless. The verses distinguish divine guidance by God’s choosing, the straight path, the book, judgment, and prophethood.

In (6:84), the advance placement of kullan, “each,” means that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were each independently guided, rather than some receiving guidance only through another. Noah’s earlier guidance shows that this mercy and chain of guidance did not begin with Abraham. Some exegetes take the pronoun in “his descendants” to refer to Noah, since he is the last-mentioned name and Lot and Elias are not Abraham’s descendants; others refer it to Abraham and explain the inclusion of Lot and Elias by taghlīb. The view that “descendants” includes only the six names in this verse, while the names in the next two verses merely add to that phrase, conflicts with the context and flow. “Thus do We reward the good-doers” apparently identifies their exalted divine guidance as the reward; kadhālika indicates its loftiness and magnificence.

In (6:85), Jesus’ inclusion among Noah’s descendants despite his connection being through his mother demonstrates that the children and descendants of a daughter count among one’s own children and descendants. This accords with conclusions drawn from the Qur’anic rules of inheritance and prohibited marriage.

For (6:86), Ishmael apparently means Abraham’s son and Isaac’s brother. Elisha, al-Yasaʿ or al-Laysaʿ, was apparently an Israelite prophet, though the Qur’an gives no account of his story. To be preferred above the nations means, first, superiority over one’s contemporaries through directly receiving God’s special guidance while others receive guidance through such persons. It may also mean preference over people of all times, because they received the guidance inherent in fiṭrah without intermediary. This preference extends to the prophets and to the fathers, descendants, and brethren joined to them, but its criterion is only direct divine guidance, not choosing, the straight path, scripture, judgment, or prophethood. Consequently, the verse cannot prove the prophets’ superiority to angels: if angels or Imams also receive this direct guidance, the prophets are not superior to them in this respect, though they may be superior in other respects.

The named prophets are arranged neither chronologically nor by rank; Noah, Moses, and Jesus occur among others despite their Qur’anically established superiority to the rest. Al-Manār groups David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses, and Aaron as prophets who also held rule or authority; it places Zachariah, John, Jesus, and Elias together for exceptional zuhd; and regards Ishmael, Elisha, Jonah, and Lot as a residual group lacking a common distinction. Al-Mizan rejects the last judgment. Ishmael was distinguished by the trial of sacrifice, his patience, and his partnership with Abraham in building the Kaʿbah; the hajj sacrifice perpetuates remembrance of his ordeal. Jonah underwent the singular trial of being swallowed by the fish. Lot endured migration with Abraham and then the ordeal of a people whose unprecedented indecency ended in their destruction, leaving only his household submitted to God, except his wife. The Qur’an gives no story of Elisha, although some narrations report that he succeeded Elias, performed miracles like those of Jesus, and faced a people afflicted by famine and drought. Thus the first six form a group marked by rule in addition to messengership, the next four by disinterest in worldly adornment, and the last four by distinct great trials and qualities. Al-Mizan finds no proof for al-Manār’s proposed relative ranking of Moses and Aaron, Job and Joseph, and David and Solomon, nor for treating ṣalāḥ as zuhd.

Verse (6:87) confirms the continuity of guidance by adding the prophets’ fathers, descendants, and brethren. Al-Rāghib defines ijtibāʾ as selected gathering and, when ascribed to God, an exclusive grace yielding blessings without the servant’s effort. Al-Mizan accepts that this accords with Qur’anic usage, but holds that its root sense here is gathering what was dispersed. God gathered these persons from their separate places and then guided them as one to a single path. This suits the theme of an uninterrupted chain of persons guided by the innate divine guidance.

That path is uniform in its times and circumstances, its constituent parts, its callers and followers, and its destination. Its outward laws can differ in breadth, concision, and elaboration according to the capacity of nations, but all rest on the one reality innate to humankind: God’s oneness and exclusive worship. Human faculties, needs, feelings, reason, desire for felicity, and fear of misery remain grounded in a fixed creation, although the forms of life and particular aims change with times. Therefore the religion to which fiṭrah calls is not restricted to one circumstance; its elements do not contradict or invalidate one another because all are nourished by tawḥīd; its guided callers deliver one religion despite differences of elaboration; and its beliefs, ethics, and laws have the one goal of monotheism and worship.

The indefinite ṣirāṭan mustaqīman emphasizes the attribute of straightness rather than a particular named path. It denotes a path wholly consistent and free from discrepancy, because it is founded on the unchanging human constitution and directs humanity toward its existential end. Those guided to it are secure from the perils and slips of the journey: it is based on truth, leads to truth, and does not leave its followers in confusion, sin, disobedience, or wretchedness.

In (6:88), God’s special guidance is the guidance by which He guided these prophets, and true guidance belongs only to Him. Its marks are that a person follows the path of the guided prophets and that his path is an internally consistent whole revolving around tawḥīd, the call of truth, servitude, and taqwá. Paths that accept some messengers but reject others, take some divine commands while abandoning others, or follow desires do not secure human felicity. They depart from fiṭrah into error and injustice, and cannot be God’s guidance, for God neither decrees injustice nor makes it a means to happiness.

God’s guidance is sheer guidance, free from error and leading to unending happiness. Yet a divine gift does not become independent of its Giver as an ordinary transferred possession does. It remains God’s gift only while its recipient adheres to tawḥīd and servitude; no one has standing or security with God except through sheer servitude. Hence even these people’s deeds would have become ineffectual had they committed shirk, the term appropriate here because the passage expounds monotheism.

In (6:89), ulāʾika signals the lofty station of this group. The group as a whole, not every individual, received the book, judgment, and prophethood; scripture was given to only some prophets, such as Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. When “the book” is used generally of prophets, it is a revealed scripture containing laws by which people’s disputes are judged. A book is not essentially sheets written with a pen; its function is to preserve meanings so they may be recalled, and thus it can include what is retained in memory or recited from memory.

The Qur’an uses “book” in three principal ways. First are revealed scriptures, especially those containing religious law. Second are records of human deeds: individual records, records of nations, a record for all humanity, and records distinguished for the wicked and righteous. Third are records of all cosmic events. Among these are an unchanging comprehensive record, perhaps with universal and individual forms, and records subject to effacement and establishment. Fixed lifetimes also belong to this category. The Torah is exceptional in being described as inscribed on tablets.

The root meaning of ḥukm is restraint or prevention. It is applied to authoritative commands because they restrict unconditioned action, to judicial rulings because they end dispute or oppression, and to propositions because they remove uncertainty. It also underlies iḥkām, firmness and compactness that resist dissolution, and the contrast of decisive muḥkam with ambiguous mutashābih. In social and practical matters, ḥukm includes rules such as obligation, prohibition, permissibility, recommendation, and disapproval, as well as rules concerning ownership, authority, guardianship, and related relations. As an act, it can mean legislating a law, issuing judicial or legal verdicts, or exercising political rule.

Because ḥukm occurs beside “the book” here, it apparently means qaḍāʾ: the prophets received legal rules and the office of judging people by them. It may, however, have a broader meaning. Prophethood is the divinely granted reception of news from the unseen, concerning realities such as divine unity, angels, and the Last Day. The book, judgment, and prophethood are accordingly fruits of the guidance that gathered the prophets: it guides them to the straight path, gives knowledge of divine laws, establishes authority to judge by them, and informs them of unseen realities.

God’s own ḥukm may be His creative decree, inseparable from the existence of what He brings into being; His legislative command; or the execution of His promise and judgment. When attributed to prophets, it means their God-given legal judgment, and some usages may also imply legislative authority. For non-prophets, the Qur’an recognizes judgment by God’s revelation but condemns legislation independently of it.

“These” who disbelieve refers to deniers of the Prophet’s call, certainly including Meccan disbelievers. The pronoun in “disbelieve in it” can refer to the preceding guidance, understood as hidāyah, but more plausibly refers to the book, judgment, and prophethood as fruits and definitions of that guidance. The indefinite qawman marks the importance of the people entrusted with it.

Al-Mizan examines and rejects the proposed identifications of this people. They cannot simply be the preceding prophets, because the description “who are not disbelievers” is present-continuous although those prophets were not present at revelation; the Prophet himself is addressed only in the following verse. They are not angels, since qawm is not ordinarily applied to angels and their belief would not console the Prophet about his community’s rejection. They are not merely the early Meccan believers or the Muhājirīn, because some apostatized or were hypocrites. Nor are they specifically the Anṣār, the Muhājirīn and Anṣār together, or all Companions: despite their collective merits, some among such groups turned back or were hypocrites, whereas the wording apparently requires complete freedom from disbelief.

The proposal that a community may be called believing although a few members disbelieve would, if valid, extend to all believers in all times rather than a chosen subgroup. Moreover, the Qur’an ordinarily identifies exceptions to a community-wide description where they exist, and none appears here. The claim that the Anṣār were meant because they had not yet rejected the call also fails: at that time they were idolaters, the passage contrasts guidance with shirk, and entrustment must preserve the message rather than assign it to people who have neither accepted nor rejected it. The identification with non-Arabs has the same defects. Nor is it enough to name believers who happen to die steadfast: such accidental continuance gives no guarantee appropriate to God’s entrustment and preservation, while many believers mix faith with shirk and cannot protect this pure guidance from corruption.

The commentary concludes that the verse consoles the Prophet: the unbelief, arrogance, and blind transgression of his people cannot destroy the guidance embodied in the book, judgment, and prophethood, because God has entrusted it to people who certainly do not disbelieve. Their shirk or deviation is inconceivable, for God’s reliance on them to preserve His path cannot involve error. Thus, God knows best, in every age He has one or more servants entrusted with the guidance given through the prophets, preserving religion from loss and guidance from extinction. These are the infallibles, the prophets and their successors, protected from shirk and iniquity. The verse may be extended to righteous believers safeguarded by taqwá, good deeds, and pure faith only if it is established that God has likewise entrusted them with preserving His guidance.

Verse (6:90) adds that those persons are truly guided by God, whose guidance attains its intended end of bringing the guided person to eternal happiness. Dhikrá is a stronger expression of reminder than dhikr, and the reminder’s address to the nations establishes the universality of the Prophet’s mission. Iqtidāʾ means following or emulating, but the Prophet is commanded to follow their guidance, not to follow the prophets themselves. His sharīʿah has abrogated their legal codes and his book supersedes theirs; what remains to follow is the direct divine guidance they received. Calling it “their guidance” honors them, though guidance belongs primarily to God. Therefore the verse does not support the claim that the Prophet and his followers observed earlier prophets’ rituals and laws unless specifically abrogated; that inference would require the command to follow the prophets themselves.

The closing command directs the Prophet to follow that divine guidance, remind all nations of it without seeking any reward, and state this disinterestedness openly. It reassures people, aids the success of the call, and removes grounds for accusation, just as the Qur’an relates of Noah and later prophets.
verses.91: Al-Mizan states: Allah is not duly honored by those who deny revelation to any mortal. They are challenged to say who revealed the Book brought by Moses, a light and guidance which they display selectively while concealing much of it, though they and their fathers were taught what they did not know. The answer is Allah; they are then to be left engrossed in vain discourse.
verses.92: Al-Mizan states: A blessed Book, confirming what preceded it, was revealed so that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it; believers in the hereafter believe in it and guard their prayers.
verses.93: Al-Mizan states: None is more unjust than one who lies against Allah by falsely claiming revelation or claiming he can produce the like of Allah’s revelation. At death, such wrongdoers will be commanded by the angels to surrender their souls and will receive humiliating punishment for speaking untruthfully about Allah and arrogantly rejecting His communications.
verses.94: Al-Mizan states: You have come to Us alone as We first created you, leaving behind what We gave you. Your alleged intercessors and Allah’s associates are absent; your ties with them are cut off, and your assertions have vanished.
verses.95: Al-Mizan states: Allah splits the grain and date-stone to germinate, brings the living from the dead and the dead from the living; how then can people be turned away from Him?
verses.96: Al-Mizan states: Allah splits the dawn, makes the night for rest, and appoints the sun and moon for reckoning—an arrangement of the Mighty, the Knowing.
verses.97: Al-Mizan states: God made the stars so that people may find their way through the darkness of land and sea; He has elaborated these signs for people who know.
verses.98: Al-Mizan states: He produced you from a single soul and gave you a dwelling-place and a repository; He has elaborated the signs for people who discern.
verses.99: Al-Mizan states: God sends down water, brings forth every kind of plant and green foliage producing piled grain, and brings forth accessible date clusters, gardens of grapes, olives, and pomegranates, alike and unlike. Their fruit and ripening are signs for a people who believe.
verses.100: Al-Mizan states: They make the jinn Allah’s associates and ignorantly ascribe sons and daughters to Him, though He created the jinn. He is exalted above such claims.
verses.101: Al-Mizan states: Allah originated the heavens and the earth; having no consort, He cannot have a son. He created all things and knows all things.
verses.102: Al-Mizan states: Allah, your Lord, is the sole god and Creator of all things; therefore serve Him, for He is Guardian over all things.
verses.103: Al-Mizan: no vision comprehends Him; He comprehends all vision, All-Subtle and All-Aware.
verses.104: Al-Mizan states that clear proofs from the Lord have come to you; whoever sees benefits his own soul, whoever is blind harms it, and the Prophet is not your keeper.
verses.105:
Al-Mizan explains that these verses answer the denial that God has revealed anything to a mortal, connect this denial with the guidance and scriptures granted to the prophets, condemn the gravest forms of injustice concerning God and revelation, describe the wrongdoers’ death, and then set out signs of divine unity and God’s names and attributes.

On (6:91), qadr may signify giving God His due regard, describing Him as He deserves, or knowing Him as He deserves. Since the surrounding discussion concerns God’s continuous guidance of prophets through book, judgment, and prophethood, the most fitting sense is that the deniers have not accorded God His due value. To deny revelation is to imply that God is not a Lord who cares for His servants’ affairs or guides them to felicity. The other senses remain possible, but interpreting qadr as failing to ascribe sufficient power to God is least suitable here. The same expression elsewhere rebukes those who lower God’s honor by equating Him with powerless beings worshiped besides Him.

The verse argues that lordship entails guiding humankind to the straight path by sending revelation and scripture to some people. It gives two proofs. First, Moses brought a Book that the Jews themselves accepted as light and guidance. Secondly, people possess religious beliefs, moral virtues, and laws which their ordinary faculties and collective reason could not independently have produced. Human reason can pursue material benefit, ward off loss, organize cooperation, and distribute interests equitably, but it cannot by itself establish the revealed teachings and laws that order society toward true happiness. Thus existing scriptures and teachings beyond collective human capacity testify to revelation.

The commentary holds that the address in (6:91) is directed to the Jews, not principally to the Arab polytheists. The appeal to Moses’ Book would not bind polytheists who did not accept it as revelation; the accusation that they displayed parts of the Book while concealing much fits the Jews; and “you were taught what you did not know” is likewise addressed to them. Their denial of revelation, despite their belief in Moses and the Torah, may have issued from hostility to Islam, an effort to incite polytheists, or a response to questions about the Prophet’s revelation. Their other reported statements contrary to their own principles show that such a contradiction was possible when falsehood served their interests.

The fact that Sūrah al-Anʿām is Meccan does not exclude an address to the People of the Book. Islam’s call was universal from its beginning; Arab polytheists and the People of the Book interacted; Meccan chapters address the People of the Book; and Jewish and Christian communities were present throughout Arabia. The chapter addresses people for their qualities, not as merely named individuals. Therefore, Jewish deviations that entail rejecting revelation suitably appear amid the refutation of those who reject monotheism, prophethood, or the hereafter. Nor does the polytheists’ awareness that Jews claimed to follow Moses’ Torah make the Torah binding evidence for them; knowing a claim is not accepting the Book as divine light and guidance.

Al-Mizan notes the readings tajʿalūnahu, “which you make into parchment,” and yajʿalūnahu, “which they make into parchment.” The latter can be understood through a rhetorical shift of address, while the former directly addresses the Jews. A proposed harmonization—that the verse was first addressed in Mecca to polytheists in the third person and was later inspired in the second person for Jews in Medina—is plausible only on its stated assumptions, but does not remove the main difficulties. It still relies on an argument from a Book the polytheists did not believe in, cannot naturally address them as recipients of prophetic teaching, restricts “the people” without warrant, concedes that Jews could have made the denial, and lacks proof for the alleged later inspiration. If the verse was revealed in Medina, however, many of these objections do not arise.

The teaching that neither the Jews nor their fathers knew is not ordinary knowledge gained through sense, imagination, or reason. It is extraordinary knowledge conveyed through revelation: religious beliefs, moral virtues, and laws. Even if people can attain general notions of God’s unity, prophethood, the hereafter, and virtue, this does not suffice to establish these truths socially. Material desire and the drive to secure worldly enjoyment bury the realities latent in fiṭrah; where materialism rules a society, inherited spiritual and moral values progressively disappear. Rulers seek their own power, while collective governments chiefly order society according to majority desire, whether virtuous or vicious, and reinterpret remaining moral values to suit prevailing practice. The surviving traces of pure teachings are therefore remnants of the prophets’ calls, and derive from God’s instruction through revelation and scripture.

The sentence is not directed to polytheists, who did not acknowledge such a share of prophetic teachings, nor to Muslims, since that would interrupt the argument without indication and introduce an unexplained shift of audience. It refutes the Jews by showing that they possess beneficial teachings which neither they nor their forefathers acquired on their own, and which must have reached them through God’s revelation to a mortal. The unqualified passive expression “you were taught” includes all revealed beliefs and laws, not Torah alone. Its passive form presents the argument without assuming its conclusion: among their knowledge is teaching neither they nor their fathers generated; God is the evident answer to who taught it, just as He is the answer to who revealed Moses’ Book. The Prophet is consequently commanded to say, “Allah,” and leave those who deny revelation to their vain sport.

On (6:92), the Qur’an is introduced as a Book revealed by God, like the true previous scriptures. Its being blessed and verifying what preceded it are signs of its divine origin, rather than proofs considered in isolation. Its blessedness, mubārak, is the abundant and enduring good God has placed in it: it resolves disputes, joins people, removes enmity, spreads security, enlightens them against ignorance and vice, brings worldly felicity, and grants eternal reward. A human fabrication, satanic impression, or deceptive imagination could not yield these divine benefits, since evil does not produce perfection. Its truthfulness and confirmation of earlier genuine scriptures are further signs, and its warning fulfills God’s purpose of guiding servants to happiness in both worlds.

Umm al-Qurá is Mecca, and because the verse adds those around it, the expression concerns its people; those around it may mean all people whose lands surround Mecca, or its neighboring lands. This honors the sanctuary from which the religious call began and spread. The purpose clause may be joined to the Book’s blessedness, but more likely joins its verification of earlier scripture: the Book was revealed so that it might verify what preceded it and warn the people. Believers in the hereafter believe in it because it calls to eternal safety and warns against everlasting punishment. Their distinguishing quality, guarding their prayers, apparently denotes inward humility and submissiveness before God in worship, though it is also commonly interpreted as observing prayer times.

Al-Mizan defines barakah as established, enduring divine good in a thing. Its manifestations differ with the sought benefit: in progeny it may be abundance or the endurance of one’s good remembrance; in food, satiating many; in time, accomplishing what normally could not be done in that span. In religious matters, even material blessing ultimately means spiritual good or worldly good leading to eternal happiness. Thus the blessing of food may be satiation, harmlessness, healing, or spiritual illumination according to the intended benefit. God grants it by bringing together the relevant causes and removing impediments.

Divine blessing does not cancel the system of causes. God’s will is not a parallel, competing cause but stands in a ṭūlī relationship to all other means and causes. Blessing in food can consist in arranging causes so that it does not harm the eater, and blessing in wealth in arranging them so that it is not wasted, lost, stolen, or plundered. Those who deny barakah because natural causes leave no room for another cause mistake God’s causal precedence for an interfering cause on the same plane.

On (6:93), the commentary identifies three supremely unjust acts: forging a lie against God, falsely claiming revelation, and saying, “I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed.” The rhetorical question calls both the Prophet and his opponents to fairness before explicit truth. In context, forging a lie against God primarily concerns attributing associates and intercessors to Him; falsely claiming revelation is distinct in intention, although it falls generally under lying about God; and claiming to reveal the like of God’s revelation mocks the Qur’an and God’s communications. The distinction prevents the second act from being a merely redundant instance of the first and accords with the later threat concerning alleged partners and intercessors.

The false claimant to revelation apparently refers in context to the Prophet’s own claim as disputed by his opponents, though the wording remains generally applicable to anyone who makes such a claim falsely. It does not naturally refer to Musaylimah, whose claim came after the migration unless the verse is treated as Medinan. Likewise, the future-oriented wording “I will reveal” does not precisely fit either the conditional boast in (8:31) or the reported present claim of ʿAbd-Allāh b. Saʿd b. Abī Sarḥ. It apparently records a polytheist’s defiant promise. The repeated man for the third wrong separates the first two cases, in which one admits revelation in principle, from the third, in which one sets oneself against God and rejects revelation itself.

The agonies of death are encompassing intensities, and the angels’ stretching out their hands signifies their beginning to punish the wrongdoers. “Give up your souls” belongs to the angels’ speech: they seize the souls painfully and announce humiliating chastisement on the day of death, in barzakh, before the further punishment of Resurrection. The unjust are those guilty of the three listed wrongs. Speaking falsely about God includes assigning Him partners or falsely attributing a rule or revelation to Him; arrogance toward His communications includes the boast of producing the like of His revelation. The command to give up the soul is existential or creational, not a legislative command subject to human choice. It signifies the soul’s separation from the body at death and supports the Qur’anic indication that the soul is not material, though joined to the body by an immaterial union.

On (6:94), people come to God alone as they were first created, having left behind the possessions and supports entrusted to them, together with the supposed intercessors they called God’s partners. Death unveils that all their affairs were always under God’s direction alone. Wealth, children, spouses, relatives, communities, apparent causes, and objects of worship had no independent influence. Drawn by worldly adornment, people mistake visible means for independent powers and become absorbed in securing material pleasures; this is the play of false imaginations that distracts them from the Creator and Director of causes. When the soul leaves the body, its material links are severed, the apparent power of these means vanishes, and the person realizes that he has had no lord but God. The verse’s severed ties and vanished assertions describe this unveiling and the collapse of the illusions on which worldly attachment rested.

Verses 6:95-99 list signs that show that God alone directs affairs. He splits seed and date-stone so that plants and trees emerge; brings living from dead and dead from living; splits the dawn; makes night a rest; and makes the sun and moon instruments of reckoning. This ordered arrangement within an ever-changing world serves human life and manifests the Mighty, Knowing One: none can overcome His regulation, and no need of His kingdom escapes His knowledge. The stars guide travelers through the darkness of land and sea, while God also has an independent will governing them in their own right; these purposes do not conflict, because they concern different aspects within a universally connected order.

Humanity, despite its multitude, comes from a single soul, apparently Adam. The preferred interpretation of mustaqarr and mustawdaʿ is that some people have been born and settled on earth, while others are temporarily deposited in the loins and wombs until their birth. The verse portrays humanity as continually inhabiting the earth while future members await their turn to settle there. Other proposed interpretations are possible, but add little. Rain then brings forth vegetation, grain, dates, grapes, olives, pomegranates, and their varying yet comparable fruits. Vegetative growth may include the growth latent in every being with vegetative power, including plants, animals, and humans.

The signs are suited to different capacities. Vegetation is plain enough to recognize through a gaze illuminated by faith rather than stubbornness. The stars and celestial events require knowledge. The origin and secrets of human souls require fiqh: theoretical learning joined with inward awareness, strenuous reflection, and perseverance.

On (6:100) and (6:101), assigning the jinn as associates to God is refuted by the fact that God created them: the created cannot be the Creator’s partner or equal. The jinn may mean devils, as in dualistic beliefs concerning Yazdān and Ahriman or beliefs that deify Iblīs, or the known class of creatures, as in the claim that God married a jinn woman and angels were born from them. In the latter case, the alleged sons and daughters are angels falsely invented and attributed to God. If the terms are broader, they include the various claims of religions and idolaters that God has children. God’s having no consort negates the possibility of a real child, and His being Creator and Originator of everything also negates it: a child is a part of its parents that develops independently, while a thing cannot create a part of itself. As Originator of the heavens and earth, God has no like from whom He could take a spouse or have children of His kind, and He knows all things.

Verse (6:102) concludes that Allah is the Lord, that there is no god but Him, that He created all things, and that He alone must be served. Since everything is His creature and existentially subordinate to Him, nothing can be His equal or share His right to worship. His guardianship means that He watches, directs, and orders all things; it reinforces the command to serve Him and warns against associating partners with Him. Verse (6:103) corrects any physical conception of this guardianship. No vision comprehends God because He transcends bodily properties, yet He comprehends every vision. His being al-laṭīf and al-khabīr means that He encompasses and knows everything, outwardly and inwardly, without one thing engaging or veiling Him from another. Ordinary sight grasps only outward accidents such as color, distance, magnitude, motion, and stillness; God comprehends both sight itself and the total realities, substances and accidents, that are present to Him.

Al-Mizan takes “the Creator of all things” without exception: everything possessing any reality or existence is created by God. The Qur’an nevertheless recognizes real causal relations among beings and attributes human acts to human agents, making command, prohibition, accountability, reward, and punishment meaningful. It affirms the universal law of causality: contingent things need causes; without a cause their existence is impossible, and when a complete cause is present with its conditions and without impediments, its effect necessarily follows. The Qur’an itself argues from causes to the Creator and from divine attributes to their consequences.

At the same time, God’s causality and agency encompass all things. Things, their actions, movements, states, effects, measures, and goals all trace to His creation, measurement, and guidance. Their essence is attributable to divine creation, while their determinate limits, transformations, stages, and ends are attributable to divine measurement. The universe is a connected and harmonious system under one Director.

The objection that sins and injustice must be excluded from God’s creation confuses existential realities with conventional and relational classifications. Everything God creates is good in its real, existential aspect. Evil, sin, injustice, obedience, and disobedience are not independent external entities; they are titles applied to acts in relation to divine law, rational standards, social order, or intended ends. Adultery and marriage, for example, do not differ in bare external motions, but in their conformity or nonconformity to law, custom, and collective welfare. Likewise, social titles such as manager, master, slave, rich, and poor are not realities added to a person’s existential essence. God’s creation encompasses the real existence of actions, while their legal and social descriptions belong to the plane of convention and assessment. Therefore, universal creation neither attributes injustice to God in the objectionable sense nor abolishes law, responsibility, reward, and punishment.

The commentary rejects the theory that God alone creates each effect by habitual custom while apparent causes have no real causal connection. This destroys the causal principle on which all reasoning, including proof of God and the Qur’an’s authority, rests. Its error is to confuse horizontal causes, which cannot independently be complete causes of one effect, with vertical causes, in which a cause is itself caused and acts through the higher cause. It also fails to distinguish a source from which an effect emanates from a means through which it emanates.

It further rejects the image of God as a retired architect who created beings initially, leaves them to an independent causal system, and only intervenes in unknown events or miracles. This view makes contingent beings dependent upon God for origination but not subsistence, though the Qur’an argues for God’s existence and unity through the continuing transformations, effects, benefits, and ordered courses of the sun, moon, stars, seasons, seas, rain, living things, and human development. These are ongoing signs of both God’s agency and His ordering of all things toward their ends. A being cannot become self-subsisting merely because it has been given existence; if it were independent in existence, it could not perish. Every being receives existence from God at its origin and continuously throughout its subsistence. The Qur’an therefore admits only that God creates every thing, continually sustains every being and event, and invisibly dominates its beginning, end, outward, and inward.

On (6:104), baṣāʾir are clear proofs through which one sees, and by extension they signify insight, knowledge, and faith, in contrast with blindness, ignorance, and disbelief. The Prophet speaks to the polytheists of the preceding arguments for God’s unity: whoever sees through them benefits his own soul, and whoever remains blind harms himself. He is not their keeper in the creational sense, for their minds and hearts are not under his control; he is only their sincere legislative admonisher and adviser. The verse is thus a parenthetical appeal through the Prophet’s voice, assuring them that his message contains no personal interest and urging their submission.

On (6:105), taṣrīf means presenting the communications in varying expressions and from different angles. Darasta means that the Prophet has learned them by reading; dārasta intensifies this meaning. Under the reading durisat, derived from wearing out and disappearing, the accusation becomes that the communications are obsolete and meaningless, like the polytheists’ description of the Qur’an as “fables of the ancients” (asāṭīr al-awwalīn). God’s repeated presentation of His communications thus has distinct consequences: the wretched fully realize their wretchedness by accusing the Prophet of learning from the People of the Book, or by dismissing the communications as worn out; while the communications become clear to those who know, through the purification of their hearts and expansion of their breasts. In this respect the verse resembles: And We reveal of the Qur’an that which is a healing and a mercy to the believers, and to the unjust—it only adds to their perdition (17:82).
verses.106:
Al-Mizan holds that the Prophet is commanded to follow the revelation concerning tawḥīd and the principles of religion, without allowing the polytheists’ proud rejection and aversion to hinder his delivery of the message. The exclusive address in “your Lord” indicates God’s particular care for him.

“There is no god but He” prevents “withdraw from the polytheists” from being understood as an approving abandonment of them to their gods. Withdrawal means neither endorsing their idolatry nor exhausting oneself trying to compel them to accept monotheism. The Prophet’s duty is to convey the message, not to control their response: God alone is their keeper and guardian. He has left them in error because they turned from the truth and proudly refused submission; had He willed their monotheism, they would not have associated partners with Him.
verses.107:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse consoles the Prophet: the polytheists cannot frustrate God through their polytheism, and their guidance or rejection is not his responsibility. Had God willed, they would have believed voluntarily, as believers do. But through pride, defiance, plotting against God, and mocking His communications, they deprived themselves of the mercy and aid necessary for faith, so that their evil plot returned upon themselves.

God’s effective will operates according to the system of means, conditions, and causes He has established in creation (takwīn). The same order governs legislation (tashrīʿ) and guidance. Guidance is available to everyone who exposes himself to divine mercy; those who reject it through iniquity, disbelief, and defiance are deprived of it, led into error despite knowing the right way, and have their hearts sealed. Were this order set aside, causality—and with it the coherence, wisdom, and purpose of creation and legislation—would collapse.

Thus, “if Allah had willed” does not mean that He would have compelled them to abandon polytheism. Compulsory belief would eliminate the human choice required for īmān (believe, faith), erase differences in degrees of perfection, and make education, discipline, and religious messages meaningless. It would transform human reality into a wholly different order. The verse instead affirms God’s absolute power to grant them voluntary faith and reassures the Prophet that he need not grieve over their refusal.

The commentary takes “keeper” (ḥāfiẓ) to concern their existential affairs—life, growth, and sustenance—and “guardian” (wakīl) to concern their religious affairs, belief, and actions. This mutually distinct reading better fits the terms than the view that ḥāfiẓ merely attracts benefit and wakīl repels loss. Neither their worldly existence nor their religious outcome is entrusted to the Prophet.
verses.108:
Al-Mizan says that the prohibition on abusing what polytheists invoke besides Allah is religious courtesy protecting the sanctity of holy things from insult, profanity, and derision. Since people instinctively defend what they hold sacred, believers’ abuse of idols can provoke ignorant, prejudiced retaliation against Allah. The stated reason therefore establishes a general prohibition of negative or blasphemous speech that leads to any negative mention of what is sacred in Islam.

“Thus have We decorated for every people their deeds” concerns zīnah: the attractive aspect that moves people toward an act. Human life depends on such pleasures. Physical pleasures, and mental pleasures that serve worldly life without harming the hereafter, belong to God’s creation and to sound fiṭrah (innate human nature); they move people to acts through which individual and human life are preserved. “He is the One Who gave to everything its creation, then guided it (to its goal) (20:50).”

Other mental pleasures arise from base desire, undermine sound human life and servitude to God, and bring misfortune in the hereafter. Because fiṭrah is God’s formation for human felicity, desires that contradict it are not rooted in God’s creation; they are satanic adornments of sin, though they occur by God’s leave. They cannot be directly ascribed to God, for this would make Him command both good and indecency, destroy the distinction underlying religious duty, reward, and punishment, and contradict the upright religion founded on fiṭrah. As the commentary notes: “Surely Allah does not enjoin indecency; do you say against Allah what you do not know? Say: My Lord has enjoined justice (7:28-29).”

This does not deny that spiritual and psychological conditions mediate obedience and sin. Such conditions directly produce their effects, while God is indirectly related to them through idhn (permission, leave, authorization), since no cause acts in His kingdom without His leave. But this differs from legislation: God does not instruct belief and disbelief alike, nor urge obedience and disobedience alike. Satan’s adornment of polytheism and sin is permitted as part of the divine test through which the system of religious call, command, prohibition, reward, and punishment is completed. In this broad sense—attribution through permission—the verse ascribes the decoration of all deeds to God.

The commentary rejects four interpretations. It rejects limiting “decoration” to commands, prohibitions, and fair religious instruction because the verse is universal and provides no basis for this restriction. It rejects the view that people simply incline to their deeds despite being shown the truth, because God must be declared free not only from legislating both good and evil but also from directly creating both good and evil inclinations without mediation. It rejects taking “deeds” to mean only good deeds, or decoration to mean mention of reward and punishment, because neither the wording nor context supports this limitation, and such decoration is not exclusive to believers. Finally, it rejects the deterministic view that God initially calls equally to obedience and sin: decoration presupposes ikhtiyār (free will, choice), since it inclines a person toward one available alternative.
