In good it is hidāyah (guidance) and tawfīq (reconciliation, divine help, God-given success); in sin it may be iḍlāl (misguidance, misleading, leaving in error) and makr (plot, scheme, contrivance, ruse), which may be ascribed to God only as retribution for prior wrongdoing, not as an initial act.

The return to God confirms that this principle covers inward and outward, good and evil deeds. People act for the attractive appearance placed before them, heedless of the concealed reality beneath it. At their return, God will disclose what they did: both God’s friends and Satan’s friends will see realities previously hidden from them.
verses.109:
Al-Mizan explains that jahd al-aymān denotes oaths sworn with the utmost possible emphasis. The polytheists’ claim that they would believe if a sign came is effectively a demand for a miracle. The Prophet is told that signs belong solely to God’s dominion and cannot be produced by anyone except by His leave.

The final question means that they will not believe even when signs come, despite the plausibility their emphatic oaths may have for believers. It is a prediction from the unseen that God has not willed their belief. The passage notes two recitations, “they will not believe” and “you will not believe,” respectively addressing believers and polytheists, while both remain part of the Prophet’s commanded response. It rejects the proposal that anna means “perhaps,” since this is, even if lexically possible, too rare a usage on which to interpret the Qur’an.
verses.110:
Al-Mizan treats this verse as the explanation of why the polytheists will not believe even if the requested signs are sent. “The first time” means before those hypothetical signs, when they did not believe in the Qur’an.

God turns their hearts so that they do not comprehend as they should, and their sight so that they do not see as they should. Consequently, they will disbelieve in the signs just as they first disbelieved in the Qur’an, and God will leave them wandering hesitantly in their transgression. This is the meaning indicated by the verse’s context.
verses.111:
Al-Mizan explains the verse as God’s answer to the polytheists’ assertion that a sign would make them believe. Their assertion is false because they ignorantly suppose signs and miracles to be independent causes that automatically produce faith. Yet signs can bring belief only if God wills.

Even if angels visibly came to them, the dead spoke with them, and all things were brought before them—in groups or manifestly face to face, testifying by speech or by their very state—they would not believe unless Allah willed it. Although causality governs creation, every cause and effect remains needy of God and works only by His leave. Most of the polytheists were ignorant of this, perhaps through lack of education rather than defiance: they mistook apparent means for self-sufficient and independent causes, and therefore thought that granted signs would necessarily yield faith.
verses.112:
Al-Mizan explains that every prophet, not the Prophet alone, is assigned enemies among the devils of humankind and jinn. Shayāṭīn are evil beings, a term used in the Qur’an chiefly for Iblīs and his descendants. Jinn are intelligent, free-willed creatures hidden from human senses by their nature; Iblīs is one of them and they differ from angels. Their waḥy is indirect communication through hints, while zukhruf al-qawl is embellished but misleading speech that resembles truth without being true. Jinn devils whisper, insinuate, and tempt human devils; human devils entice one another and secretly exchange plots.

Their enmity and deceptive exchanges occur by God’s permission: had He willed otherwise, they would not have acted so. As signs themselves affect belief only by His will, all affairs depend on God’s will and leave. Therefore their hostility and fabricated claims, including associating partners with God, cannot overcome His authoritative will; the Prophet is to leave them and what they forge rather than be distressed by their disruption. In this respect the verse corresponds to the previous command to withdraw from the polytheists.

The apparent attribution to God of appointing these enemies does not make Him directly responsible for evil, sin, or polytheism. The commentary concludes that blessings and good deeds are attributable to God directly or through intermediaries; evil and sin are directly attributable to other than Him, such as Satan or the ego; and evil and sin are indirectly attributable to God through His existential and creational permission. He permits them as implications of the trial through which the divine call of commands, prohibitions, rewards, and punishments is completed. This is part of a world in which human growth and perfection occur gradually.
verses.113:
Al-Mizan explains that iqtirāf means earning or acquiring, and that “it” refers to the misleading waḥy, or suggestive speech, of the preceding verse. The opening conjunction joins the stated end to other unmentioned divine purposes: God did not prevent the prophets’ enemies from exchanging embellished, misleading words so that the hearts of those who deny the hereafter might incline to them, accept and be pleased with them, and acquire the evil they are to acquire.

These outcomes lead to their wretchedness in the hereafter, a destination they summon through the state for which they have prepared themselves. God aids both those headed for salvation and those headed for wretchedness to realize their capacities and complete their journey toward the end their readiness and disposition (lisān al-istiʿdād) seek: “All do We aid—these as well as those—out of the bounty of your Lord, and the bounty of your Lord is not confined (17:20).”
verses.114: Al-Mizan states that Allah alone should be sought as judge, for He revealed the well-elaborated Book. Those given the Book know it came from the Lord in truth, so the Prophet should not be among the disputers.
verses.115: Al-Mizan states that the Lord’s word has been fulfilled in truth and justice, beyond anyone’s power to alter; He is the Hearing, the Knowing.
verses.116: Al-Mizan warns that obeying most people on earth leads away from Allah’s path, because they follow uncertainty and mere speculation.
verses.117: Al-Mizan states that the Lord knows best who has strayed from His way and who follows right guidance.
verses.118: Al-Mizan commands believers in Allah’s communications to eat that over which Allah’s name has been mentioned.
verses.119: Al-Mizan asks why believers should not eat that over which Allah’s name was mentioned, since He has already detailed what is forbidden, apart from necessity. Many lead others astray through ignorant desire, but the Lord knows best those who exceed His limits.
verses.120: Al-Mizan commands abandoning both outward and inward sin; those who acquire sin will be repaid for what they acquired.
verses.121:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as a connected argument: God alone is to be followed in His elaborated Book; following most people leads astray because they rely on uncertainty and speculation; and believers must distinguish lawful slaughter from carrion by eating what was slaughtered in God’s name and refusing what was not. Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the verses were occasioned by polytheists asking why Muslims ate animals they killed but not those “killed” by God. The purpose is to establish God’s rule and explain the difference.

On (6:114), the commentary explains that the initial fāʾ makes the question a consequence of the preceding clear proofs and of the Qur’an’s confirmation of the Torah and Gospel. Citing Majmaʿ al-bayān, it notes that ḥakam, unlike ḥākim, denotes one fit to be referred to for judgment because he judges only by truth; tafṣīl is clarification that removes ambiguity. Thus no worshipped god or supposed affiliate should be sought as judge when Allah sent the Qur’an, whose teachings are distinctly arranged without confusion; only such a One deserves judgment. The address assuring the Prophet that those given the Book know its truthful divine source both consoles him and shows the polytheists that his message rests on clear proof. “With truth” means revelation is neither satanic suggestion nor soothsayers’ speech, nor revelation corrupted by devils.

On (6:115), kalimah can denote a divine decree that will certainly be fulfilled, though it may also denote created beings brought forth by God’s creative command. In this context, Al-Mizan holds that the Lord’s accomplished word apparently means Islam together with Muḥammad’s prophethood and the Qur’an: a scripture embracing previous scriptures and their principal divine teachings, whose coming had been mentioned in them. Its accomplishment is the final realization of this call after the gradual development of religion and law through the prophets, culminating in the Muhammadan religion; Islam contains the essence of the preceding religions and more. God knows best.

Its being accomplished ṣidqan means that the call’s contents and descriptions are realized outwardly; its being accomplished ʿadlan means that it is balanced, internally non-contradictory, and gives everything its true measure without error, deficiency, or injustice. “There is none who can change His words” explains both qualities: neither God, who does not reverse His decree or fail His promise, nor any creature, which cannot overcome Him, can alter it. Other exegetes identify the word with the Qur’an—sometimes excluding legal rulings from “words” because they can be abrogated—with religion, or with God’s proof; another view takes ṣidq as concerning Qur’anic reports and ʿadl its laws. “The Hearing, the Knowing” may mean that God hears calls and knows real needs, hears events through messenger-angels while knowing them directly, or hears speech and knows deeds.

On (6:116), kharṣ can mean lying or guessing and speculation; the latter better fits the context, since uncertainty and speculation explain why obeying most people diverts one from God’s way. Conjecture may be unavoidable and acceptable in particular worldly affairs, where certainty is rare. It cannot be relied upon, however, regarding genuine human felicity or eternal wretchedness, or the beliefs and laws bearing on them: God, creation’s purpose, resurrection and the hereafter, prophethood, scripture, and divine law. In the servant-Lord relationship, knowledge and certainty are required, for speculation remains inseparable from ignorance and cannot enable proper service to a Lord whose demands are unknown. Reason itself establishes this, and the following verse confirms it by God’s knowledge.

On (6:117), aʿlam may plausibly be either absolute or comparative. God alone possesses independent, original knowledge of the straying and the guided; but, when knowledge bestowed by God is included, He knows best because others know only what He grants them. The bāʾ in bi-man, concerning those guided, indicates that the same particle is implied in the preceding man concerning those who stray.

On (6:118), the preceding premises establish that God deserves obedience above all others. The verse therefore requires adherence to His ruling and rejection of desire-based, ignorant claims of lawfulness, including the devil-inspired disputes later mentioned. Together with (6:121), it establishes the central distinction: eat what legally counts as slaughtered, mudhakká, and not what counts as carrion, maytah, despite polytheist objections. The fāʾ shows that this ruling follows the prior argument, and food over which Allah’s name is mentioned is a slaughtered offering for God.

On (6:119), God has already made forbidden foods clear, with an exception for compulsion; an animal slaughtered in God’s name is not among them and may be eaten. Those who lead people astray from ignorant desire are transgressors of God’s limits, including polytheists who deny a difference between what people slaughter and what God causes to die and demand that both be eaten or both avoided. Mā lakum is a rhetorical question meaning, in effect, what benefit or justification can there be in not eating it; it has also been read as a negation, meaning that they have no right not to eat it. The verse indicates that prohibited foods had been outlined before this sūrah. A translator’s note qualifies the resulting chronology: reports of revelation order and comparison with other verses may instead indicate that the verse refers to a later verse in this sūrah, or that the sūrah’s order differs from its order of revelation.

On (6:120), the unrestricted wording includes every sin, open or hidden. Contextually, it prepares for the prohibition of food over which Allah’s name was not mentioned; because (6:121) emphatically calls this fisq, Al-Mizan infers that it is an inward sin. Outward sin is what everyone recognizes as evil and leading to misery, such as polytheism, oppression, and mischief; inward sin is what initially seems unobjectionable, such as carrion, blood, or pork, and is learned through divine teaching, though reason can sometimes discover it. Proposed alternatives—public versus private sins, bodily versus heartfelt sins, and several distinctions involving adultery, lovers, or marrying one’s stepmother—do not fit the context and mostly lack evidence. The promised recompense justifies the prohibition by warning of painful retribution.

On (6:121), the prohibition complements the command to eat lawful slaughter. Since eating food over which Allah’s name was not mentioned is transgression and all transgression must be avoided, it is incumbent to avoid it. The devils’ friends are the polytheists, whose objection about eating what people kill but not what God kills means carrion. Their claim is satanically inspired and false: carrion is fisq, whereas legally slaughtered meat is not forbidden. Obeying them by eating carrion risks leaving īmān and becoming like them—by adopting their custom or becoming their friends and affiliates, awliyāʾ. The warning follows the prohibition, rather than the command to eat lawful slaughter, because the polytheists sought to have believers continue eating dead meat, not to have them refrain from meat slaughtered in Allah’s name.
verses.122: Al-Mizan portrays the guided as raised from death and given a light for life among people, unlike the disbeliever trapped in inescapable darkness whose deeds are made alluring.
verses.123: Al-Mizan states that God places chief sinners in every town to plot, though, without realizing it, they plot only against themselves.
verses.124: Al-Mizan relates that, when a communication comes, they refuse belief unless given what Allah’s messengers receive. Allah best knows where to place His message, and the guilty plotters will suffer humiliation and severe chastisement.
verses.125: Al-Mizan states that Allah expands the breast for Islam of whomever He wills to guide, but makes the breast of whomever He wills to lead astray constricted and tight, as if ascending upward, and lays uncleanness upon those who do not believe.
verses.126: Al-Mizan identifies this as the Lord’s straight path, whose communications have been made clear for a people who mind.
verses.127:
Al-Mizan interprets the sequence beginning at (6:122) as a contrast between believers and disbelievers in guidance and error. Before divine guidance, a person is like one dead and deprived of perception and movement; approved belief revives him and gives him a light by which he distinguishes good from evil and benefit from harm. The disbeliever is instead in the darkness of spiritual death and ignorance, unable to discern these things or escape toward eternal happiness. Thus, at its initial level, death signifies ḍalāl or kufr, life signifies guidance or īmān, light is the knowledge resulting from īmān, and darkness is ignorance. Light cannot plausibly mean either īmān itself or the Qur’an in this context.

The commentary nevertheless maintains that the believers’ life and light are not merely figurative. Those connected with their Lord possess an enduring life that does not end with bodily death: under His guardianship, they are free from weariness, misery, pain, fear, and danger, and enjoy divine proximity, peace, and unending happiness. Their outward conduct may resemble that of others, but their cognition, will, perception, and aims exceed ordinary human capacities. Just as human beings have a higher life than animals, and animals than plants, believers given divine knowledge, faith, certitude, and devotion possess a higher share of life and light. Qur’anic descriptions of the good life, of hearts, eyes, and ears that fail to yield their proper fruit in the heedless, and of believers strengthened by a special rūḥ all support this conclusion.

A report narrated by both Shias and Sunnis from the Prophet says, “Whoever practices what he knows, God will provide him—or teach him—what he does not know.” Al-Mizan uses this to explain that when īmān is firmly rooted in the soul, a person’s opinions and actions are formed in accordance with it, just as any deeply rooted virtue or vice shapes them. The light therefore enables discernment amid social life and the choice of acts conducive to true happiness. Mathal means a description or attribute; the commentary prefers to understand the phrase as omitting “he is” in “like him whose likeness is that he is in utter darkness,” rather than positing the longer omitted phrase, “the likeness of one who.”

“Thus” (kadhālika) connects the embellishment of the disbelievers’ deeds to the preceding general analogy: absorbed and enchained by deeds made beautiful to them, they cannot emerge from darkness into felicity and light. Al-Mizan rejects the view that it compares believers and disbelievers merely by saying that each group’s deeds are embellished in its own eyes, since that does not fit the immediate context.

Regarding (6:123), the commentary holds that the verse completes this account: in every town, major sinners plot against religion, the prophet, and believers, but their plots neither free them from darkness nor harm anyone but themselves. The “great sinners” are specified because they initiate these plots, while the general public follows them. Jaʿl has the same sense here as in the granting of light in (6:122) and means khalq: God created these major sinners so that they might plot. Their plotting is therefore an end connected with their creation, comparable to the creation of many jinn and humankind for hell. A translator’s note qualifies that this evildoing and damnation are not primary ends willed in themselves (bi-al-dhāt), but inevitable consequences of human creation, willed accidentally (bi-al-ʿaraḍ) within a whole that is good overall. Al-Mizan rejects an alternative reading that treats the two uses of kadhālika and jaʿl as parallel transformations: a merciful transformation of believers and an empowerment of sinners to plot.

Makr is a hidden scheme intended to cause another’s loss and frustrate his purpose. Yet God has no personal interest to be damaged by His religion; His call benefits those addressed by it. Consequently, those who scheme against God’s communications in fact damage themselves, though their darkness prevents them from perceiving it.

In (6:124), the pronouns refer to these great sinners, not to all polytheists. Their statement demands the office of risālah, including the public religious call, rather than merely religious teachings; otherwise, they would have spoken of prophets rather than messengers. Since they did not accept human messengership, their demand is mocking, akin to demanding that revelation be given to an important man. Allah’s reply establishes that He alone knows where to place His message, and their plots bring humiliation (ṣaghār) and severe punishment. The reference cannot include every polytheist: a universal demand to be messengers would leave no recipients of the mission; the reply would not suit such an incoherent demand; and the threat explicitly concerns guilty plotters, identifying the people already described as great sinners. A translator’s note observes that the lexical distinction invoked between nabī and rasūl conflicts with the use of “send” for both in 22:52, and notes that the author favors elsewhere a distinction deduced from narrations.

For (6:125), ṣadr is the receptacle of knowledge and intuition, and sharḥ al-ṣadr is its expansion so that it receives true teaching rather than rejecting it. Islam means taslīm to God. When God expands a person’s breast for Islam, that person receives and retains true beliefs and righteous deeds through an inner light that reveals them; the blinded heart, by contrast, cannot distinguish truth from falsehood or right from wrong. This spiritual light and softness of heart define the divine guidance described in the verse.

The verse is an alternative expression of (6:122). The consequential fāʾ shows their mutual implication: the one revived and given light accepts the beliefs and actions illuminated by it; correspondingly, the one whom God wills to guide has his breast opened to submit to Him. Submission is thus itself a light from God, and those who submit are upon a light from their Lord.

Iḍlāl is the opposite of guidance and manifests as a constricted breast that refuses truths because it cannot admit them. Ḥaraj denotes the extreme of tightness; “as though he were ascending upwards” explains this constriction by comparison with a vessel that cannot receive what exceeds its capacity. Rijs, defilement or uncleanness, stands here for ḍalāl. It is laid “upon” unbelievers as something overshadowing and separating them from others. Although the surrounding verses chiefly concern shirk, “those who do not believe” is unrestricted and therefore includes disbelief in God as well as rejection of His revealed beliefs and practices.

Al-Mizan rejects the claim that this verse means guidance and misguidance are exclusively from God with no real involvement of any other factor. Its purpose is to define their nature when God guides or misguides, not to deny other causal attributions. An event may be attributed both to God, who creates its means and conditions, and to other real factors; denying this would undermine universal causality and, with it, rational inference. It also rejects an argument that identifies expansion and constriction of the breast with motives or inclinations to believe and disbelieve. The two may accompany one another, but they are not identical; the argument mistakes concomitant events for the same event and reads a rational proof into a text that does not state it.

“This” in (6:126) refers to this established divine custom: God opens the breast of the guided for Islam and tightly constricts that of the astray. It is His straight path, an unchanging and unremoved custom, so that believers are characterized by openness to submission and disbelievers by its opposite. The verse gives a decisive, inclusive and exclusive account of guidance and misguidance. Its communications are clear to those who take heed and attend to the intrinsic truths and innate beliefs God has placed within them, by which they can recognize truth and falsehood.

The abode of peace (dār al-salām) in (6:127) is paradise: a dwelling immune from outward and inward defect, including death, decay, disease, poverty, sorrow, anxiety, and bereavement. God’s awliyāʾ also participate in this peace in the present world because they see God, rather than themselves, as the sole possessor of all things. They consequently fear no future loss and grieve over no past loss; being occupied solely with their Lord, they live with Him in inward seclusion. He is their guardian because, during their worldly journey, they followed the light of guidance placed in their hearts and illuminating their sight and insight. Al-Mizan rejects the view that al-salām here is a divine name and that the phrase means God’s own abode, since the context does not support it. It also holds that the pronouns refer not merely to the nearest antecedent, “a people who mind,” but principally to those whom God wills to guide, whose blessings the verses explain.

Finally, Al-Mizan defines hidāyah as an attribute of action: guidance is either showing someone the way (irāʾat al-ṭarīq) or taking him to the goal (al-īṣāl ilá al-maṭlūb). Accordingly, al-Hādī, like mercy and sustenance, describes God through His action toward creatures. His existential or creational guidance (al-hidāyat al-takwīniyyah) directs every species and individual, through creation, growth, maturation, and transformation, toward its ordained acts and perfection. His legislative guidance (al-hidāyat al-tashrīʿiyyah) consists in the true beliefs, righteous deeds, commands, prohibitions, encouragements, warnings, promises, and threats that He legislates.

Legislative guidance in turn includes both showing the way, which leaves a person able to be thankful or unthankful, and taking one to the goal. The latter is the special opening of the breast described in (6:125): a spiritual readiness that embraces true beliefs and righteous deeds without finding them burdensome. It is called light because it reveals what the heart should accept and reject. This guidance leads to the straight path, which is God’s religion in its teachings and rulings. Its parts contain no internal contradiction and do not fail to reach their end, because they express the single reality of pure monotheism and rest upon the unchanging innate nature of humankind. Nor is there conflict among its travelers: every prophet calls to the same religion as Adam and the final prophet, differing only in how concisely or fully that one religion of monotheism and submission is expounded.
verses.128: Al-Mizan states that, when all are gathered, the jinn and their human friends will acknowledge their mutual profit and their appointed end; God will decree the Fire to be their abiding abode, except as Allah wills.
verses.129: Al-Mizan says God authorizes some wrongdoers over others because of what they earned.
verses.130: Al-Mizan states that jinn and humankind will be asked whether messengers from among them conveyed God’s communications and warned them of that Day. Deceived by worldly life, they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers.
verses.131: Al-Mizan states: God does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are heedless.
verses.132: Al-Mizan says all have degrees according to what they do, and God is not heedless of their deeds.
verses.133: Al-Mizan states that the self-sufficient, merciful Lord may remove people and replace them with successors, as He raised them from another people’s seed.
verses.134: What you are promised will occur, and you cannot thwart God.
verses.135:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as explaining the wilāyah (authority, guardianship, friendship) granted to some wrongdoers over others, especially the authority of devils over disbelievers. This does not make God unjust: on the Day of Resurrection, those who associated partners with God and sinned will recognize that they chose their course themselves. Though worldly life deceived them, they had received God’s communications and warning of the Last Day. Divine decree (qaḍāʾ) neither removes free choice nor conflicts with it; God has decreed that certain people will follow demonic leaders by their own volition. Neither God nor the devils compel them to choose polytheism, sin, and wretchedness. God is needless of them, created them through mercy, and called them toward it; they wrong themselves and therefore do not succeed.

On (6:128), the commentary explains that istikthār of humankind by the jinn does not mean that the jinn literally brought humans into being. Rather, they gained many humans within their sphere of deceptive and tempting influence through wilāyah. Al-Mizan describes this as a reciprocal relationship: followers voluntarily seek their own interests in following their leaders, while leaders gain an interest in controlling their followers’ affairs. Humans gain access to worldly pleasures and personal interests through the jinn’s enticements, and the jinn gain what they seek through human compliance. Thus the human friends of the jinn confess that each profited from the other until they reached their appointed end.

That ajal is not the end of earthly life, but the limit set for their being or the degree they actualize through their deeds. By voluntarily pursuing evil and mutual profit, they arrive at the decreed state of wrongdoers and disbelievers. Their confession shows that, although this end was appointed by God, they reached it through free choice. The commentary therefore considers it possible that the jinn here are specifically devils that whisper in the hearts of humans and jinn. A translator’s note qualifies the exposition by observing that wilāyah and tawliyah ordinarily convey authority, hierarchy, and control rather than equal friendship: “Some of us profited by others” need not indicate benefit on both sides, and may primarily refer to the devils’ benefit from authority over their human followers.

God’s verdict is that the Fire is their mathwá, a settled place where they remain; “to abide in it” reinforces this permanence. The exception, “except as Allah wills,” means that this decree does not diminish God’s continuing power: He can remove them from the Fire, though He does not. The ending, “surely your Lord is Wise, Knowing,” addresses the Prophet and explains the judgment.

Verse (6:129) applies the same principle to the authorization of some wrongdoers over others. Followers accept leaders’ temptations, commit injustice, and consequently come under the leaders’ wilāyah. The bāʾ in bi-mā indicates causality or exchange: this authorization is retribution for their wrongdoing, not an arbitrary divine initiative. The shift to God’s first-person speech, addressed to the Prophet rather than the polytheists, is treated as a confidential mode of address that indicates their unworthiness to be addressed directly.

The commentary reads (6:130) as answering the objection that, although wrongdoers acted freely, they may have been unaware that their sins would lead to perdition, demonic authority, and exclusion from salvation; punishing such heedlessness would be unjust. God refutes this by asking whether messengers came with His communications and warning of the Day of Gathering and Reckoning. Their admission completes the proof against them: they rejected the message knowingly, not through ignorance. “From among you” means that the messengers, considered collectively in relation to jinn and humankind, were of their own kind rather than unfamiliar creatures such as angels; it does not establish that each group had messengers from its own kind.

The repeated testimony records two distinct confessions: first, that messengers conveyed the communications and warning; second, that the hearers were disbelievers. The commentary rejects the view that the repetition merely distinguishes witnessing disbelief in this world from testifying to it in the hereafter, since both would reduce to the same testimony. Worldly life’s deception explains how people possessing both knowledge and choice nevertheless followed damnation: when truth appeared to them, base desires and vices covered it and blinded them to it.

On (6:131), Al-Mizan explains that God’s established custom is not to destroy towns while their people are unaware of what He requires of them and of the consequence of refusing Him. Such destruction would be injustice by God, which is impossible for Him. Although God decrees their end and authorizes some over others, He does not cancel their ability to obey or their freedom of choice. They choose polytheism and disobedience, receive messengers and warnings, reject them, and persist in transgression; authority by wrongdoers and the Fire then follow as their penalty. They thus bring destruction upon themselves knowingly and voluntarily. “Destroying towns” here means decreeing their wretchedness in this world and punishment in the hereafter, not necessarily an exterminating punishment in this world.

Verse (6:132) means that both jinn and humankind differ in their deeds and therefore in their degrees, while God is not heedless of any of those deeds. Verse (6:133) gives the general ground for denying divine injustice. Ẓulm is putting something where it does not belong, whether through an act or a wrongful omission. It may arise from need—seeking gain or avoiding loss for oneself or another—or from inner wickedness and indifference to another’s suffering. God is free of both: He is absolutely self-sufficient and possesses an all-encompassing mercy that He bestows upon everything according to its condition and capacity. He can therefore remove people and replace them with whatever successors He wills, just as He brought them forth from the seed of a people He removed. The use of mā, “what,” rather than man, “whom,” conveys vagueness suggestive of the breadth of His power.

Verse (6:134) concerns the divinely ordained resurrection and retribution promised and threatened through revelation. It will certainly occur, and no one can evade or prevent any of God’s promises and decrees; it reinforces the preceding promise of reward and threat of punishment.

For (6:135), makānah denotes one’s present position or condition, while ʿāqibat al-dār is the final outcome and idiomatically the success of attaining one’s goal. The command to the polytheists to act according to their condition is a threat in imperative form: they may continue in their polytheism and injustice, while the Prophet continues to adhere to his belief and call to monotheism. They will soon learn whose effort succeeds; the Prophet will succeed, whereas the unjust cannot. The commentary rejects the interpretation that “I too am acting” is God’s speech about executing resurrection and retribution, because the context and the ensuing comparison of the two sides make the Prophet the speaker.
verses.136: Al-Mizan condemns the polytheists’ invented division of God-created crops and cattle between Allah and their associates: they preserve the associates’ share but transfer Allah’s share to them, an evil judgment.
verses.137: Al-Mizan states that the polytheists’ associates made the killing of their children appear fair, thereby ruining them and obscuring their religion. Had Allah willed, they could not have done this; the Prophet is told to leave them with their fabrications.
verses.138: Al-Mizan reports that the polytheists, on the basis of their false beliefs, restricted certain crops and cattle to whomever they chose, prohibited riding some animals, and omitted Allah’s name over others. They forged these rules against Allah and will be requited for them.
verses.139: Al-Mizan recounts their rule that what was in these animals’ wombs belonged to men and was forbidden to women, unless stillborn, when both could share it. Allah will recompense their false attribution; He is Wise and Knowing.
verses.140: Al-Mizan declares lost and astray those who ignorantly kill their children and falsely forbid the provision Allah has given them; they are not rightly guided.
verses.141: Al-Mizan says that Allah produces trellised and untrellised gardens, palms, varied seed-produce, olives, and pomegranates. People may eat their fruit, must pay its due at harvest, and must not be extravagant, for Allah does not love the extravagant.
verses.142: Al-Mizan says Allah made cattle for burden and as carpets; eat His provision, not following Satan’s footsteps, for he is an open enemy.
verses.143: Al-Mizan challenges those who claim prohibitions concerning sheep and goats: did Allah forbid their males, their females, or what their females’ wombs contain? They must produce knowledge if truthful.
verses.144: Al-Mizan similarly challenges claims of prohibition regarding camels and cows: were their males, females, or unborn offspring forbidden, or did they witness Allah enact this? None is more unjust than one who forges lies against Allah to mislead without knowledge; Allah does not guide the unjust.
verses.145: Al-Mizan states that revelation forbids an eater only carrion, poured-out blood, swine flesh, which is unclean, and an animal over which a name other than Allah’s has been invoked. verses.146: Al-Mizan states that Jews were forbidden every clawed animal and the fats of oxen and sheep, except fat borne on their backs, in the entrails, or mixed with bones. This was a punishment for their rebellion, and Allah is Truthful.
verses.147: Al-Mizan says: tell deniers their Lord’s mercy is all-encompassing, but His punishment cannot be averted from the guilty.
verses.148: Al-Mizan reports the polytheists’ claim that, had Allah willed, neither they nor their fathers would have associated partners with Him or forbidden anything. The response demands knowledge for this claim, since they merely follow uncertainty and speculation, as earlier deniers did before tasting punishment.
verses.149: Al-Mizan says Allah’s argument is conclusive; had He willed, He would certainly guide all.
verses.150:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as a refutation of polytheists who invented rules about crops, cattle, and food and ascribed them to Allah. Their allotment of portions to Allah and to their alleged associates was baseless, falsely attributed to God as a sacred obligation, and contemptuous of Him: they favored the idols by protecting the idols’ share while allowing Allah’s share to pass to them. “In their make-believe” marks their claim as false, while the associates are called theirs because the polytheists themselves treated those gods as Allah’s partners.

Regarding the killing of children, the common recitation means that their associates made this practice attractive to most polytheists. The idols’ hold over their hearts and their illusory devotion to them made child sacrifice seem commendable for winning the gods’ favor. This concerns children generally, not specifically the burying alive of daughters. Other exegetes identify the associates as devils, idol-house custodians, or deviators; Tafsīr al-Qummī reports that they were their forefathers. Ibn ʿĀmir’s recitation instead means that the associates killed the children and that this killing was made attractive. The intended ruin is chiefly the polytheists’ destruction through ingratitude, injustice to people, and the confusion of religion by making falsehood appear true, although one reading takes the first pronoun as referring literally to the slain children.

The commentary explains ḥijr as prohibition: the polytheists claimed that certain crops and cattle could be eaten only by persons they selected. A report identifies these as offerings to their gods, available only to the gods’ male servants. Their prohibition of animals’ backs refers to such consecrated cattle as al-sāʾibah, al-baḥīrah, and al-ḥāmī; their failure to mention Allah’s name refers principally to slaughtering animals for idols in the idols’ names. Other interpretations connect it with abstaining from riding designated pilgrimage offerings or with any use of animals without Allah’s name. Their rule concerning what was in the wombs of consecrated camels made a live-born fetus lawful for men alone, but a stillborn one lawful for both men and women; other views take it to mean milk, or both milk and offspring. Their very false attribution will return upon them as a burden and punishment.

The commentary holds that killing children without knowledge and forbidding Allah’s provisions are the reasons for their loss and deviation. The subsequent argument establishes that the foods are provision from God, lawful by reason and not prohibited by revelation. Allah’s production of trellised and untrellised gardens, palms, edible grains, olives, and pomegranates demonstrates their lawfulness; the command to eat establishes permission, not obligation or recommendation. Trellised plants are supported climbing plants such as vines, whereas untrellised trees stand on their trunks.

The harvest due is a fixed right of the poor in crops and fruit, to be given on the harvest day; reason requires it and divine law confirms it. It is not identical with the later, specified rite of zakāh, since some of these produce items are not subject to zakāh and the verse is Meccan whereas zakāh was legislated in Medina. It may nevertheless have been a root of zakāh, as Meccan verses often briefly outlined later Medinan laws. The prohibition of extravagance is unrestricted and addresses everyone: owners must not wastefully consume, overgive, or spend improperly, while recipients must not waste what they receive. Interpretations limiting the prohibition to owners, charity collectors, consuming before harvest, withholding an obligation, or spending in disobedience conflict with this unrestricted context.

Ḥamūlah denotes large load-bearing animals, while farsh denotes small animals close to the ground or liable to be trodden upon. The command to eat them confirms their lawfulness, and following Satan’s footsteps means declaring unlawful, without knowledge, what Allah has made lawful. The eight pairs enumerate sheep, goats, cows, and camels, each in male and female forms, and challenge the polytheists to say which sex or unborn offspring Allah supposedly prohibited. Another view makes the repeated “two” refer to tame and wild kinds.

Their claim could arise only from rational or transmitted evidence, or from having witnessed Allah’s enactment of the prohibition. Since they have neither, the rhetorical question exposes them as the most unjust: they forge lies against Allah and mislead people without knowledge, and Allah does not guide the unjust. Revelation then limits prohibited food to carrion, poured-out blood, swine flesh, and that over which other than Allah’s name has been invoked, while necessity excuses one who neither desires it nor exceeds the limit.

The restrictions imposed on Jews do not contradict the original lawfulness of good foods. Every clawed animal and most fat from oxen and sheep were forbidden to them as punishment for rebellion, except fat carried on their backs, contained in the entrails, or mixed with bones. Al-ḥawāyā means entrails; the commentary prefers reading the phrase as “what the entrails carry.” If the polytheists deny the message, the Prophet must warn them that Allah’s mercy is all-encompassing, yet His punishment cannot be averted from the guilty. Mercy is mentioned first so that warning does not make them despair.

The polytheists argued that, had Allah willed otherwise, they and their forefathers would neither have committed polytheism nor prohibited anything. Al-Mizan holds that the premise is true but their conclusion false. They infer that Allah’s not compelling them proves His approval of their acts; in fact, it proves that He has left them free to choose either polytheism or faith, and either invented prohibitions or obedience. Thus Allah may command them to abandon polytheism and false prohibitions, and Allah—not they—has the conclusive argument.

Had Allah willed, He could have guided all by forcing belief; His not doing so grants freedom of choice. In the takwīnī sense, His permission, idhn, gives servants the capacity to act or refrain and removes impediments to their choice. In the tashrīʿī sense, He commands them to avoid polytheism. Legislative commands and prohibitions depend on, and do not contradict, this existential freedom.

The command to bring witnesses that Allah forbade these foods is a challenge exposing their inability and their lie. Even if they produce testimony, the Prophet must not endorse it, because no such prohibition exists and their testimony follows base desire. Endorsing them would mean following the desires of people who reject Allah’s signs, deny the hereafter, and equate creatures, such as idols, with their Lord.

Among the transmitted reports, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and the Imams relate that when allocations to idols and to Allah became mixed, the polytheists restored the idols’ share but left Allah’s share with the idols, even directing irrigation accordingly. Tafsīr al-Qummī glosses ḥijr as prohibited and jannāt as gardens. Shuʿayb al-ʿAqarqūfī reports Imam al-Ṣādiq’s explanation that the harvest due is a bundle of ears and a handful of dates at the owner’s estimation, preferably before the crop is taken home. Imam al-Riḍā reportedly said that no duty remains if poor people are absent at harvest.

Muʿāwiyah b. al-Ḥajjāj reports from Imam al-Ṣādiq that crops have two rights: the collected tithe or half-tithe, and the owner’s harvest-day gift, given bundle after bundle. Imam al-Riḍā explains that giving with both hands at harvest is extravagance; one should give handful after handful or bundle after bundle. Muṣādif reports that Imam al-Ṣādiq rebuked him for dismissing a beggar without first giving to three beggars. Another report says an Anṣārī gave away his entire harvest and left nothing for his family; the Imam identifies this as extravagance. Al-Mizan says this applies the Meccan verse to a later Medinan case, rather than giving its occasion of revelation. Likewise, Ibn Jarīj’s report that the verse was revealed over Thābit b. Qays b. Shammās is rejected as an occasion of revelation, though it may be an application of the verse.

Imam al-Ṣādiq is reported to have instructed giving to every Muslim who comes, and, if only a polytheist comes, giving to him. A report from the Prophet glosses the harvest due as every ear that falls from the shock. Ibn ʿAbbās’s report that the verse was abrogated by tithe and half-tithe, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s claim that zakāh abrogated every Qur’anic charity, are rejected: whether the harvest gift is obligatory or recommended, it does not conflict with zakāh. A further report describes Medinans placing palm clusters in the mosque so beggars could strike them and take what fell.

Tafsīr al-Qummī reports that the Prophet explained the eight pairs as tame and wild sheep, tame and wild goats, tame and wild cows, and two-humped and one-humped camels, all lawful. Al-Mizan leaves open whether azwāj has the same meaning here as in the related verse cited by that report.

A report from Imam al-Ṣādiq states that only what Allah has forbidden in His Book is unlawful; the Prophet’s prohibition of donkey meat at Khaybar was to preserve donkeys for carrying loads, not because donkeys are intrinsically unlawful. Al-Mizan notes other reports prohibiting fanged animals and clawed birds and leaves their legal treatment to jurisprudence. If additional prohibitions are established, they may be understood as the Prophet’s prohibition of khabīth things, which Allah approved. A report attributed to Tafsīr of ʿAlī b. Ibrāhīm says Jewish kings denied the poor bird meat and cattle fat, so Allah forbade these to them for their transgression. Finally, Imam al-Ṣādiq explains Allah’s conclusive argument on the Day of Resurrection: one who knew will be asked why he did not act, and one who claims ignorance why he did not learn. Al-Mizan calls this one application of the verse.
verses.151: Al-Mizan presents God’s injunctions as prohibiting association of anything with Him, while commanding kindness to parents; it forbids killing children from fear of poverty, since God provides for both parents and children. It also forbids open and hidden indecencies and the killing of a life God has made inviolable, except where justice requires it. These commands are given so that people may apply reason.
verses.152: Al-Mizan commands that an orphan’s property be handled only in the best manner until the orphan reaches maturity; that measures and weights be given justly within the limits of human capacity; that speech be just even against a relative; and that God’s covenant be fulfilled. These injunctions are meant to make people mindful.
verses.153: Al-Mizan calls people to follow the straight path and not other ways, which lead them away from God’s way. This injunction is given so that they may guard against evil.
verses.154: Al-Mizan states that God gave Moses the Book as a completion for the doer of good, an elaboration of all things, guidance, and mercy, so that its recipients might believe in meeting their Lord.
verses.155: Al-Mizan says the revealed Book is blessed; follow it and guard against evil so mercy may be shown.
verses.156: Al-Mizan says the Book precludes claiming only two groups before them received it, and ignorance of their study.
verses.157:
Al-Mizan holds that the injunctions in (6:151-153) are universal laws of divine religion: abstention from polytheism, unkindness to parents, indecencies, unjust killing—including killing children for fear of poverty—wrongful dealing with orphans’ property, deficient measure and weight, unjust speech, breach of God’s covenant, and following ways other than God’s. The same principles appear in the preaching of earlier prophets, and religion cannot be complete and sound while lacking any of them.

The phrase introducing the injunctions as what God has “forbidden” does not conflict with the presence of positive commands, because the Prophet is reciting the divine wording as revealed. Polytheism comes first because it is a grievous iniquity that God does not forgive; all sins in some way return to it, just as good deeds return to monotheism. Kindness to parents is therefore among the greatest sins to neglect, second only to associating partners with God. Human society depends upon reciprocal love and mercy between generations: parents naturally care for dependent children, while grown children must care for parents when age renders them dependent. If this bond is widely neglected, people lose interest in begetting and raising children, family formation and parenthood decline, and society’s bonds disintegrate beyond repair, depriving people of happiness in this world and the next.

Imlāq means lack of wealth and provision. The prohibition of killing children addresses an Arab practice in famine and drought, when children were killed out of fear of hunger. The stated reason is that parents are not their children’s providers: God provides for both. Al-fawāḥish are evil and indecent acts, including adultery, sodomy, and accusing chaste women of adultery. Apparently, their apparent and concealed forms are acts committed openly and privately. Because the carnal soul strongly desires such acts, their legalization would remove their stigma and spread them, cutting off progeny, destroying the family, and ultimately destroying society. Permitting murder and similar indecencies likewise removes public security and shakes the foundations of society.

The prohibited soul may be understood as one whose killing God has forbidden, or as one whom God has consecrated in His legislation by protecting his blood and right. Some exegetes regard murder as a separately repeated instance of indecency, emphasized for its enormity; the killing of children is similarly singled out for its special relevance to Arabs, some of whom treated fatherhood as ownership and poverty as a justification for killing children. The inviolable soul is that of a Muslim or a non-Muslim under a peace treaty with Muslims, a muʿāhid; it may be killed only for a just cause, namely retaliation, qiṣāṣ or qawad, or a religious penalty, ḥadd.

The prohibition on “approaching” an orphan’s property includes every form of expenditure, investment, and dealing with it, all of which must preserve it in the best possible way. Its duration is until the orphan attains both physical puberty and intellectual maturity. This does not make the property permissible to use afterward; rather, the subject of guardianship ends when the person can manage his own property. Full measure and weight require no diminution. The assurance that God imposes no duty beyond capacity answers the objection that exact fairness is impossible in ordinary dealings, and may apply both to fair weights and to the care of orphan property.

Just speech concerns words that can confer benefit or loss upon others, especially in legal rights: testimony, judgment, and fatwá. Affection, sympathy, or kinship must not lead a person to alter the truth for a favored party and violate another’s right. Majmaʿ al-bayān reports that this command has wide application, including confessions, testimony, wills, legal rulings, judicial verdicts, governmental laws, religious beliefs, and enjoining good and forbidding evil. God’s ʿahd most plausibly means the religious duties He has decreed, since this is the Qur’an’s common use of the term, it is ascribed to God, and it occurs among universal commandments. It may also mean a person’s or mutual commitment made in God’s name, in which case attributing the covenant to God reminds the parties that He is the true other party to it.

The central point of verse (6:153) is not merely the command to follow the straight path, which serves as a prelude, but the prohibition of departing from God’s way and becoming divided within religion. The initial conjunction may, according to readings of anna or an, link the verse to the preceding commands; the reading inna makes it a new statement. The straight path is free of internal contradiction and of failure to bring its travelers to their destination; it is also free of disagreement among its parts and among those who adhere to it. Other paths necessarily bring failure and discord because they proceed from unregulated satanic desires, whereas God’s way rests upon fiṭrah and khilqah.

The commentary takes “my path” to refer to the Prophet, who is the speaker commanded to convey these injunctions and who consistently refers to God in the third person. Other exegetes apparently take it as God’s path, which requires a shift in the speaker at “His way.” Either reading identifies the foregoing principal injunctions as the straight path.

The distinct endings of the three verses correspond to their subjects. The first set of prohibitions is plainly evil to innate human nature; reason suffices to recognize its evil once desire and dark emotion cease to veil the intellect. The second set requires, beyond reason, mindfulness of the social benefits and harms that reason recognizes: society cannot endure if the weak are neglected, dealings are unfair, courts and governments are unjust, and truth is suppressed. The third ending concerns taqwá. Complete religious taqwá requires recognizing God’s prohibitions through reason and mindfulness, then abstaining from deviant ways. It means abiding by fiṭrah, the basis of religion. Those who pursue desire, cling to worldly life, and are deceived by its adornment abandon taqwá and sound reason without heeding the consequences. Since personal desires are divergent and lack a unifying rule, their followers do not remain on one path; religious taqwá can thus be hoped for only by adherence to the straight path free from contradiction and conflict.

Rūḥ al-maʿānī reports Quṭb al-Rāzī’s explanation that the first ending calls the Arabs to recognize practices they shamelessly committed, while the second calls them to remember virtues they already observed. Al-Mizan rejects this: historical reports do not support the claim that pre-Islamic Arabs consistently protected orphan property, gave full measure, or spoke justly, and the account reduces tadhakkur to mere remembrance rather than its Qur’anic sense. Rūḥ al-maʿānī also reports al-Rāzī’s view that the first duties are evident while the second are hidden and intricate, requiring strenuous thought to find a balanced course. The commentary finds this broadly similar to its own explanation but rejects the claimed intricacy: slight reflection discloses these evils; the verse’s mindfulness concerns the matters stated, not an added notion of balance; balance applies only to the first two commands; and the capacity clause already addresses it. It also rejects Abū Ḥayyān’s reported view that the verse’s primary theme is the command to follow the path merely because it includes all duties; the verse’s flow makes that command a preparation for the prohibition of other ways.

Verse (6:154) explains that universal, concise principles were subsequently differentiated and elaborated where needed. God gave Moses a complete Book to remedy the deficiency of those who had done well under the concise legislation, to detail the rules branching from it as required by the Children of Israel, and as guidance and mercy so that they might believe in meeting their Lord. “Then” therefore marks the giving of Moses’ Book as a complement and elaboration of earlier universal commandments, not an event after the Qur’an. On this account, proposed omissions in the verse or attempts to connect it to Abraham’s story are contrived. “Him who would do good” is a generic description of any good-doer, not a particular person. Interpretations that make the completion God’s favor to Moses, believers, prophets, Abraham, or Moses’ rank in Paradise are judged weak. “All things” means what was necessary or beneficial to the Children of Israel and those after them. The purpose that they believe in their Lord’s meeting suggests that Israelites were reluctant, or even refused, to believe in the Last Day; this is supported, the commentary says, by the present Torah’s lack of resurrection teaching and historians’ reports that some Israelite tribes denied the hereafter.

The blessed Book revealed to the Prophet has the special qualities just described for Moses’ Book, and must therefore be followed with taqwá in order to receive mercy. The particle an in verse (6:156) means “lest you say” and refers to its revelation. The two earlier communities are the Jews and Christians, recipients of the Torah and Injīl. Other prophetic books either contained principles without an elaborate legal system, contained no legal code, or were unknown to the Qur’an’s first audience. Thus the Qur’an removes the excuse that an elaborate revealed law belonged only to Jews and Christians and that its study had been inaccessible to others.

In verse (6:157), “they” in the claim that its audience would have been better guided refers to those earlier recipients of scripture. Ṣadaf means iʿrāḍ, turning away or evading. The faʾ in “so indeed” makes the arrival of clear proof, guidance, and mercy the answer to both proposed excuses. Bayyinah here is used for the Book because of its manifest proofs and guidelines. Consequently, none can claim an excuse for noncompliance; rejecting and turning away from God’s communications is the height of injustice and earns an evil chastisement.
verses.158: Al-Mizan states that, when some signs of the Lord come, belated belief will not benefit one who had not previously believed or earned good through belief; both sides are told to wait.
verses.159: Al-Mizan states that the Prophet has nothing to do with those who divide their religion into sects. Their affair belongs to Allah, who will inform them of what they used to do.
verses.160:
Al-Mizan connects these verses with the preceding discussion: they threaten those who abandon the straight path and divide into factions, dissociate the Prophet from religious deviation, promise reward for good brought on the Day of Judgment, and affirm the fulfilment of divine retribution.

Regarding (6:158), the commentary takes the question as a rhetorical negation, uttered after admonition and the religious call have proved ineffective. The coming of the angels, the Lord, or some signs of the Lord are inevitable events joined to God’s just and conclusive judgment, by which the obstinate are exterminated. The angels’ coming means their descent with punishment. The Lord’s “coming” is His liqāʾ (meeting, vision): the complete unveiling of His absolute oneness on the Day of Resurrection, when veils are removed. It is called ityān, or coming, because what was hidden becomes manifest and what was absent becomes present; God’s Holy Precinct transcends physical properties. Some exegetes instead interpret it as the coming of the Lord’s command.

The coming of some signs means an event that changes people’s condition so that choice and free will are no longer available. It may be death, which transfers a person from action to retribution in barzakh; disbelief and defiance becoming second nature, so that truth can only be verbally admitted from fear; or an unavoidable punishment that compels belief. Such compelled belief cannot save, because beneficial belief must be freely chosen. Thus all three events bring a just, decisive judgment. Those whom no admonition or proof affects are, in reality, awaiting it, whether or not they recognize this.

Some exegetes regard the question as derision of polytheists who demanded to see the Lord, have angels descend, or receive signs like those of former prophets. Al-Mizan allows that this may explain the first half, but holds that it does not fit the latter half, which explains the reality and character of the events rather than merely mocking their demand.

Faith on that day benefits neither one who had failed to believe willingly beforehand nor one who believed but did not earn good through that belief, having disregarded God’s laws and immersed himself in sin and disobedience. Repentance is then unavailable. Their desperate resort to īmān in order to avert punishment does not profit them, nor can punishment be averted from the guilty. The thrice-repeated expression “your Lord” consoles and strengthens the Prophet against polytheists who gloried in their own lords and idols: he will either prevail in his mission or his Lord will decisively judge between him and them. “Wait; we too are waiting” therefore conveys a serious, real threat, not an empty one.

An objection says that the signs cannot be the polytheists’ requested miracles: God’s established practice would be to exterminate a people who rejected such signs, while the nation of the Prophet of Mercy would not be exterminated. Al-Mizan replies that this nation too remains subject to God’s just and decisive judgment. The verse does show generally that faith without good deeds is insufficient, but not without qualification. It concerns those who had an opportunity both to believe and to act righteously, yet failed to do so; it does not apply to one who believes voluntarily and dies before having an opportunity for good deeds. What profits is voluntary faith not ruined by sin or contaminated by evil.

Regarding (6:159), Al-Mizan holds that those who divide religion include polytheists and, because of the shared quality of religious division and disagreement, Jews and Christians; the sense is not confined to these groups or to Muslim sects, but is universal. The verse applies the preceding universal commandments, from the prohibition of polytheism to that of leaving God’s way. Its past tense does not restrict division to the past, but denotes a quality occurring in the past, present, or future. The Prophet, who calls to truth and monotheism and embodies Islam in his practice, is distinct from all who break religion into sects under different leaders. They do not follow his path of unity and avoidance of division. Their splitting, despite knowledge, arose from transgression among themselves; their matter is with their Lord, who will unveil what they did and hold them accountable for it.

Regarding (6:160), Al-Mizan first explains the verse independently as an expression of divine favour and justice: a good deed receives at least ten like it, whereas an evil deed receives no more than its equivalent. God may multiply the reward for good further and may pardon evil altogether. In its context, however, unity around truth is treated as a good deed and deviation from it as an evil deed. The verse’s primary concern is not a numerical limit on punishment, as though every evil received only one punishment, but the kind and quality of recompense: good yields good and more, while evil—here, prohibited deviation—yields an evil consequence like itself, not anything desirable.
verses.161: Al-Mizan presents the speaker as guided by his Lord to the straight path: a most right religion, the faith of Abraham the upright one, who was not of the polytheists.
verses.162: Al-Mizan: Prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are all for Allah, the Lord of the nations.
verses.163: Al-Mizan says He has no associate; the speaker is commanded and first to submit.
verses.164: Al-Mizan asks why one should seek a lord other than Allah, the Lord of all things. Each soul earns evil only against itself; none bears another’s burden; and all return to their Lord, who will inform them of their differences.
verses.165:
Al-Mizan explains that these final verses summarize the Prophet’s mission, show that he practices what he preaches, and gather the chapter’s proofs against polytheism.

The straight path is a clear way and a qiyam religion. Whether qiyam is understood as an abbreviated qiyām or as qayyim, it conveys that the religion sustains its followers: it is free from internal contradiction and failure to reach its end, and, being founded on fiṭrah, upholds welfare in this world and the hereafter. It is Abraham’s ḥanīf faith: he inclined to the level course of monotheism and did not deviate into polytheism.

Nusukī means every act of worship, although it commonly denotes sacrifice or the sacrificial animal offered for God. The Prophet is commanded to declare that he follows the divine guidance he calls others to follow; this removes suspicion and supports the truthfulness of his message, since a truthful caller practices what he preaches. Prayer is separately mentioned because of God’s special care for it. Life embraces every action, quality, act, and abstention, while death includes what pertains to it and is rooted in one’s life.

The declaration dedicates prayer, all worship, life, and death alike to Allah, Lord, Owner, and Director of the affairs of all nations. It is not a division in which worship denotes practical sincerity while life and death merely acknowledge God’s command or ownership; that reading is contrived. Rather, it affirms sincere servitude in every aspect: the Prophet takes and leaves nothing except for God, lives only for Him, and seeks death only in His way. He has been commanded to this complete servitude.

“First of those who submit” means first in rank and degree, not in time: the Prophet possesses the highest degree of submission, though submitters existed before him. The interpretation that he is only the first submitter in his own nation imposes an unwarranted qualification and rests on the erroneous claim that Abraham was first in the absolute sense, whereas Noah is described as among those who submit (10:72). Nor do the passages concerning Abraham and Ishmael, including (2:128), or the naming of Muslims in (22:78), establish that view.

Verses (6:164) and (6:165) contain three comprehensive proofs of monotheism, concerning creation’s origin, human life in this world, and the return after it. Since Allah is the Lord of all things, everything is His servant and subject to His lordship; no other lord can rightly be served. Every person’s acts and beliefs adhere to that person alone, and no one bears another’s burden. Because all return to God, who requites them by unveiling the realities of their acts, and none can escape His retribution, He alone must be worshiped.

Human life is governed by a divinely designed system of succession in the earth and differences of age, strength, gender, wealth, power, and knowledge. God made this system to test people through what He has given them. He governs their happiness, advancing the obedient toward their ordained felicity and leaving wrongdoers on their knees; therefore He alone deserves service and worship. Khalāʾif may mean that generations succeed one another or that humanity has been made God’s vicegerent in the earth. The chapter closes by joining God’s swift requital of evil with His forgiveness and mercy.
